Scattered loosely through a space, with no sharp center or focus.
Never cutting corners, however long or dull the job.
Standing in public defiance of a ruling party or state.
Unmoved by something and unconcerned with how it turns out.

mnemonics: Diffident shares Latin fidere, to trust, with confident; the dif- (from dis-, not) marks a person who does not trust their own ability.

senses.definition: A lament in song, by which mourners give voice to their grief for the dead.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A sorrowful song that people sing or play to grieve a death.

examples.text: The village band marched ahead of the hearse, playing a dirge so slow that each step took two beats.
Sailors sang a dirge on deck as their shipmate's body, sewn into canvas, was lowered into the sea.
With its slow, gloomy chords, the band's new single sounds more like a dirge than a dance track.
Every year on the anniversary of the mine collapse, the town choir sings a dirge for the miners who never came home.

distractors.lemma: A small, catchy tune with homespun words, easy to pick up by ear.
An ecstatic choral chant first performed at ancient Greek wine festivals.
A high harmony part that a few voices add over everyone else's melody.
A short burst of praise to God that a congregation sings together.

mnemonics: Dirge comes from dirige, the opening Latin word of a chant in the church's service for the dead, which is why a dirge is a song of mourning.

senses.definition: Break the hold of an error or illusion on someone's mind.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To clear up someone's wrong idea about something.

examples.text: Let me disabuse you of the idea that the job is easy; most new hires quit within a month.
One look at the real sales figures disabused investors of the belief that the company was growing.
A week of camping in the rain disabused him of any romantic notions about living off the land.
Her first paycheck, after taxes and rent, quickly disabused her of the notion that she would soon be rich.

distractors.lemma: Mistreat a person or misuse a thing, causing harm.
Knock out a machine or system's ability to function.
Hand out sums from a pool of money held in trust.
Wash one's hands of something in public, denying any tie to it.
Strike a lawyer's name from the roll of those allowed to practice.

mnemonics: Disabuse joins dis-, undo, with an old sense of abuse, to deceive: to disabuse someone is to undo a deception.

senses.definition: Pulling against other accounts or views, so that they cannot be reconciled.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Out of step with each other, so they cannot all be right.

examples.text: The two maps gave discordant locations for the spring, one placing it north of the ridge and the other south of it.
Her cheerful public statements were discordant with the gloomy figures in the company's own report.
The two doctors gave discordant readings of the same X-ray, one seeing a fracture and the other nothing at all.
The polls were so discordant, ranging from a ten-point lead to a five-point deficit, that no one could call the race.

distractors.lemma: Trusted to keep a confidence and to handle awkward matters quietly.
So downcast after a loss or letdown that every attempt to cheer you up fails.
Prone to long detours away from the main subject.
Lacking the basic politeness owed to other people.
Having a refined eye that picks out the best from the merely good.

senses.definition: Sour-sounding, with tones that jar when heard together.

mnemonics: Discordant comes from Latin dis-, apart, and cor, heart: discordant views come from hearts set apart.

senses.definition: A mismatch that turns up when two versions of the same figures, facts or story are compared.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: When two numbers or stories about the same thing do not line up.

examples.text: The twins' birth certificates showed an odd discrepancy: one named the hospital as St. Mary's, the other as County General.
A discrepancy between the recipe's ingredient list and its steps left me unsure whether to add two eggs or three.
The museum label dated the vase to 1820 and the catalog said 1870, and nobody on staff could explain the discrepancy.
Engineers traced the test drone's crash to a discrepancy between its altitude sensor and its GPS reading.

distractors.lemma: Good sense about what to keep to oneself and when to stay quiet.
The shaky, crumbling condition of a body or building that age has used up.
The act of letting others in on information they had not been given before.
Extended, careful reasoning put into words on some topic for listeners or readers.
A frantic state in which someone has run out of good options and grabs at any that remain.

mnemonics: Discrepancy comes from Latin discrepare, to sound different: when two accounts do not sound the same, there is a discrepancy.

senses.definition: Make remarks meant to shrink the standing of a person, group or piece of work in others' eyes.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To put down someone or their work with sneering remarks.

examples.text: My grandmother would never disparage another cook's food at the table, even when the stew was burned.
In interviews he likes to disparage his early paintings as clumsy copies of better artists.
It seems unfair to disparage the volunteers' work when they gave up every weekend to finish it.
The new manager made a habit of disparaging the old filing system, calling it a relic that only dinosaurs could love.

distractors.lemma: Break up a crowd or cluster so that its members drift off separately.
Get a messenger, vehicle or shipment on its way to where it is needed.
Knock a tidy layout out of place, leaving it jumbled.
Unhook or pull loose a part that was locked onto another.
Produce facts or reasoning that a claim cannot stand up against.

mnemonics: Disparage contains par, from the Latin for "equal": to disparage someone is to talk as if they are below par.

senses.definition: Unlike one another in their basic makeup, sharing few or no features.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Of very different kinds, with almost nothing alike about them.

examples.text: The book ties together disparate topics, from medieval farming to modern banking.
The new manager had to unite two disparate teams, one cautious and formal, the other loose and fast.
Her friends were a disparate group: a retired judge, a teenage skateboarder and a beekeeper.
It is hard to compare such disparate jobs as nursing and stock trading.

distractors.lemma: Pushed by a lack of options into acting rashly or at great risk.
Spoken in a way meant to make someone seem unimportant or bad.
Coolly detached, so that personal feelings play no part in one's view.
Having a bad name because of dishonest or shabby behavior.

mnemonics: Disparate shares a Latin root, parare, with separate: disparate things are so unlike that they seem to belong in separate worlds.

senses.definition: Act out a pretense so that others are misled about what one is thinking or planning.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To put on an act so people cannot tell what is really going on in your mind.

examples.text: A good poker player learns to dissemble, keeping a calm face even while holding a winning hand.
Asked about the layoffs, the spokesman chose to dissemble, giving vague answers that hid what he knew.
To keep the surprise party secret, Tom had to dissemble for weeks, acting bored whenever his wife mentioned her birthday.
Small children rarely dissemble well; their faces show exactly what they feel.

distractors.lemma: Undo the screws and joints of a device until its parts lie separately.
Pass ideas or research along through many outlets so that word of them travels far.
Call another person or thing to mind by having a similar look or nature.
Spread so thin in the air or over time that it can no longer be noticed.
Cast a vote against a decision that the rest of a group supports.

mnemonics: Dissemble comes from the same Latin root as simulate: to dissemble is to simulate a feeling so the real one stays hidden.

senses.definition: Put news, knowledge or findings into wide circulation so that the public at large comes to hear of them.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To pass news or knowledge around until it is known far and wide.

examples.text: Medieval monks helped disseminate classical learning by copying ancient texts by hand and sending them to other monasteries.
Before the printing press, it could take years to disseminate a new idea across Europe.
A single post can disseminate a rumor to millions of people before anyone checks whether it is true.
The library helps disseminate local history by putting old newspapers online for free.

distractors.lemma: Keep up a pretense that masks one's real opinions or plans.
Pick up on the small features that set one thing apart from a similar one.
Crumble away into loose fragments until the original object is gone.
Cut a group down to a small remnant through heavy killing or destruction.

mnemonics: Disseminate comes from the Latin for "seed," the root of seminal and seminar: to disseminate ideas is to scatter them like seed.

senses.definition: An uneasy tension between beliefs, statements or actions that point in opposite directions.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A jarring mismatch between what someone believes, says or does.

examples.text: The company's green advertising, set beside its record of polluting rivers, created a dissonance that customers could not ignore.
After moving abroad, he felt a nagging dissonance every time his new job required him to do something his upbringing called rude.
Learning that his favorite athlete had cheated left Marco with a dissonance he could not shake: he still admired the man but hated what he had done.
The cheerful tone of the narration, laid over such grim events, produces a dissonance that unsettles many readers.

distractors.lemma: A poet's trick of reusing one vowel sound across several neighboring words.
The full, ringing quality of a sound that echoes and carries well.
How much ground someone must cover to get from one spot to another.
The legal winding-up of a company, marriage or other formal bond.

senses.definition: In music, a grating combination of notes that leaves the ear waiting for relief.

mnemonics: Dissonance comes from Latin dis-, "apart," and sonare, "to sound": ideas in dissonance sound wrong together, like clashing notes.

senses.definition: Grow rounder and tighter as whatever is inside pushes its skin or walls outward.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To puff out and get tight because it is overfilled.

examples.text: As the hot-air balloon filled, its fabric began to distend until every seam was pulled taut.
If you block the nozzle while the tap is fully open, the garden hose will distend and may burst.
The veins in his neck seemed to distend as he strained to lift the heavy crate.
Left in the hot car, the sealed carton of juice had distended into a tight, rounded block.

distractors.lemma: Break someone's concentration with something louder or more interesting.
Run a liquid through a still so that its purest or strongest part is collected.
Turn up for a lecture, service or other gathering as one of those present.
Keep insisting on a point while others push back against it.
Head downward by stairs, slope or ladder toward lower ground.

mnemonics: Distend shares the Latin tendere, "to stretch," with extend and tension: a distended belly is stretched out from inside.

senses.definition: Unwilling to let any fact or argument loosen one's grip on a cherished position.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Treating your own opinions as rules nobody may argue with.

examples.text: My uncle is dogmatic about steak: there is one correct way to cook it, his, and no argument will move him.
A dogmatic scientist would have thrown out the surprising data; she rewrote her theory instead.
A dogmatic editor, she struck out any sentence that broke one of her grammar rules, even when the rule made the prose worse.
The book club fell apart because one dogmatic member insisted that every other reading of the novel was wrong.

distractors.lemma: Belonging to the world of the stage and its performances.
Good at choosing gentle words that keep tempers calm in a dispute.
Leaving people guessing about what is meant or intended.
Plodding on toward a goal long after most people would have stopped.

senses.definition: Having to do with the formal teachings of a religion or school of thought.

mnemonics: Dogmatic comes from dogma, a belief that an authority says must not be questioned: a dogmatic person treats their own opinions that way.

senses.definition: Giving good grounds to suspect that something is not genuine or above board.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Seeming untrue or shady enough that you would want to check it first.

examples.text: He offered the dubious excuse that his alarm clock had failed three days in a row.
The used-car dealer's dubious paperwork listed three different mileages for the same vehicle.
Historians treat the diary as dubious because its paper was made decades after the events it describes.
The so-called gold watch the stranger was selling for ten dollars looked dubious, and its color was already rubbing off.

distractors.lemma: Reliably doing one's chores and obligations without complaint.
Built with two of something where one would usually do.
Tough enough to shrug off rough handling, weather and the years.
Of a metal, able to be pulled long and thin, bending rather than snapping.

senses.definition: Of a person, holding back belief in something while still weighing it up.
Of a result, hanging in the balance with no clear sign of which way it will go.

mnemonics: Dubious shares its Latin root with doubt: a dubious claim is one you have good reason to doubt.

senses.definition: Bursting with joyful excitement that one cannot easily hold back.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So happy and excited that it seems to bubble out of you.

examples.text: Still ebullient after the wedding, she hugged every guest and danced until the band packed up.
The ebullient fans sang and waved flags all the way home after the surprise victory.
Even on gray Monday mornings, our ebullient receptionist greets everyone with a joke and a wide smile.
His usually ebullient letters turned short and flat during the long, lonely winter.

distractors.lemma: Ready to go easy on those who slip up or break the rules.
Able to speak or write clearly and movingly.
Combative in manner, always looking for someone to quarrel with.
Restoring moisture and suppleness to chapped skin.

mnemonics: Ebullient comes from the Latin ebullire, "to boil over": an ebullient person bubbles over with joy.

senses.definition: Built from hand-picked pieces of many unrelated traditions or fields.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Mixing bits from many different styles or sources in your own way.

examples.text: The festival's eclectic lineup put a brass band, a punk group and a solo harpist on the same stage.
The garden was eclectic: a raked gravel bed, an English rose border and a cactus patch shared one small yard.
As a teacher she was eclectic, borrowing a game from one method and a drill from another.
The town museum's eclectic collection places Roman coins, Inuit carvings and early video games in neighboring rooms.

distractors.lemma: Running on power that flows through wires and cables.
Quirky in habits or dress, in a way that makes one stand out.
Overflowing with joy to the point of jumping or shouting.
Able to give a lot under tension and then snap back unharmed.

mnemonics: Eclectic comes from the Greek eklegein, "to pick out": an eclectic person picks out the best from many sources.

senses.definition: A remedy's or plan's power to bring about the change it aims at.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: How well something, like a medicine or plan, actually does the job it is meant to do.

examples.text: Clinical trials showed the new vaccine's efficacy: it prevented illness in nine out of ten people.
Since sales fell even while the ads ran, the manager doubted the campaign had any efficacy at all.
Teachers wanted proof of the reading program's efficacy before using it in every classroom.
Economists disagree about the efficacy of rate cuts: some say they revive spending, others say they change nothing.

distractors.lemma: The quality of using little time, energy or money for a given amount of work.
Outrageous nerve, shown without a trace of embarrassment.
A logical slip that leaves an argument's conclusion unsupported.
Bubbly, sparkling liveliness in a person's manner.

mnemonics: Efficacy sounds like effect, so it measures how well something achieves its effect.

senses.definition: A piece of verse composed in mourning, usually looking back on a life that has ended.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A poem of grief written after someone dies.

examples.text: Years after her brother's death, the poet finally finished the elegy she had been drafting in notebooks since the week he died.
Scholars think the poet wrote the elegy within a month of his wife's death, though he never showed it to anyone.
In the closing stanza of the elegy, the speaker stops mourning the dead soldier and begins to celebrate his life.
When the family dog died, my nine-year-old wrote a four-line elegy and taped it above his empty bowl.

distractors.lemma: A life-size carving of a person, often lying on top of that person's tomb.
A quiet refinement that looks effortless and is never showy.
A condition in which the body treats a harmless substance as an attacker.
The property or influence that outlives the person who left it.
The set words a congregation says or sings together each time it worships.

mnemonics: Elegy comes from the Greek elegos, a song of grief, and an elegy is still a poem that grieves for the dead.

senses.definition: Using language with such grace and force that listeners or readers are stirred or won over.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Able to find the right words and say them in a way that stirs people.

examples.text: The best man's toast was so eloquent that by its last line half the guests were wiping their eyes.
In just ten sentences, Lincoln's Gettysburg Address made an eloquent case that the soldiers buried there had not died in vain.
Even in his second language, the novelist was eloquent, always finding the exact word to stir his readers.
The student's eloquent essay about her grandmother's journey to America was so moving that two of the judges wept.

distractors.lemma: Pleasing to the eye in a polished, understated way.
Holding a high, honored place among the leaders of a profession.
Hard to stop once talking, and quick to fill any silence.
Forever just out of reach, however hard one tries.
Built up with layer upon layer of careful detail.

senses.definition: Of a gesture or expression, conveying a message as plainly as speech would.

mnemonics: Eloquent comes from the Latin e-, out, and loqui, to speak: an eloquent person speaks out with skill.

senses.definition: Improve a story or report in the telling by slipping in colorful touches that go beyond what actually happened.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To stretch the truth when you tell something, so it sounds more exciting.

examples.text: Every time Grandpa told the fishing story, he would embellish it, and the trout grew a few more inches.
Tempted to embellish her job application, she turned a summer internship into a management role, and the lie was soon discovered.
The witness stuck to what she had seen and refused to embellish her account with guesses about the driver's motives.

distractors.lemma: Skim money for yourself from accounts that your job put in your charge.
Stiffen someone's nerve so that they speak or act with less fear.
Pull someone into the middle of a conflict, so they become one of its parties.
Process a body after death so that it holds its form for viewing or burial.

senses.definition: Give a plain object or room a fancier look by adding trimmings, carving or other ornament.

mnemonics: Embellish contains the French bel, beautiful (as in belle): to embellish a story is to make it prettier than the truth.

senses.definition: Resting on real-world trials and measured results instead of on argument from first principles.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Backed by looking and testing, not just by thinking it through.

examples.text: The economist's elegant model fell apart once empirical studies showed that real shoppers did not behave the way it predicted.
Rather than follow the planting guide, the gardener took an empirical approach, trying three spots and noting which tomatoes thrived.
Some philosophers say moral truths can be known by reason alone, while others insist all knowledge rests on empirical observation of the world.

distractors.lemma: Having to do with an emperor's reign or the lands it controls.
Haughtily commanding toward others, with no thought that they might refuse.
Spoken with heavy weight on each word to drive the point home.
Pressing enough that failing to act is not an option.
Quick to put yourself in another's place and feel their hurt or joy.

mnemonics: Empirical comes from the Greek empeiria, experience: empirical knowledge is learned by experience and testing, not by theory.

senses.definition: Follow a rival's or hero's lead closely, aiming to reach their standard and perhaps pass it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To follow in someone's footsteps, hoping to do as well or better.

examples.text: The rookie studied hours of tape on the veteran goalkeeper, hoping to emulate his calm when a striker lined up a penalty.
The apprentice watched the head chef's knife work for months, determined to emulate her speed without losing a fingertip.
As a young writer, he tried to emulate Hemingway, cutting his sentences short and stripping out every extra adjective.
Many startups emulate the habits of famous founders, hoping that copying their routines will bring the same success.

distractors.lemma: Have its origin in something and travel out from it to whatever is nearby.
Lift the legal chains of slavery or second-class status from a group.
Pack up and resettle in a foreign nation, giving up the one you came from as home.
Break oil or fat into tiny droplets held evenly through a watery liquid.

senses.definition: Mimic a different machine in software so that its programs run unchanged.

mnemonics: Emulate comes from the Latin aemulus, a rival: you emulate people when you try to match or even beat them.

senses.definition: Breed a reaction in others, or a new state of affairs.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make people come to feel something, such as trust or fear.

examples.text: Returning every client's call within an hour helped her engender trust among customers who had been let down before.
The referee's inconsistent calls engendered so much anger that fans booed him off the field.
Teachers who praise effort rather than talent tend to engender a love of challenge in their students.
Secret salary deals engender resentment, because workers eventually find out what their colleagues earn.

distractors.lemma: Leave something open to injury or ruin through careless or harmful acts.
Grow puffed and distended from taking in too much blood or fluid.
Rise over and around something until it is lost from view.
Claim every bit of someone's attention for a long stretch.

senses.definition: Father or produce offspring.

mnemonics: Engender shares its Latin root with generate (generare, to beget): to engender trust or anger is to generate it.

senses.definition: Short-lived, with an end that comes soon after its start.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Here for a very short while and then gone.

examples.text: Viral dance trends are ephemeral; by the time parents learn one, teenagers have already moved on to the next.
The monks spent weeks on the sand painting, knowing it was ephemeral and would be swept away the day it was finished.
The pop-up restaurant was ephemeral by design, open for just six weekends before the chef moved on.
Her interest in the guitar proved ephemeral, and the instrument was gathering dust by spring.

distractors.lemma: Off to the side, at the margins of a space or a topic.
Possessing an unearthly lightness and grace.
Having to do with the skin's surface layer, the part that sheds and renews itself.
Raging through a whole population in a sudden wave.
Solemn and mournful enough to darken any gathering.

mnemonics: Ephemeral comes from the Greek epi, on, and hemera, day: something ephemeral lasts about a day.

senses.definition: A pointed bit of wit in a line or two of prose or verse, easy to quote and hard to forget.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A clever one-liner that sticks in people's minds.

examples.text: Guests at the dinner party waited for the old novelist's next epigram, since one dry line from him could end any argument.
The playwright's characters trade epigrams like tennis volleys, each witty line topping the last.
Her wedding toast ended with a sly epigram about marriage so neat and funny that guests repeated it for weeks.
The senator was better known for her epigrams than for her bills, and reporters waited all session for her next quotable jab.

distractors.lemma: Someone else's words placed on the page before a story starts, to set its tone.
The last word of a book or play, set apart from the plot that came before it.
A wired message paid for by the word, so senders cut every spare one.
One self-contained stretch of a longer story, often released on its own.

mnemonics: Epigram and telegram both end in gram, Greek for something written. Think of an epigram as a telegram of wit: short, because every word counts.

senses.definition: Hide your real position behind wording loose enough to be taken either way.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To talk in a fuzzy way on purpose so no one can pin you down.

examples.text: Pressed by his daughter about whether they were getting a puppy, Dad began to equivocate, offering a string of maybes and we'll-sees.
Asked point-blank whether he had read the report, the manager would only equivocate, saying he had looked at parts of it and grasped the general idea.
Rather than admit she had no interest, she chose to equivocate, calling her calendar "complicated" and promising to circle back about the project.
The doctor refused to equivocate; she told the family plainly that the treatment had failed.

distractors.lemma: Put two things on the same footing, as though one stood for the other.
Make the case for a plan or reform and urge others to back it.
Stir a remembered scene or emotion back to life in someone.
Bring a sacred name or a legal right into play to strengthen your case.

mnemonics: Equivocate joins the Latin aequus, equal, and vox, voice: words that speak with two equal voices, so no one can tell which meaning you intend.

senses.definition: Possessing a scholar's depth of learning, shown in wide reference and exact detail.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very well read, with deep knowledge of many subjects.

examples.text: The erudite tour guide could quote Dante in Italian, explain the chemistry of fresco paint and date a church by its windows.
Her erudite review, packed with references to centuries of earlier novels, was far more than the usual plot summary.
The night watchman never finished high school, but decades of reading on his shift had made him surprisingly erudite about Roman history.
The erudite biography runs to two hundred pages of footnotes that cite sources in five languages.

distractors.lemma: Jerky and uneven in behavior, swinging between states without warning.
Off the mark because of a mistaken fact or faulty reasoning.
Off course or out of line, whether in where it goes or how it behaves.
Quick to snap, interrupt or insult, with no thought for courtesy.

mnemonics: Erudite comes from the Latin e-, out of, and rudis, rough or untaught (as in rude and rudimentary): an erudite person has been taught out of roughness.

senses.definition: Confined to and understandable by only an enlightened inner circle.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So specialized or obscure that only a few insiders understand it.

examples.text: The physicist explained her esoteric theories using mathematical notation that baffled the general public.
The podcast's jokes are so esoteric that you need to have read every comic book since 1960 to get them.
The secret society guarded its esoteric rituals from outsiders for centuries.
At the wine tasting, the expert's esoteric talk of soil chemistry and barrel toasting left most guests nodding politely.

distractors.lemma: Quirky and offbeat, with personal ways that others find peculiar.
Strikingly foreign and unfamiliar, as if brought from a distant land.
Airy and graceful, with an almost weightless, dreamlike quality.
Wide-ranging in taste, borrowing freely from unrelated traditions.

mnemonics: Esoteric comes from the Greek eso, within: esoteric knowledge stays inside a small circle, while exoteric knowledge is for outsiders.

senses.definition: Remarks in honor of someone who has died, recalling the good in their life.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The kind words said about a person at their funeral.

examples.text: His sister delivered a touching eulogy at the funeral, remembering his kindness and humor.
The jazz magazine printed a eulogy for the late pianist, praising sixty years of music and generosity to younger players.
Standing beside the coffin, the coach gave a eulogy that recalled every season the old groundskeeper had worked.
She stayed up the night before her grandfather's memorial service, writing a eulogy that would do justice to his life.

distractors.lemma: An admission of fault offered to someone you have wronged.
A likeness drawn between two different things to make one easier to grasp.
Musical smoothness in the sound of words or speech.
A discredited program of selective human breeding, aimed at pushing out traits its backers disliked.

senses.definition: Lavish words of praise for a living person, a cause or a thing.

mnemonics: Eulogy joins Greek eu (good) and logos (word): good words spoken about someone, usually at a funeral.

senses.definition: A tactful label that dresses up a grim or awkward fact.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Mild words that cover a harsh fact, as when "let go" stands in for "fired."

examples.text: The listing called the cramped apartment "cozy," a euphemism that every renter in the city knows how to decode.
Military briefings sometimes use "collateral damage" as a euphemism for civilians killed by mistake.
Rather than tell the class their hamster had died, the teacher reached for a euphemism and said it had gone to live on a farm.
The memo called the price increase a "pricing adjustment," a euphemism that fooled no one.

distractors.lemma: Giddy elation so strong that it carries you away.
A one-line nugget of wisdom about how the world works.
Remarks from a mourner that celebrate a life now over.
Sweetness of sound in a line of verse or a stretch of speech.

mnemonics: Euphemism comes from Greek eu (good) and pheme (speech): speaking of a bad thing in good-sounding words.

senses.definition: So faint and brief that it slips away even as you notice it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Fading away almost as soon as it shows up.

examples.text: The smell of cut grass was evanescent, strong for a moment as the mower passed and then gone on the breeze.
The puffs of breath in the frosty air were evanescent, curling upward and gone a second later.
Her smile was evanescent, flickering across her face and vanishing before anyone else at the table saw it.
The firefly's glow was evanescent, gone before I could point it out to my daughter.

distractors.lemma: Sparkling with fizz, or with lively high spirits.
Slipping around questions instead of meeting them head-on.
Plain for anyone to notice, with nothing hidden about it.
Glinting with a play of many hues across its surface.

mnemonics: Evanescent comes from Latin evanescere, to vanish; the English word vanish grew from the same root.

senses.definition: Act on a problem that is already present so that it grows harder to bear or to fix.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To turn an existing problem into a bigger one.

examples.text: Scratching the rash will only exacerbate the infection and prolong your recovery.
Shouting at a frightened dog tends to exacerbate its panic rather than calm it.
The airline's decision to cancel ten more flights only exacerbated the crowding at the gate.
Taking the shortcut through the marsh exacerbated our delay, since we lost another hour in the mud.

distractors.lemma: Stretch an account past the truth by inflating how big or important something was.
Tear into someone's work or conduct in public with bitter, cutting words.
Pull out a plant, pest or practice, root and all.
Give someone a sudden rush of happy energy.
Open up the ground with shovels or machines to get at what is below.

mnemonics: Exacerbate shares a root with acerbic (Latin acerbus, bitter): to exacerbate a bad thing is to make it more bitter.

senses.definition: Lift suspicion off a person by showing that the fault lay with someone else or with no one.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To take the blame off someone by showing the facts.

examples.text: Everyone blamed the new bookkeeper for the leaked memo until the server log exculpated her: it was sent a week before she started.
Everyone blamed the dog for the missing cake until crumbs turned up in Theo's bed and exculpated her.
The replay showed the referee had waved play on, which exculpated the goalkeeper the fans had booed all week.
A letter found two centuries later helped exculpate the servant who had been hanged for the theft.

distractors.lemma: Undo the moral debt of a misdeed by paying a price for it.
Clean up a text for polite readers by cutting its crude passages.
Press a lesson into a pupil's thinking until it becomes second nature.
Condemn a person's actions in a stinging public rebuke.

mnemonics: Exculpate is Latin ex (out of) plus culpa (blame), the root of culpable: it takes someone out of blame.

senses.definition: Calling for action at once because putting it off would cause harm.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Needing to be handled now, not later.

examples.text: The ambassador cut short her holiday when a coup in the capital created exigent circumstances that demanded her immediate return.
When the dam began to leak, the exigent situation forced officials to evacuate the town overnight.
Police may enter a home without a warrant under exigent circumstances, for instance if someone inside is screaming for help.
A fire alarm in the server room was an exigent problem that pulled every technician off their other work.

distractors.lemma: Falling short in quantity, leaving almost nothing to work with.
Old but still around to be seen or read today.
Brought in from beyond the thing being examined, not produced inside it.
Outside the reach of a tax or rule because of one's status.

senses.definition: Expecting more effort or care from others than is fair.

mnemonics: Exigent comes from Latin exigere, to demand, the same root as exact: an exigent problem demands action now.

senses.definition: End a charge or suspicion against someone through an official decision in their favor.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To formally find that someone was not to blame.

examples.text: After the audit found no missing funds, the treasurer was fully exonerated.
The board of inquiry moved to exonerate the captain after reviewing the logbooks.
The league's investigation exonerated the coach, finding that the players had changed the scores without his knowledge.
The ethics panel exonerated the senator, ruling that every gift had been reported on time.

distractors.lemma: Go through a group of things by number, citing them in turn.
Treat a figure or relic as worthy of worship.
Settle what is owed to a worker for time and effort given.
Irritate a person so much that their temper starts to fray.

mnemonics: Exonerate comes from Latin ex (off) and onus, oneris (a burden): to exonerate someone is to lift the burden of blame off them.

senses.definition: Chosen because it gets results now, with questions of fairness set aside.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Done because it helps you now, not because it is right.

examples.text: Blaming the intern was expedient for the manager, though everyone knew it was unfair.
Rather than fix the leaking roof, the landlord took the expedient route of painting over the water stains before the inspection.
The king was merciful only when mercy was expedient, never out of kindness.
The student found it expedient to praise the teacher's poems the week before grades were due.

distractors.lemma: Brisk and businesslike, getting a job done in short order.
Accepting the commands of those in charge and carrying them out.
Eagerly awaiting an event one believes is near.
Considered cheap enough to lose without much regret.
Stated outright in precise terms instead of hinted at.

senses.definition: Handy and effective for the task at hand.

mnemonics: Expedient comes from Latin expedire, to free the feet: an expedient choice frees you to move toward what you want, right or not.

senses.definition: Strike out an entry or a passage so that the record no longer shows it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To wipe something off the books as if it was never there.

examples.text: After the doping scandal, the club expunged the former champion's name from every trophy plaque in the hall.
The school lets a student expunge one failed course from the transcript by retaking it.
Soviet censors expunged purged officials from group photographs, painting over their faces.
The moderators expunged every post that named the victim, so not a line of it remains in the archive.

distractors.lemma: Give a full, careful account of what an idea means.
Draw down a supply of something until less of it is left.
Raise public doubts about the truth of a statement or the good faith of a person.
Hurry a job or order along, cutting its waiting time.

mnemonics: Expunge comes from Latin pungere, to prick, as in puncture: scribes pricked dots under a name to strike it from a list.

senses.definition: Speak or write of someone or something in glowing, admiring terms.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To talk up something's good points with real warmth.

examples.text: The critic's review extolled the young poet's ear for rhythm and compared her to the masters.
Reviewers extolled the phone's battery life, calling it the best they had ever tested.
Every time we visited, Uncle Ray would extol his new electric car, praising its range and speed until everyone groaned.
In every interview, the chef would extol the tomatoes from her grandfather's farm as the best in the country.
The travel guide extols the little harbor town, calling its sunsets the finest on the coast.

distractors.lemma: Win money or favors from someone by holding a threat over them.
Rally people with a fervent appeal to do something.
Remove a part or substance from the thing it is lodged in.
Throw a member out of an institution for good.
Be overcome with triumphant glee and show it.

mnemonics: Extol comes from Latin extollere, to lift up: when you extol someone, you lift them up with praise.

senses.definition: Not pertinent to the matter under consideration.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Irrelevant or completely unrelated to the current topic.

examples.text: The speaker meandered through several extraneous anecdotes that confused the audience.
Students should edit out extraneous details to keep their essays concise.
The detective dismissed the extraneous clues that led away from the primary suspect.
During the negotiation, the mediator asked both parties to ignore extraneous grievances.
The meeting ran an hour over because people kept raising extraneous complaints about parking instead of discussing the budget.

distractors.lemma: Delivered on the spot, with no script or rehearsal.
Far outside the normal run of things, in a way that amazes.
Calling for all the energy and force a person can muster.
Counting in a wrongdoer's favor, so the blame weighs less.

senses.definition: Beyond what is needed; not essential to the whole.
Coming from outside the thing it is found in, rather than belonging to it.

mnemonics: Extra means outside, so extraneous things are extra and out of place.

senses.definition: Using humor that is out of place, so that a weighty topic sounds trivial.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Cracking jokes at a time that calls for a straight face.

examples.text: Asked by the judge whether he understood the charges, he gave a facetious bow and said, "Only the fun ones."
When the doctor asked how he had broken his arm, Leo gave a facetious answer about wrestling a bear, and she did not smile.
At the funeral reception, his facetious comment about the open bar earned him cold stares.
Even his facetious toast at the wedding, which predicted the couple would last a week, made the bride's mother wince.

distractors.lemma: Glib and shallow, treating a hard question as if it were easy.
Existing only on paper or in someone's imagination.
Bothered by the smallest flaw, mess or slip in standards.
Stirring up feuds between rival camps inside a party or group.
Hitting just the right note in word or deed.

mnemonics: Facetious goes back to Latin facetia, a joke or witty remark: a facetious person turns things into a joke, even when a joke is out of place.

senses.definition: Based on faulty reasoning or a mistaken belief, and so likely to mislead.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Based on a flawed argument or incorrect logic.

examples.text: The economic proposal rested on fallacious assumptions about consumer behavior.
The ad's claim that one celebrity's success proves the diet works is plainly fallacious.
The lawyer exposed the fallacious reasoning behind the witness testimony.
It is fallacious to assume that because two events happened together, one must have caused the other.

distractors.lemma: Lying idle between plantings, with no crop sown.
Smutty and suggestive, playing up sex to draw attention.
Given to wisecracks when the mood calls for gravity.
Touchy and quarrelsome, so that keeping the peace is a struggle.

senses.definition: Intended to deceive or trick.

mnemonics: Fallacious comes from Latin fallere, to deceive, the same root as false: a fallacious argument leads you to a false conclusion.

senses.definition: Brainless and blandly content, never noticing how little sense it makes.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Silly and empty, said with a satisfied air and no idea how it sounds.

examples.text: The host kept a fatuous grin on his face even as his guest described losing her home in the flood.
The candidate's fatuous answer, "I just love this country a whole lot," drew laughter from the debate audience.
The new manager kept up a fatuous cheer through the crisis, beaming "Let's stay positive!" as the servers went down.
The ad's fatuous slogan, 'Water: now wetter!', became a joke across the country.

distractors.lemma: Kidding around about weighty things when a sober tone is called for.
Fussy about cleanliness and precision to an unusual degree.
Leading to a wrong conclusion because the argument has a hidden flaw.
Prone to breaking into hostile cliques that fight among themselves.
Able to kill, or bad enough to doom a plan.

mnemonics: Fatuous shares a root with infatuated, from Latin fatuus, 'foolish': people who are infatuated often say fatuous things.

senses.definition: Quick to drop one loyalty or love for another, so that no one can count on it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Quick to lose interest in a friend, partner or team and move on.

examples.text: Her fickle loyalties made it difficult for anyone to trust her.
The fickle crowd cheered one moment and jeered the next.
He was a fickle suitor, swearing eternal love to a new woman every few weeks.
Fans are fickle: last season they adored the coach, and now they want him fired.

distractors.lemma: Flaring into a burst of temper at the smallest spark.
Fussy, rejecting food or things that are not just so.
Invented for a story or a lie, with no basis in fact.
Open to error; never certain to get things right.

senses.definition: Varying from hour to hour in ways no one can forecast.

mnemonics: Fickle goes back to Old English ficol, meaning deceitful: a fickle lover's vows do not hold.

senses.definition: Make a public show of ignoring a rule, law or custom.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To break a rule in plain sight because you don't care about it.

examples.text: The neighbors flouted the town's fireworks ban, setting off rockets from the beach where the sheriff could see them.
He flouted the library's silence rule by taking a phone call at full volume in the reading room.
He chose to flout convention by wearing sneakers to the gala.
Protesters gathered in the square at midnight to flout the curfew in full view of the police.

distractors.lemma: Make a showy display of what one owns or can do.
Flail and stumble while getting nowhere.
Make a dramatic exit to let everyone see one is offended.
Prosper and spread, growing stronger season by season.

senses.definition: Laugh at with contempt and derision.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Mocking or making fun of something with disrespect.

examples.text: Critics began to flout the outdated traditions of the academy.
It is unwise to flout the wisdom of experienced mentors.
The satirist used his column to flout pompous politicians.
Instead of debating, they preferred to flout opposing theories.

distractors.lemma: Praising an achievement with genuine admiration.
Supporting a cause through financial donations.
Whispering secrets behind closed doors.
Greeting strangers with polite hospitality.
Documenting historical events with accuracy.

mnemonics: Flout rhymes with out: people who flout a rule step out of it in plain sight, as if daring anyone to stop them.

senses.definition: Feed the anger of a group until it breaks out into conflict or revolt.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To stir up anger in people so that trouble breaks out.

examples.text: Rival fans were seated apart, but one man ran along the fence trying to foment a brawl between the two ends.
Anonymous accounts posted fake stories to foment anger between the two neighborhoods before the vote.
Rather than calm the crowd, the speaker chose to foment its rage, pointing at the police line and shouting.
The cook spent the voyage whispering complaints about the rations, hoping to foment a mutiny before they reached port.

distractors.lemma: Hurt or harass a victim over and over.
Grieve openly over a loss or a missed chance.
Saddle someone with a burden they never agreed to take on.
Rail loudly and bitterly against a person or policy.

senses.definition: Soothe an aching body part with hot, damp packs.

mnemonics: Foment comes from Latin fovere, 'to keep warm': to foment a revolt is to keep feeding its heat until it boils over.

senses.definition: Get in ahead of an expected trouble so that it never arrives.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To deal with a problem early so it never gets a chance to happen.

examples.text: Hoping to forestall complaints, the airline handed out meal vouchers before anyone asked for them.
The city trimmed dead branches all summer to forestall the power cuts that winter storms usually bring.
A quick apology from the chef forestalled the scathing review the diner had threatened to write.

distractors.lemma: Turn one's back on a habit with a solemn vow.
Comb woods and fields for anything edible.
Pay for a broken rule by losing a right or a stake.
Say ahead of time how things will turn out.
Pass up a treat or benefit by one's own choice.

mnemonics: Forestall comes from Old English foresteall, an ambush, literally a standing in front of someone on the road: to forestall something is to get in its way before it arrives.

senses.definition: Owing its occurrence to luck or coincidence rather than to anyone's design.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The result of luck or coincidence, not of anyone's plan.

examples.text: Their meeting was fortuitous: both had missed the same train and ended up sharing a taxi.
Penicillin's discovery was fortuitous, since Fleming noticed the mold only because he had left a dish uncovered.
Nothing about the timing was fortuitous; the leak had been planned for weeks.
A fortuitous gust of wind blew the lost kite back into the boy's arms.

distractors.lemma: Thrown in for no good reason and hard to excuse.
Snaking along with bend after bend instead of running straight.
Turning up in every place you look.
Hovering over someone out of concern for how they are faring.
Morally rotten and grossly unfair to those it touches.

senses.definition: Turning out well through a stroke of luck.

mnemonics: Fortuitous comes from Latin fors, 'chance', the same root as fortune: a fortuitous event is left to chance.

senses.definition: Stubbornly resistant to authority or control.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Unruly and hard to control, often quarrelling with those in charge.

examples.text: The fractious crew refused to follow the captain's navigation orders during the storm.
Dealing with a fractious legislature made it nearly impossible to pass new reforms.
The teacher struggled to maintain order among the most fractious students in the classroom.
The fractious horse grazed calmly until someone brought out its harness, then fought every attempt to fit it.

distractors.lemma: Amounting to a sliver of the total, often too little to matter.
Likely to break, crack or fail under slight pressure.
So panicked that every move becomes hurried and scattered.
Felt between brothers, or between comrades who treat each other as kin.

senses.definition: Easily irritated or annoyed.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Grouchy, touchy, and easily set off by minor inconveniences.

examples.text: Lack of sleep left him feeling unusually fractious throughout the morning meeting.
The toddler became increasingly fractious as bedtime approached without a nap.
Even the normally mild-mannered scholar grew fractious under the relentless questioning.
An incorrigibly fractious young man

distractors.lemma: Fascinated by ancient history and archaeological artifacts.
Fabricated from synthetic materials in a laboratory setting.
Faithful to traditional customs and religious practices.
Famed for extraordinary artistic achievements and paintings.

senses.definition: Unpredictably difficult in operation; likely to be troublesome.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Hard to manage or handle because it tends to cause problems.

examples.text: The old machinery proved too fractious for the new factory workers to operate safely.
Navigating the fractious legal system required the assistance of seasoned attorneys.
Economists worried about the fractious nature of the emerging global market.
Rockets were much too fractious to be tested near thickly populated areas
Fractious components of a communication system

distractors.lemma: Constructed with sturdy timber and reinforced steel beams.
Designed for maximum energy efficiency in cold climates.
Dedicated to preserving rare botanical specimens.
Filled with bright colors and intricate geometric patterns.

mnemonics: Fractious shares a root with fracture, Latin frangere, 'to break': a fractious group keeps breaking the rules and breaking into quarrels.

senses.definition: Inclined to economize, stretching money and supplies as far as they will go.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Good at making money and supplies last, with few treats or extras.

examples.text: Being frugal, she packed her own lunch every day and put the money she saved toward her tuition.
His frugal habits, from darning socks to buying day-old bread, let him retire at fifty.
Her frugal grandmother washed and reused every plastic bag and saved the string from parcels.
Rising prices have pushed many families to become more frugal, cooking at home and canceling subscriptions.

distractors.lemma: Gripped by deep winter cold, with ice on every surface.
Running wild and wary of people, despite a tame or farmyard ancestry.
Belonging to the kingdom of molds, yeasts and mushrooms.
Facing forward or coming straight at something head-on.
Paying off well, with plenty to show for the effort.

mnemonics: Frugal comes from Latin frux, 'fruit' or 'produce': a frugal person makes every bit of the harvest last.

senses.definition: Inclined to fill every silence with long, idle chatter.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Liking to talk on and on, even when nobody asked.

examples.text: The garrulous barber kept stopping his scissors to finish each anecdote, so a simple trim took an hour.
Voicemails from my garrulous aunt always ran out of recording time before she reached the point of her call.
During the long bus ride, his garrulous companion never stopped talking.
The professor became remarkably garrulous whenever the topic turned to vintage cars.

distractors.lemma: Always grumbling and finding something to whine about.
So loud in color that it looks tasteless.
Of giant size, far bigger than usual.
Sociable by nature and drawn to crowds and parties.

mnemonics: Garrulous comes from Latin garrire, 'to chatter': a garrulous seatmate chatters for the whole flight.

senses.definition: Needle or taunt a person over and over until they are stung into action.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To poke at someone with words or dares until they finally do something.

examples.text: His teammates goaded him into jumping off the high dive, chanting until he climbed the ladder.
The chess hustler goaded passing tourists with jeers about their nerve until one finally sat down to play.
Reporters tried to goad the mayor into a shouting match, but he only smiled and moved on.
The defense lawyer goaded the witness with sarcastic questions until she lost her composure on the stand.

distractors.lemma: Brag and smirk after coming out ahead of someone.
Gape in disbelief at some startling sight.
Carve a furrow into wood with a curved chisel.
Slip up in a way that earns a laugh rather than real harm.

senses.definition: Keep a herd moving by jabbing the animals with a spiked rod.

mnemonics: A goad was first a pointed stick for driving cattle; to goad someone is to keep poking at them until they move.

senses.definition: Thriving on company and at ease mixing with many people.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Loving company and finding it easy to strike up talk with anyone.

examples.text: Her gregarious brother knew everyone at the party within twenty minutes, while she stayed by the snack table.
Shy as a child, he grew into a gregarious adult who hosted dinners for a dozen friends every week.
Sales jobs suit gregarious people who would rather spend the day meeting new clients than working alone at a desk.
A gregarious host, she made sure no guest stood alone for more than a minute.

distractors.lemma: Flagrantly awful, far past the bounds of an ordinary mistake.
Heavy with consequence, the sort of harm people mourn for years.
Unable to stop chattering even when listeners edge away.
Puffed up with showy ambition and a taste for the colossal.

senses.definition: Of animals, banding together in herds or flocks by instinct.

mnemonics: Gregarious comes from Latin grex, 'flock', also found in congregate: a gregarious person likes to be part of the flock.

senses.definition: A sly talent for scheming and outwitting others through deceit.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Sneaky cleverness that helps someone fool others.

examples.text: Posing as a clumsy tourist with her map held upside down, the spy photographed every warship in the harbor; her guile fooled even the patrol officers.
In poker, guile counts for more than luck: a strong player will sigh and slump over a winning hand to lure others into raising.
The detective's guile was her best tool: she pretended to believe every lie the suspect told until he contradicted himself.
Without an ounce of guile, the child confessed to breaking the vase.

distractors.lemma: The uneasy sense, or the plain fact, of being to blame for a wrong.
A members' body for one craft or trade, which trains apprentices and sets fees.
Shameless cheek in asking or taking more than one is owed.
Steering advice that points someone toward a sensible choice.

mnemonics: Guile is the root of beguile: someone with guile can beguile you into trusting them.

senses.definition: Stale from being trotted out again and again by speakers and writers.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Tired and predictable; everyone has seen or heard it before.

examples.text: The pop song's hackneyed rhyme of 'fire' with 'desire' made the reviewer groan.
Real-estate listings are full of hackneyed labels, so every cramped flat becomes 'cozy' and every shabby one 'full of character'.
The painting teacher told students to skip hackneyed subjects such as sunsets over the sea and to draw the bus depot instead.
Every war film that year repeated the same hackneyed scene of a soldier kissing a photo of his sweetheart.

distractors.lemma: Visibly ravaged by hardship, with the face drawn tight.
Dashed off on impulse and poorly judged, more whim than plan.
Born under a bad star, so that little ever goes right.
Frazzled by being pulled in many directions at once.

mnemonics: Hackneyed comes from the hackney, a horse kept for hire; ridden by everyone, it ended up worn out, like an overused phrase.

senses.definition: A long, fiery speech that rails at its listeners or stirs them to action.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A long, loud rant that listeners are made to sit through.

examples.text: The activist delivered a fiery harangue from the steps of city hall.
The neighbor's harangue about our barking dog went on so long that the pizza on the table went cold.
Every Thanksgiving, Grandpa's harangue about the price of gasoline began before the turkey was carved.
At the gate, the passenger delivered a harangue about delays and rude staff while the agent nodded silently.

distractors.lemma: An advance messenger whose coming means a larger event follows close behind.
The courtroom step at which a defendant formally answers guilty or not guilty.
The smooth teamwork of people who see eye to eye.
A fresh scoring of a familiar tune for a different set of players.

mnemonics: Harangue comes from Medieval Latin harenga, a speech given to a crowd. It also starts like harass, which is what a harangue does to its listeners.

senses.definition: Someone who organizes life around good food, comfort and other delights of the senses.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A person whose top priority is having a good time.

examples.text: Asked what gave life meaning, the hedonist answered without hesitation: warm baths, ripe peaches and long naps.
She rejected her ascetic upbringing to become a devoted hedonist in Paris.
Only a true hedonist would book a week at a spa to recover from a week at the beach.

distractors.lemma: A healer who prescribes remedies made from leaves, roots and flowers.
Someone who dodges questions with vague, noncommittal replies.
A person who values human reason and dignity above religious authority.
A writer or performer who earns a living by being funny.

mnemonics: Hedonist comes from Greek hedone, "pleasure": a hedonist lives to chase it.

senses.definition: Leadership so dominant that one state or class sets the terms for everyone else.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being the top power that others must follow.

examples.text: After the Soviet Union collapsed, commentators described a period of American hegemony in which no rival could check Washington's influence.
One search company's hegemony is so complete that its name has become a verb for looking something up online.
For centuries, Rome's hegemony over the Mediterranean meant that nearly every port answered to the emperor.
Hollywood's hegemony in world cinema leaves little screen time for films made in smaller countries.

distractors.lemma: A hurried exodus by people running from peril at home.
Uniform makeup in which each part matches the rest.
A swollen, all-consuming sense of one's own greatness.
The pleasing effect of chords that support a melody.

mnemonics: Hegemony comes from Greek hegemon, "leader": a nation with hegemony leads and the rest follow.

senses.definition: An opinion condemned by a church or other ruling body for departing from its official teaching.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Believing or saying something your church or group has ruled is wrong.

examples.text: Early church councils met to settle which teachings were orthodox and which were heresy.
In the strictly traditional academy, questioning the canon was treated as intellectual heresy.
The bishops excommunicated the philosopher, ruling that his writings on the soul were heresy.
In a newsroom that revered the printed page, proposing to publish only online was heresy.

distractors.lemma: A report passed along secondhand by someone who never witnessed the events.
The inborn link that makes relatives resemble one another in build and coloring.
The system of shields, crests and colors by which noble families marked their identity.
The part of a nation's past that it chooses to protect and celebrate as its own.

mnemonics: Heresy comes from Greek hairesis, "a choosing": a heretic chooses a belief of his own over the official one.

senses.definition: A person who makes a habit of challenging whatever a society treats as beyond question.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A person who loves to knock down ideas that everyone else treats as untouchable.

examples.text: The young economist was an iconoclast who publicly tore apart the theories her professors had built careers on.
An iconoclast in the kitchen, he served dessert first and mocked every rule of fine dining.
Known as the league's iconoclast, the coach threw out decades of standard strategy and won anyway.
Every few decades a linguist turns iconoclast and declares the rules of school grammar a myth.

distractors.lemma: A specialist who forecasts growth, prices and jobs for banks or governments.
An expert who reads Homer and Virgil in the original and teaches about the ancient world.
Someone whose refined taste in one pleasure, from cigars to opera, others defer to.
A celebrity so admired that fans copy the person's look and style for years.

senses.definition: One who wrecks holy statues and paintings, believing that honoring them is wrong.

mnemonics: Iconoclast joins Greek eikon, "image", and klastes, "breaker": first a smasher of holy images, now a smasher of sacred ideas.

senses.definition: The giving of divine honors to a carved, cast or painted image.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Bowing down to a statue or object and treating it like a god.

examples.text: Roman officials ordered Christians to burn incense before the emperor's statue, a rite the believers refused as idolatry.
Some reformers whitewashed church walls, fearing that painted saints encouraged idolatry.
The law forbade carving any image of the god, lest worshippers slide into idolatry.
Early travelers often misread respect for ancestors as idolatry when they saw families bowing before carved tablets.

distractors.lemma: The body of beliefs a movement uses to explain the world and justify its aims.
A stretch of time so calm and pleasant that it seems lifted from a pastoral poem.
The personal blend of vocabulary, habits and pronunciation by which one speaker can be recognized.
A fixed expression that a learner would misread by taking each word literally.

senses.definition: Admiration so extreme that it treats a person or thing as holy.

mnemonics: Idolatry joins idol with Greek latreia, "worship": it is the worship of an idol.

senses.definition: Fixed in a way that no force, effort or passage of time can alter.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Set for good; no one and nothing can ever alter it.

examples.text: Her routine was immutable: up at five, a run at six and at her desk by seven, every day for twenty years.
The contract contained immutable clauses that could not be renegotiated by either party.
Medieval scholars taught that the heavens were immutable, untouched by the decay of the world below.
Young people often treat their tastes as immutable, then find them changing completely within a decade.

distractors.lemma: Free of every smudge, stain and stray crumb.
Of two liquids, impossible to dissolve one in the other in any proportion.
Having a body that can fight off a given infection before it causes illness.
So personal in style that every attempt to reproduce it falls short.

mnemonics: Immutable holds Latin mutare, "to change", as in mutation; the im- means not, so it cannot change.

senses.definition: Having or revealing little emotion or sensibility; not easily aroused or excited.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Not reacting outwardly at all, whatever you may feel inside.

examples.text: Her impassive expression made it impossible to guess whether she liked the offer.
The interpreter kept an impassive face, showing neither shock nor amusement, while translating the ambassador's insults word for word.
Through the whole tense auction the collector sat impassive, raising one finger now and then without a flicker of feeling.
Poker players learn to look impassive so that opponents cannot read their hands from their faces.
The cat met the dog's frantic barking with an impassive stare, not even twitching an ear.

distractors.lemma: Barring every attempt to cross from one side to the other.
Quick to leap into choices on a whim and count the cost afterward.
Given to harmless pranks and teasing grins.
Shamelessly bold, with no embarrassment about giving offense.

mnemonics: Impassive joins im-, not, to the Latin root of passion (pati, to suffer or feel): an impassive face shows no passion.

senses.definition: Ordering people about from a lofty height, as if one's every wish were law.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Bossy in a grand, high-and-mighty way that treats others as servants.

examples.text: The new landlady pinned imperious notices in the hallway: no guests after nine, no cooking fish, no questions.
The toddler's imperious cry of "Juice, now!" sent both grandparents running to the kitchen.
Used to a house full of servants, the old aristocrat was imperious even with the paramedics, ordering them to wipe their boots.
In an imperious letter, the billionaire instructed the town council to move the road that spoiled his view.

distractors.lemma: Likely to lead to injury or disaster.
Below the threshold at which the eye, ear or touch can register it.
Safe from decay, so it survives the centuries intact.
Scornful toward God and holy things, in word or deed.

mnemonics: Imperious comes from Latin imperium, "command", the root of empire: an imperious person gives orders like an emperor.

senses.definition: Cheeky or nosy in a way that ignores the respect a person or moment deserves.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Talking back or asking nosy things when you should mind your manners.

examples.text: The impertinent intern corrected the chief executive's grammar in front of the whole board.
My grandmother would not tolerate impertinent answers, and any child who talked back was sent from the table.
The cadet's impertinent grin during the inspection earned him a week of extra drills.
The butler raised an eyebrow at the impertinent guest who demanded a tour of the owner's private study.

distractors.lemma: Bound to end or fade after a while.
Refusing to repent, however plain the harm one has caused.
Left without force or influence, so one's efforts achieve nothing.
Coming and going rather than continuing without a break.
Refusing to give up a plan or argument long after others would have dropped it.

senses.definition: Not pertinent to the matter under consideration.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Having nothing to do with the topic you are currently discussing.

examples.text: The attorney objected because the opposing counsel raised impertinent details.
He introduced several impertinent facts that confused the main argument.
The committee dismissed the suggestion as entirely impertinent to the agenda.
Please remove these impertinent remarks from the final report.
Mentioned several impertinent facts before finally coming to the point

distractors.lemma: Extremely important to the final outcome.
Relating directly to personal property rights.
Incapable of being measured accurately.
Showing persistent effort despite obstacles.
Derived from incorrect mathematical assumptions.

mnemonics: Impertinent is in- (not) plus pertinent, relevant: an impertinent remark was first one that did not belong, and the word came to mean cheeky.

senses.definition: Able to withstand a force or influence without being changed or troubled by it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So thick-skinned that insults, pain or pressure have no effect.

examples.text: The mule was impervious to coaxing and shouting alike, and the cart stayed where it was.
The dictator seemed impervious to world opinion, shrugging off every sanction and protest.
The novelist was impervious to bad reviews; she never read them and began each new book the morning after a launch.
The old sea captain seemed impervious to cold, standing on deck in shirtsleeves through the January gale.

distractors.lemma: Lordly and bossy toward those one considers beneath one.
Rushing headlong into action before thinking it through.
Spread all through something, from its center to its edges.
Connected with an emperor's rule and the lands under it.

senses.definition: Of a material, sealed tight against water, damp and fumes.

mnemonics: Impervious comes from Latin per, "through", and via, "way"; with im- in front, nothing finds a way through.

senses.definition: Keeping up a hostility that no apology, gift or appeal will ever ease.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So angry or hostile that no peace offering will ever work.

examples.text: Each rival faction proved implacable, walking out of every round of peace talks.
Twenty years on, she still held an implacable grudge against the partner who had emptied their company accounts.
The striking miners faced an implacable owner who refused every offer and vowed to starve them out.
The cat remained implacable after the bath, hissing at us from under the bed for two days.

distractors.lemma: Within the reach of a rule or law, so that it governs the case.
Too far-fetched for a sensible listener to accept.
Escaping the fingertips because it is so fine or insubstantial.
Carried by what is left unsaid, so the listener must read between the lines.

mnemonics: Implacable shares Latin placare, "to calm", with placate; the im- means not, so it cannot be calmed.

senses.definition: Hold a person or thing responsible for an act or quality, usually a bad one such as a fault or a selfish motive.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To claim that someone caused something or has some quality, often a bad one.

examples.text: The crash report did not impute any blame to the pilot, pointing instead to a faulty sensor.
Critics were quick to impute the company's losses to its new chief executive, though the slump began years earlier.
We should not impute selfish motives to her gift just because she mentioned it in a speech.
Readers often impute a narrator's opinions to the author, which annoys many novelists.

distractors.lemma: Steep someone in a belief or mood until it becomes part of them.
Tell or teach someone something, so they come to know it too.
Act as a drag on a plan or a movement, so it advances only with difficulty.
Sever a hand, foot or whole limb from the body as a medical treatment.

senses.definition: In law or accounting, assign a value to something by estimating it from other figures.

mnemonics: Impute shares a root with compute: Latin putare, 'to reckon'. To impute is to reckon a fault into someone's account.

senses.definition: Present only in a first faint form that is likely to grow.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: In its first early stage and likely to get bigger.

examples.text: Linguists tracked the incipient spread of a new slang word, heard so far only in a few city schools.
The band's incipient fame showed in the small crowd that now sang along to its first single.
An incipient smile tugged at her mouth as she read the first line of the letter.
Economists saw rising home sales as a sign of an incipient recovery after two hard years.

distractors.lemma: Weak in flavor and dull to the senses.
Able to read a situation sharply and see what is really going on.
Never letting up, from one minute to the next.
Broke to the point that creditors cannot be paid.
Pressing a request so hard that saying no becomes difficult.

mnemonics: Incipient comes from Latin incipere, 'to begin' (in- 'on' + capere 'to take'): something incipient is just taking hold.

senses.definition: Living in poverty so deep that getting through each day is a struggle.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Having so little money that food and rent are out of reach.

examples.text: The scholarship covers fees for indigent students whose families could never pay them.
In the 1800s, indigent widows often ended their days in the county poorhouse.
After the flood took his farm and his savings, the once-comfortable rancher found himself indigent at sixty.
Once a wealthy merchant, he died indigent, and the parish paid for his funeral.

distractors.lemma: Stung into resentment by what feels like an injustice or a slight.
Rooted in a region since the earliest times on record.
Soft-hearted in granting wishes and slow to say no.
Keeping at one's work with patient care, hour after hour.
Dug in on a position and unwilling to give an inch.

mnemonics: Indigent comes from Latin indigere, 'to be in need': indigent people need help just to get by.

senses.definition: Preferring idleness to effort, so that work is put off or left undone.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Lazy; would rather lounge around than do any work.

examples.text: His indolent attitude toward his studies, skipping lectures and never opening a book, led to failing grades.
She spent an indolent summer afternoon dozing in a hammock while the weeds took over the garden.
Once he had tenure, the professor grew indolent and reused the same lecture notes for twenty years.
Too indolent to cook, he lived on cereal and takeout for most of the year.

distractors.lemma: Treating superiors with bold, deliberate contempt in words or manner.
Filled with a scent or flavor that brings a particular thing vividly to mind.
Showing sorrow openly in one's face, voice or mood.
Refusing to let others hold beliefs or live in ways one disapproves of.
Living in deep poverty, with nothing to spare and often nothing at all.

senses.definition: Of a tumor or other illness, getting worse only slowly and with little discomfort.

mnemonics: Indolent comes from Latin in- 'not' + dolere 'to feel pain': the indolent avoid the pain of hard work. Doctors still call a slow, painless tumor indolent.

senses.definition: So vast or moving that every attempt to put it into words falls short.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Too big a feeling or experience for any words to do it justice.

examples.text: Standing at the canyon rim at sunset, she felt an ineffable awe; every phrase she tried in her journal that night seemed too small.
The symphony left the audience with an ineffable sense of peace that nobody could quite describe afterward.
Asked to describe holding her newborn daughter, she gave up and said the joy was ineffable.
The mystic spoke of an ineffable truth that lay beyond the reach of language.

distractors.lemma: Making no real difference to the problem it was meant to solve.
Wasteful in how it works, so that much of the energy or money put in is lost.
Falling outside the group that may apply, compete or receive a benefit.
Genial in company, greeting others with a ready smile and easy chat.

senses.definition: Of a name or word, barred from speech by religious law.

mnemonics: Ineffable comes from Latin in- 'not' + effari 'to speak out': something ineffable cannot be spoken.

senses.definition: Moving forward in a way that nothing can stop or turn aside.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Always pressing on, and impossible to halt however hard people try.

examples.text: Year by year, the glacier made its inexorable advance down the valley, burying the old hiking trail.
No new law could halt the inexorable rise in rents once the tech firms moved into the neighborhood.
Despite every effort to save the factory, its decline proved inexorable.
Rising sea levels pose an inexorable threat to towns along the coast.

distractors.lemma: Bound up with another thing so closely that one cannot be had without the other.
Leaving everyone at a loss as to why or how it happened.
Beyond any pardon, since nothing about the situation lessens the fault.
Wildly overpriced, asking far more than the thing is worth.
Never running dry, however much is drawn from it.

senses.definition: Of a person, deaf to every plea for mercy or a change of mind.

mnemonics: Inexorable comes from Latin in- 'not' + exorare 'to win over by pleading' (orare, 'to pray'): no prayer can stop it.

senses.definition: Harmful to something, or tending to hold back its growth or success.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Bad for something, making it hard for it to grow or do well.

examples.text: Layers of paperwork are inimical to small businesses, which cannot afford a compliance team.
The harsh desert climate is inimical to most forms of plant life.
High humidity can prove inimical to delicate electronic instruments.
Constant interruptions are inimical to the deep focus that good writing needs.

distractors.lemma: One of a kind, in a style that others try for and never manage.
Kept to the smallest amount needed.
Knowing each other so well that nothing is held back between them.
Coming so soon that there is little time left to prepare.

senses.definition: Feeling or showing ill will toward a person or group.

mnemonics: Inimical comes from Latin inimicus, 'enemy' (in- 'not' + amicus 'friend'): something inimical acts like an enemy.

senses.definition: Wicked conduct, especially cruel injustice done to others.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Behavior so unfair and cruel that it counts as evil.

examples.text: The preacher thundered against the iniquity of landlords who evicted widows in the dead of winter.
The novel lays bare the iniquity of a mill town where children worked fourteen-hour shifts for pennies.
Rigging the water contracts so that the poorest districts paid double was an iniquity the new mayor vowed to undo.
The tyrant's iniquity knew no limits: he jailed critics without trial and seized their farms.

distractors.lemma: The era of the earliest great civilizations, now thousands of years gone.
The quality of turning up in every place one looks.
A probe ordered by officials to get to the bottom of a public failure.
A stream of yearly payouts bought with a lump of savings.
A knack for finding resourceful ways around obstacles.

mnemonics: Iniquity comes from Latin iniquus, 'unjust' (in- 'not' + aequus 'equal, fair'): iniquity treats people in a cruelly unfair way.

senses.definition: Posing no danger and giving no one reason to take offense.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Safe and mild; it won't hurt or upset anybody.

examples.text: The joke seemed innocuous to him, but it reopened an old family quarrel.
He made an innocuous comment about the weather to break the tension.
