Despite its fearsome fangs, the snake is innocuous; its venom is too weak to hurt a person.
The email looked innocuous, just a simple invoice, until the attachment installed a virus.

distractors.lemma: Low-key in appearance, so that the eye slides past it.
Jarring because it clashes with the setting or the rest of the group.
Present in numbers far beyond any attempt at a tally.
Pioneering fresh approaches where others stick to the old routine.
Part of one's makeup from the first day of life.

mnemonics: Innocuous comes from Latin in- 'not' + nocuus 'harmful', from nocere 'to harm' (as in noxious): innocuous things do no harm.

senses.definition: So bland in taste or spirit that it leaves no impression at all.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Bland and dull, with no real flavor or spark.

examples.text: Winter tomatoes from the supermarket are often insipid, pale and watery inside.
The film's insipid dialogue made even its talented cast sound bored.
After a decade of insipid pop songs, critics welcomed a band with something sharp to say.
The candidate's insipid speech, full of safe phrases, drew polite applause and no headlines.

distractors.lemma: In its first stage, with most of its growth still ahead.
Quietly destructive, with the damage hidden until it is well advanced.
Undaunted by peril, and eager to go where others hold back.
Sunk so deep in debt that the bills can no longer be paid.

mnemonics: Insipid comes from Latin in- 'not' + sapidus 'tasty' (from sapere 'to taste', the root of savor): insipid things have no savor.

senses.definition: Turned inward as a community or person, so that events and people beyond a small circle hardly register.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Cut off from the wider world and not curious about it.

examples.text: The village was so insular that a family who moved there twenty years ago is still called the newcomers.
Critics said the firm's insular culture, where executives hired only old friends, left it blind to new rivals.
The tiny expat community stayed insular, socializing only with one another and never learning the local language.
Academic fields can become insular when scholars write only for one another.

distractors.lemma: Having no answer that anyone can find, however long they work at it.
Spoken or done with open scorn that wounds the person it targets.
Breaking the chain of command by disregarding orders.
Testing everyone's patience past its limit, often through smugness.

senses.definition: Having to do with islands or the people who live on them.

mnemonics: Insular comes from Latin insula, 'island' (as in peninsula): insular people live as if on an island, cut off from everyone else.

senses.definition: Holding out against every remedy or method applied to it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So stubborn or tangled that nothing you try seems to fix or control it.

examples.text: After forty years of failed peace talks, the border dispute looked intractable.
His back pain proved intractable: neither surgery nor three different medications brought any relief.
Bamboo planted along the fence became an intractable pest, sprouting back no matter how often they dug it out.
Homelessness in the city seemed intractable until a new housing program cut it in half within five years.

distractors.lemma: Surviving with every part still in place.
Dying without a will, so the law decides who inherits.
Felt or valued, yet lacking any substance a hand could grasp.
Designed to be handled and played with rather than merely looked at.

mnemonics: Intractable comes from Latin tractare, to handle: an intractable problem is one nobody can get a handle on.

senses.definition: Refusing to give ground or accept any compromise, however strong the arguments or appeals.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Refusing to budge or meet the other side halfway, no matter what.

examples.text: The landlord stayed intransigent, rejecting every offer to split the cost of the repairs.
Talks collapsed after twelve hours because both sides remained intransigent on the pension question.
Her intransigent refusal to consider any other venue meant the wedding had to wait a full year.
No amount of evidence moved the intransigent senator, who voted against the bill for the sixth time.

distractors.lemma: Short-lived and impermanent, holding only for a limited stretch.
In grammar, belonging to the class of verbs that never pass their action on to an object.
Waging a guerrilla war on the state from within its borders.
Happening in fits, with gaps between the bursts.
Present in a thing by its very makeup, not lent to it by circumstance.

mnemonics: Intransigent comes via Spanish from Latin transigere, to settle a deal. Add in- (not) and you get someone who will not settle.

senses.definition: Deliver something in such numbers that it piles up faster than anyone can clear it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To bury someone under a flood of things, like calls, emails, or tasks.

examples.text: After the ad aired, viewers inundated the station with complaints, and the phone lines jammed for hours.
When the bakery offered free cake online, orders inundated its tiny kitchen within the hour.
New managers are often inundated with paperwork in their first weeks, leaving little time to meet the team.
During tax season, accountants are inundated with so many last-minute clients that they barely sleep.
After the newspaper ran its story, the shelter was inundated with donated coats and had to rent a storage unit.

distractors.lemma: Break from old practice by trying out fresh designs or methods.
Plant a damaging idea about someone through sly remarks.
Ripple up and down along its length in a rolling motion.
Brood over a clutch of eggs, sitting on them day and night.

senses.definition: Spread water over land until it lies submerged.

mnemonics: Inundate comes from Latin unda, a wave: to inundate is to send wave after wave over something.

senses.definition: Grown old in a habit or pastime, so that it now marks the person.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Stuck with a habit for so many years that it is part of who you are.

examples.text: An inveterate gambler, he has bet on the horses every Saturday for forty years and cannot imagine stopping.
My grandfather is an inveterate nail-biter; at ninety, he still chews them whenever the news comes on.
An inveterate hoarder, she has kept every newspaper delivered to her house since 1985.
An inveterate interrupter, the senator was still cutting off his own allies thirty years into his career.

distractors.lemma: Having a body with no bony spine running down the back.
Flipped so that what was on top now sits at the bottom.
Still whole and honored because no one has dared to break it.
Quick to dream up original gadgets, schemes or solutions.
Swollen far past any sensible measure.

mnemonics: Inveterate shares the Latin root veter-, old, with veteran: an inveterate habit is a veteran habit that has grown old with you.

senses.definition: Prone to sudden flashes of temper set off by minor irritations.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Quick to blow up in anger, even over little things.

examples.text: Passengers learned to tiptoe around the irascible bus driver, who barked at anyone fumbling for change.
Even a two-minute delay could set off the irascible manager, who once threw a stapler over a typo.
The chef grew irascible whenever the kitchen fell behind, snapping at anyone who asked a question.
Weeks of poor sleep left her irascible, and she lost her temper at the slightest noise.

distractors.lemma: Able to be rubbed away so that no mark is left.
Absurd enough to draw mockery instead of respect.
Lacking any basis in sense or evidence.
Overpowering every attempt to hold out against it.
Glinting with a rainbow of hues that seem to slide across the surface.

mnemonics: Irascible and irate both come from Latin ira, anger: an irascible person turns irate at the smallest thing.

senses.definition: Taking one's trade or duty on the road, staying only briefly wherever it leads.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Working on the road and never staying long in one spot.

examples.text: Itinerant knife sharpeners once pushed their grinding wheels through the streets, calling out for dull blades.
In the 1800s, itinerant peddlers carried pots, needles and ribbons to farmhouses miles from any store.
Before radio, itinerant musicians carried news and songs from one market town to the next.
An itinerant photographer, she drives her camper van from one county fair to the next, taking portraits for a few dollars each.

distractors.lemma: Moving forward through repeated cycles of draft, test and revise.
Coming with something unavoidably, simply because of what that thing is.
Put in place as a stand-in, meant to be swapped out once a lasting choice is made.
Beyond any chance of being wrong in what it says or teaches.

mnemonics: Itinerant shares the Latin root iter, a journey, with itinerary: an itinerant worker's whole life is an itinerary.

senses.definition: Speaking in clipped, minimal phrases and leaving much unsaid.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Talking very little and keeping answers short.

examples.text: Asked how the surgery went, the laconic doctor said only, 'Fine. He'll live,' and went back to scrub in.
The general sent a laconic report of the victory in three words: 'Town is ours.'
The laconic rancher answered the reporter's long questions with a nod, a shrug, or 'Yep.'
Readers love the novel's laconic hero, who says in five words what other characters take a page to say.

distractors.lemma: Going about a task in a lazy, offhand way, as if it hardly mattered.
Quick to well up and sob at sad moments.
Flat and uninspiring, falling well short of what was hoped for.
Instantly recognized everywhere and treated as an emblem of what it represents.

mnemonics: Laconic comes from Laconia, home of the Spartans, who were famous for short replies. To a king's threat beginning 'If I invade,' they answered only 'If.'

senses.definition: Speak or write of in glowing terms, holding up as worthy of honor.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To say in public how great someone or something is.

examples.text: Engineers still laud the old stone bridge, which has outlasted three earthquakes without a single crack.
Critics who once mocked the band now laud its early albums as classics.
Speaker after speaker rose at the dinner to laud the retiring nurse for forty years of patience and skill.
Historians still laud his patient diplomacy, which ended the war without another shot fired.

distractors.lemma: Fill the hold of a boat or wagon with freight.
Bring up a subject only by hint, trusting the listener to catch on.
Disguise stolen or criminal cash so that it looks like honest income.
Thread so many asides and flourishes through a talk that it drags.

mnemonics: Laud comes from Latin laus, praise, as does laudable. Applaud has a different root, but it still helps: to laud someone is to applaud them with words.

senses.definition: Heavy and slow-moving, with every action seeming to take great effort.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Feeling so tired and slow that even small tasks seem hard.

examples.text: Weeks after the flu, he was still lethargic, napping twice a day and struggling to climb the stairs.
The usually playful puppy seemed lethargic, lying in its bed and ignoring the ball.
After a month of polar darkness, the research crew grew lethargic, dragging themselves through even simple chores.
By the tenth hour of the flight, even the restless toddlers had turned lethargic, slumped quietly in their seats.

distractors.lemma: Carrying enough force or poison to end a life.
Having an immune system that treats a harmless substance as a threat.
Belonging to the official rites a congregation performs together in worship.
Poetic and full of feeling, with the lilt of a song.

mnemonics: Lethargic comes from Greek lethe, forgetfulness (the river of forgetting), plus argos, idle: a lethargic person seems to have forgotten how to get moving.

senses.definition: Lightheartedness that breaks into a grave mood, whether as welcome relief or as disrespect.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Jokes and fun at a serious time.

examples.text: On the eve of the hardest climb, the guide's silly campfire songs offered some welcome levity.
Many readers felt the comedian's levity about the earthquake was cruel while families were still searching the rubble.
Even a hint of levity during the flag ceremony at the military academy earned cadets an extra hour of drills.
The flight director's pun crackled over the radio, a rare bit of levity on a nerve-racking launch day.

distractors.lemma: Gentleness in judging or punishing someone who has done wrong.
The quality of getting to the point quickly and stopping.
Staying power over a great many years, in a life, a career or a product.
A sum that people are made to pay by order of a ruler or state.

senses.definition: Physical lightness, the property of having little weight.

mnemonics: Levity comes from Latin levis, light, the same root behind elevate and lever: levity is a light touch where weight is expected.

senses.definition: Fond of talking and quick to fill any silence with conversation.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very chatty, and hard to stop once started.

examples.text: A loquacious child, she asked questions from breakfast until bedtime and narrated every game she played out loud.
In her loquacious letters, which ran to twenty pages, she described every meal, every neighbor and every change in the weather.
The loquacious radio host could fill a three-hour show alone, without a single guest or caller.
A loquacious witness can be a gift to a lawyer, offering far more detail than any question asked for.

distractors.lemma: Bursting with ripe, mouth-watering flavor.
Loose and informal, in the style people use when chatting.
Wearing a long, mournful face or a slow, dirge-like tone.
Gifted at finding the right words and making them ring true.

mnemonics: Loquacious comes from Latin loqui, to speak, also found in eloquent and soliloquy: a loquacious person speaks and speaks.

senses.definition: Written or spoken in a way that makes even hard ideas simple to grasp.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So clear that anyone can follow it without effort.

examples.text: Unlike the jargon-filled memo from the legal team, the engineer's lucid two-page note explained the recall in words any customer could follow.
Lincoln's lucid argument, built step by step from points both sides accepted, left his opponent little room to wriggle.
The instructions were so lucid that I put the bookcase together without once checking the diagrams.
The subway map was so lucid that tourists who spoke no Japanese found the right line on the first try.

distractors.lemma: Played up with gory or scandalous detail to grab attention.
Wildly unreasonable, the kind of idea that makes people snort in disbelief.
Bringing in handsome profits for those who take it on.
Shaking or white-faced with rage.

senses.definition: Able to reason and recognize people again after a period of mental fog.
Glowing or glassy, so that light shines from it or through it.

mnemonics: Lucid comes from Latin lucere, to shine: a lucid explanation lets light into a murky subject.

senses.definition: Sending out light of its own, whether dim or brilliant.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Giving off its own light, so it glows or shines.

examples.text: At midnight the lava flow was still luminous, a slow orange river creeping down the dark slope.
Paper lanterns, luminous with the candles burning inside them, floated up over the river during the festival.
On summer evenings the fireflies turned the meadow into a field of tiny luminous specks blinking on and off.
Through the fog, the lighthouse lamp was a luminous smudge that grew sharper as the boat drew closer.

distractors.lemma: Taking up a lot of space, or made of a large amount of material.
Hinting at a divine power close by, so that people grow hushed and awed.
Giving a sign that trouble or danger is on its way.
Bringing in handsome returns to whoever takes it on.

senses.definition: Of writing or a performance: unusually clear, vivid and beautiful.

mnemonics: Luminous comes from Latin lumen, light, the same root as illuminate: something luminous gives off light.

senses.definition: Big-hearted enough to forgive insults and to treat a beaten or weaker opponent with generosity.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Willing to forgive and be generous, even toward people who opposed you.

examples.text: It was a magnanimous gesture to forgive his old rival and offer him a partnership.
She was magnanimous in victory, praising the hard work of the opponents she had just beaten.
Rather than gloat over the result, the winner gave a magnanimous speech thanking her opponent's supporters and promising to serve them too.
Showing a magnanimous spirit, he overlooked the insults and welcomed his critics into his home.

distractors.lemma: Backed by every single member, with not one voice against.
Too timid to take a stand or face danger.
Fond of grand, showy words that sound more impressive than they are.
Lively and full of energy, especially in speech or movement.

mnemonics: Magnanimous joins Latin magnus, great, and animus, spirit: a great-spirited person rises above grudges.

senses.definition: Use a sham or overstated ailment as cover for dodging one's duties.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To play sick to get out of doing your job.

examples.text: The ship's doctor suspected the sailor meant to malinger, since his limp came back only when the decks needed scrubbing.
Some actors malinger before shows they dread, inventing a sore throat so the understudy has to go on.
Teammates grumbled that the striker liked to malinger, since his hamstring always tightened before away games in the rain.
Video showed the worker lifting heavy boxes at home, proof that he chose to malinger rather than return to his job after his back healed.

distractors.lemma: Be slow to leave, hanging back when it is time to go.
Run down a person's reputation with spiteful lies.
Subject someone in one's care to cruelty or neglect.
Go haywire because of a fault, giving wrong results or none.

mnemonics: Malinger comes from French malingre, sickly: a malingerer acts sickly to dodge work.

senses.definition: Open to being shaped or changed by others; used of people, beliefs or plans that give way under pressure.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Easy for other people to shape or sway.

examples.text: Young children often have malleable minds that absorb both good and bad influences easily.
The senator proved malleable under pressure, changing his vote after a single meeting with lobbyists.
An inexperienced intern is often malleable and eager to adopt whatever approach the boss prefers.
Public opinion can be surprisingly malleable during a well-funded media campaign.

distractors.lemma: Awkward and clumsy, in actions or in dealing with people.
Reeking of rot or sweat, so that the air around it turns foul.
Filled with spite and set on wrecking other people's lives or plans.
Restless and resentful, nursing grievances that no change ever seems to settle.

senses.definition: Able to be beaten flat or worked into a shape without breaking apart, as gold and copper are.

mnemonics: Malleable comes from Latin malleus, hammer: a malleable metal, or a malleable mind, can be hammered into a new shape.

senses.definition: Soggy with tears and syrupy feeling, from too much drink or too little restraint.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Weepy and soppy in a way that feels like too much, often because of drink.

examples.text: By closing time the karaoke bar was full of maudlin regulars, slurring old love songs and weeping into their beer.
Critics dismissed the singer's new album as maudlin, a dozen songs about dead dogs and empty porches, each weepier than the last.
The memorial plaque's maudlin poem, all broken hearts and angels' tears, struck the family as more embarrassing than comforting.
She kept her retirement speech short and light, determined not to give a maudlin farewell.

distractors.lemma: Acid-tongued, with humor meant to leave a sting.
Part of the dull daily routine, with no spark of novelty.
Dwelling on graves, gore and disaster more than a healthy mind would.
Jumbled, with ideas or parts in no sensible order.
On its last legs and unlikely to recover.

mnemonics: Maudlin comes from Magdalene, once pronounced maudlin, because Mary Magdalene was often painted weeping.

senses.definition: Making a practice of lying, with little regard for the truth.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Lying often, so that what you say cannot be trusted.

examples.text: The mendacious witness was discredited when the defense played security footage that contradicted every detail of his story.
The mendacious applicant listed a law degree, but the university said it had no record of him.
Historians now regard the diplomat as mendacious, since nearly every victory his letters home described never happened.
The mendacious salesman swore the used car had never been in an accident, though its frame was visibly bent.

distractors.lemma: Brazen enough to try what most people would never dare.
Owning nothing and asking for one's keep from day to day.
Gaudy and cheap, built to dazzle rather than to last.
Carrying an unspoken threat that makes people uneasy.

senses.definition: Intentionally untrue.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Deliberately false and deceptive.

examples.text: The article contained several mendacious statements designed to mislead investors.
A mendacious rumor circulated through the village before the election.
The contract was voided due to mendacious clauses hidden in the fine print.
Detectives uncovered a mendacious scheme to defraud the insurance company.
A mendacious statement

distractors.lemma: Requiring immediate attention from emergency personnel.
Marked by an absence of color or pigment.
Showing a lack of basic manners and courtesy.
Belonging to a bygone era of classical philosophy.
Exhibiting excessive pride in one's achievements.

mnemonics: Mendacious comes from Latin mendax, lying, which is related to mendum, a flaw, the source of mend and amend: a mendacious story is full of flaws that need mending.

senses.definition: Prone to abrupt reversals of temper or intention that others cannot foresee.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Changing mood or mind so often and so fast that others are always caught off guard.

examples.text: Her mercurial boss could praise a report in the morning and tear it apart by lunch.
The singer's mercurial temper meant an interview could turn from warm to hostile with a single question.
Investors grew wary of the mercurial founder, who reversed the company's strategy three times in one year.
Spring weather in the mountains is mercurial, with sunshine giving way to hail in a matter of minutes.

distractors.lemma: Driven by pay above all, with loyalty going to whoever offers more.
Inclined to let an offender off lightly rather than demand the full penalty.
Tied to the business of trading goods for profit.
Significant enough to change a decision or an outcome.
Drawn from army life and the waging of combat.

senses.definition: Involving the liquid metal mercury, whether as an ingredient or as the cause of an illness.
Sharp-witted and full of darting energy in talk or thought.

mnemonics: Mercurial comes from Mercury, the swift messenger god, and the metal named after him, which slides and splits apart unpredictably.

senses.definition: Thorough down to the smallest particular, letting no slip pass however minor.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So careful that even the tiniest part of a job is done right.

examples.text: The artisan was meticulous in his restoration of the old manuscript, matching each faded letter by hand.
Her meticulous research meant that even the brand of soap in the novel's 1920s kitchen was right for the period.
We admired the meticulous craftsmanship of the antique cabinet, where not a single joint showed a gap.
A meticulous gardener, she trimmed the hedge with hand shears until every leaf stood in line.

distractors.lemma: Quick to interfere in affairs that belong to someone else.
Game for a hard challenge and slow to back down.
Gaudy in a way meant to dazzle buyers who look no closer.
Good enough to be singled out for a medal or a commendation.

mnemonics: Meticulous comes from Latin metus, fear: a meticulous worker is almost afraid of making even one small mistake.

senses.definition: Reduce the harm, force or seriousness of something bad, without removing it entirely.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To soften the damage that something bad can do.

examples.text: The city planted trees along the highway to mitigate the noise from traffic.
New safety rules were introduced to mitigate the risks of factory work.
She took medicine to mitigate the symptoms of her seasonal allergies.
Diplomats worked for weeks to mitigate the tensions between the two nations.

distractors.lemma: Serve as a strong reason pushing a decision one way or the other.
Have a disagreement argued out by lawyers in front of a judge.
Make a long journey to a new home region, often on a yearly cycle.
Hack at a body or object until it is scarred and misshapen.

senses.definition: Make a wrong or crime seem less serious, as facts offered in someone's defense can.

mnemonics: Mitigate comes from Latin mitis, mild: to mitigate damage is to make it milder.

senses.definition: Bring an upset or offended person back to a calmer frame of mind.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To settle someone down after they have been annoyed or hurt.

examples.text: The coach tried to mollify his benched striker by promising him the full second half next week.
A quick, sincere apology was enough to mollify the neighbor whose fence our dog had dug under.
Nothing the mayor said could mollify the crowd, which kept shouting until he left the stage.
The referee's quick explanation of the rule did little to mollify the furious home coach.

distractors.lemma: Fuss over and pamper someone far past what is good for them.
Rework a few features of a thing while keeping its overall form.
Puzzle someone so completely that no explanation they try will fit.
Leave someone red-faced and crushed with embarrassment.

senses.definition: Take the stiffness out of a material.
Soften the edge of a criticism or a demand so it stings less.

mnemonics: Mollify comes from Latin mollis, soft: you mollify an angry person by softening their mood.

senses.definition: Brooding and short-tempered, with a gloom that shuts other people out.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Wrapped up in a sour mood and wanting to be left alone.

examples.text: At the wedding he sat alone at the bar, morose and silent, waving off anyone who asked him to dance.
The candidate spent election night morose and short with his aides, glaring at the returns without a word.
Grandpa turns morose every February, muttering at the gray sky and leaving his crossword unfinished.
The novel's hero is a morose detective who answers every friendly question with a grunt and a scowl.

distractors.lemma: Slipping toward extinction after its best days have passed.
Sarcastic with a sharp sting, in a way that leaves its target smarting.
In the mood for romance and quick to flirt.
Hot-faced with shame over one's own blunder.

mnemonics: Morose comes from Latin morosus, peevish or hard to please: a morose person sulks and will not be cheered.

senses.definition: Part of the routine of daily life, and so dull rather than remarkable.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Plain and everyday, the kind of thing nobody would bother to talk about.

examples.text: The astronaut's video diary surprised viewers by dwelling on the mundane side of orbit: brushing teeth, fixing a fan and logging meals.
He sought to escape his mundane routine by planning an adventurous trip abroad.
Fans picture rock stars partying every night, but most of a tour is mundane: long drives, sound checks and hotel laundry.
Most of a lighthouse keeper's life was mundane: polishing brass, logging the weather and trimming wicks.

distractors.lemma: Gracious and assured in company, never awkward or crude.
Worth raising because it speaks directly to the issue at stake.
Guided by compassion in dealing with those who cannot defend themselves.
Said or done without a shred of thought behind it.
Dishonest by habit, with stories that seldom match the facts.

mnemonics: Mundane comes from Latin mundus, world: mundane things belong to the ordinary everyday world.

senses.definition: The deepest point of a decline, before any recovery begins.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The very bottom, when things could hardly sink any further.

examples.text: Sleeping in his car after losing both his job and his apartment, he felt he had reached the nadir of his life.
That bitter argument, when neither spoke for a year, was the nadir of their long friendship.
The team's nadir came with a 9-0 home loss, after which the owner fired the whole coaching staff.

distractors.lemma: A single point in a network, joined by links to other points.
The hub around which a whole affair revolves.
What a long argument boils down to once the extras are stripped away.
The seat of an infection, from which it spreads through the body.

senses.definition: In astronomy, the imagined point under an observer's feet, on the part of the sky the earth hides.

mnemonics: Nadir comes from Arabic nazir, opposite: the nadir is the point opposite the zenith, the very bottom.

senses.definition: In its first stirrings, still far from the form it will take.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Just getting started, and still a small version of what it may become.

examples.text: Only two years old, the nation's nascent space agency had yet to launch anything heavier than a weather balloon.
The nascent garden club met in a church basement, with eight members and one borrowed pair of shears.
A nascent feeling of doubt began to grow in his mind as the salesman kept talking.
The town's nascent music scene consists of three bands and one small club that opened last spring.

distractors.lemma: Having to do with the passages behind the nostrils.
In the dark about a matter, having never been told or taught.
Born and raised in a place rather than having moved there.
Turned out in crisp, well-pressed clothes.

mnemonics: Nascent comes from Latin nasci, to be born, the root of natal and renaissance: a nascent thing has just been born.

senses.definition: Too loosely drawn to grasp, with no firm outline or substance.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Fuzzy and unclear, so you cannot say exactly what it is.

examples.text: The brochure's wording stayed nebulous: the pills would 'support balance,' though it never said balance of what.
Her job title, 'vision lead,' was so nebulous that even her manager could not say what she did all day.
The contract's nebulous wording about reasonable delays led to a long fight over who was at fault.
The guest rule said only 'within reason,' a phrase so nebulous that every doorman read it differently.

distractors.lemma: Great in count, too many to list easily.
Wonderful enough to make people gasp with delight.
Stirring the awe one feels before the sacred.
Plotting deeds so wicked that decent people recoil from them.

senses.definition: Of the vast glowing clouds of gas that drift between the stars.

mnemonics: Nebulous comes from Latin nebula, mist: a nebulous idea is misty, with no clear outline.

senses.definition: Wicked in intent and usually unlawful in method.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Meant to hurt people or break the law, often in secret.

examples.text: The forged will turned out to be part of a nefarious effort to cut the old man's daughters out of their inheritance.
Behind the friendly loan app lay a nefarious design: it copied every borrower's contacts and threatened them when payments were late.
The rival stable's nefarious trick, slipping a sedative into the favorite's feed, came to light after the race.
Auditors later found the nefarious purpose behind the shell companies: hiding bribes paid to port officials.

distractors.lemma: Spanning a wide assortment of types, forms or activities.
Hanging by a thread, with collapse only a slip away.
Belonging to the onlooker, who gets the thrill without taking the risk.
Drawn to crowds and company, and restless when left alone.

mnemonics: Nefarious comes from Latin nefas, a crime against divine law (ne-, not, plus fas, what is right): a nefarious act is the opposite of what is right.

senses.definition: A raw recruit to some field, with little practice behind them.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A newcomer who is still finding their feet in some pursuit.

examples.text: As a neophyte at the climbing gym, she spent her first week learning how to tie knots and fall safely.
The chess club pairs each neophyte with an experienced player who explains the basic openings.
Wine experts sometimes forget that a neophyte cannot yet tell a merlot from a cabernet.
Even after a year in office, the senator was still seen as a neophyte who did not know how deals got made.

distractors.lemma: An infant in the days just after birth.
A sworn foe, the rival a hero is fated to clash with.
A wizard whose spells summon spirits from the grave.
A person whose fretting far outruns any real danger.

senses.definition: A new convert being taught the principles of Christianity by a catechist.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A person newly converted to Christianity who is receiving religious instruction.

examples.text: The bishop spent hours answering the theological questions of each eager neophyte.
During the ceremony, the neophyte made a public profession of faith before the congregation.
Catechists guided every neophyte through the foundational doctrines of the church.
The ancient text details the specific rites performed for a neophyte before baptism.

distractors.lemma: An ordained priest responsible for maintaining parish records and archives.
A wandering philosopher who questions traditional religious dogmas.
A secular musician hired to perform hymns during Sunday services.
A monastery librarian tasked with translating sacred manuscripts into Latin.

senses.definition: A plant that is found in an area where it had not been recorded previously.

mnemonics: Neophyte comes from Greek neos, new, and phytos, planted: a neophyte is newly planted in a field.

senses.definition: Bury the meaning of something under confusion, usually to hide what is really going on.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To muddle a message on purpose so the real point stays hidden.

examples.text: When asked about the missing funds, the treasurer tried to obfuscate the problem with a flood of acronyms and charts.
The insurance policy seemed written to obfuscate what was covered, burying every exclusion in footnotes.
A good teacher makes a hard idea clear instead of using jargon to obfuscate it.
Rather than admit the delay, the airline sent a vague notice that seemed meant to obfuscate the real reason.

distractors.lemma: Get ahead of a problem so that it never needs solving.
Stand up front at a wedding or a game and see that it goes by the book.
Be smothered until one can no longer draw breath.
Put someone under a duty they cannot honorably refuse.

mnemonics: Obfuscate comes from Latin fuscus, dark: to obfuscate is to darken a point until no one can see it clearly.

senses.definition: Lowering oneself before people in power through endless flattery and eager agreement.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Always praising and agreeing with an important person, hoping to win their favor.

examples.text: Hoping for a good score, the singer opened with an obsequious speech about the celebrity judge's genius before singing a single note.
Surrounded by obsequious courtiers, the monarch rarely heard an honest opinion.
Each time the wealthy donor toured the museum, the director turned obsequious, agreeing with his every opinion of the paintings.
Tired of obsequious assistants who called every draft a masterpiece, the novelist hired an editor known for blunt criticism.

distractors.lemma: Unaware of things that everyone else in the room can plainly see.
Approaching a subject from the side instead of head-on.
Grating on everyone nearby through rudeness, boasting or noise.
Unable to let go of a single idea or habit, returning to it again and again.

mnemonics: Obsequious comes from Latin obsequi, to comply, literally to follow after: an obsequious person follows the boss's every wish.

senses.definition: Unmoved by any reason, plea or pressure to give up a position already taken.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very stubborn; once you decide something, nobody can talk you out of it.

examples.text: Even after three doctors told him to rest, the obstinate runner insisted on racing the next day.
The obstinate juror would not change her vote, though the other eleven spent two days walking her through the evidence.
No argument could sway the obstinate teenager, who wore shorts to school all through a freezing January.
When the waiter said the kitchen had closed, the obstinate diner simply sat down and repeated his order.

distractors.lemma: Staying away from drink, sweets or other treats one has sworn off.
Belonging to the medical work of seeing mothers safely through childbirth.
Flaunting money or taste so loudly that it begs for admiration.
Out of date to the point that nobody makes or uses it any more.

senses.definition: Of a problem, stain or illness, persisting through every attempt to clear it up.

mnemonics: Obstinate comes from Latin obstinare, to persist, a relative of stare, to stand: the obstinate stand their ground and will not budge.

senses.definition: Dense about hints and implications that most people pick up at once.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Not catching on, even when the point is right in front of you.

examples.text: He was being deliberately obtuse, pretending not to understand that 'we should talk later' meant 'please leave now.'
Even the most obtuse reader will notice that every villain in the novel wears green.
I hinted three times that the party was a surprise, but my obtuse brother still asked her what time it started.
Is the committee really so obtuse that it cannot see why nobody applies for these jobs?

distractors.lemma: Dealing in theory so deep or remote that it baffles anyone outside the field.
Out of place and too loud for its setting, so that nobody can ignore it.
Digging in one's heels and staying put however hard others push.
Tucked away from fame, with only a small circle aware of it.

senses.definition: Of an angle, opening past 90 degrees but short of 180.
Of a shape or tip, rounded or flattened rather than coming to a sharp point.

mnemonics: Obtuse comes from Latin obtusus, blunted: an obtuse mind is dull rather than sharp, like an angle too wide to come to a point.

senses.definition: Intrusive in a meddling or offensive manner.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being overly eager to give unwanted help or advice in an annoying way.

examples.text: The officious security guard demanded to inspect my identification three times.
We grew tired of the hotel manager and his officious interference in our vacation.
An officious clerk made us redo every form in blue ink, though no rule required it.
She resented her neighbor's officious advice on how to prune her rose bushes.

distractors.lemma: Formal and on the record, rather than said privately or off the cuff.
Getting real results when put into practice.
Fawning, and keen to obey or flatter people with power.
Dreamed up and passed off as real.

mnemonics: Officious comes from Latin officium, "duty", the root of office: an officious person treats every matter as their duty to manage.

senses.definition: Weighing on a person as a burden, through the labor, expense or duty it requires.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Hard and tiring to do, like a heavy load you have to carry.

examples.text: The loan's onerous terms meant she worked a second job for ten years just to keep up the payments.
My duties weren't onerous at all; I only had to greet the guests at the door.
Caring for two hundred cows alone, milking before dawn and mending fences until dark, made for an onerous life.
Nobody wanted to be club treasurer once the role, with its weekly reports and yearly audits, became so onerous.

distractors.lemma: Sending a scent into the air that people nearby can pick up.
Off the mark, because the facts or reasoning behind it were wrong.
Hinting darkly that some harm or misfortune is on its way.
So vile that people recoil from it in loathing.
Belonging to the world of sleep and the visions it brings.

mnemonics: Onerous comes from Latin onus, "burden", the same onus as in "the onus is on you".

senses.definition: Closed to outside understanding, with its reasoning or inner workings kept out of view.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Hard to make sense of, because you can't see the thinking or the details behind it.

examples.text: The orchestra's hiring was opaque; players learned who got the open seat from a list on the door, with no reasons given.
The app's rules for ranking posts are opaque, so even popular creators cannot say why their views suddenly dropped.
His reasons for quitting remained opaque; he simply cleared his desk and left without a word.
The philosopher's prose is so opaque that students read each paragraph three times before it makes sense.

distractors.lemma: Lavish in a way that announces how much money was spent.
Coming at a well-chosen moment for the task at hand.
Tuned to give the top result that the circumstances allow.
Belonging to lenses, vision and the science of how we see.
Grand and theatrical, with emotions sung or played at full volume.

senses.definition: Of a surface or substance, keeping light out entirely.

mnemonics: Opaque comes from Latin opacus, "shaded": an opaque explanation leaves its meaning in the shade.

senses.definition: Scornful public blame aimed at a person or group for behavior seen as disgraceful.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A harsh wave of public shame and criticism directed at someone.

examples.text: When reporters showed that the charity's donations had paid for his yacht, the director met with such opprobrium that old friends crossed the street to avoid him.
The referee faced the opprobrium of the entire stadium after his call cost the home team the final.
Crossing the picket line earned him the lasting opprobrium of the coworkers who had stayed out on strike.
When diners learned the chef had been serving reheated frozen meals as 'made fresh daily', the opprobrium online forced the restaurant to close.

distractors.lemma: Harsh, unjust rule that holds a people down by force.
Lavish wealth on which no expense has been spared.
Seizing each passing chance for personal gain, even at others' expense.
Cloudiness that keeps light, or meaning, from getting through.

senses.definition: A state of extreme dishonor.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A deep and lasting sense of shame or humiliation.

examples.text: He lived in deep opprobrium following his conviction for fraud.
The fallen general retreated into solitude to escape public opprobrium.
Centuries later, the tyrant's name is still synonymous with absolute opprobrium.
She preferred exile to living under the heavy burden of local opprobrium.
The name was a by-word of scorn and opprobrium throughout the city

distractors.lemma: A condition of supreme happiness and satisfaction.
The legal procedure for claiming lost property.
An elevated status granted by academic achievement.
A temporary leave of absence from duties.
The ceremonial blessing of a new building.

mnemonics: Opprobrium comes from Latin probrum, "a shameful act": opprobrium is the scorn heaped on someone who commits one.

senses.definition: Showing off riches or importance so openly that the display itself becomes the point.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Flashy on purpose, to let everyone see how much money or power you have.

examples.text: Rather than an ostentatious mansion, the founder bought a modest bungalow and drove a ten-year-old car.
She arrived at the small country wedding in an ostentatious sable coat and a diamond tiara.
Guests rolled their eyes at the host's ostentatious habit of leaving the price tags on the paintings in his hallway.
Neighbors mocked the ostentatious fountain in the dentist's front yard, a marble copy of a Roman original lit up all night.

distractors.lemma: Claimed for public view, but possibly a cover for something else.
Splitting people into camps that argue hotly and at length.
Pushing one side of a disputed question instead of treating it fairly.
Checking and rechecking one's own work out of a sense of duty.

mnemonics: Ostentatious comes from Latin ostentare, "to keep showing": an ostentatious person keeps showing off what they own.

senses.definition: Soften how bad something appears or feels while leaving its root untouched.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make a problem, mistake, or bad situation seem less severe than it is.

examples.text: A generous bonus may palliate the sting of a pay freeze, but it will not stop good staff from looking elsewhere.
No apology could palliate the cruelty of what he had posted about his sister.
He attempted to palliate his tardiness by blaming the sudden transit strike.
Historians accuse the general's memoir of trying to palliate his part in the burning of the village.

distractors.lemma: Feel through the skin for clues to what is wrong inside the body.
Dust a blossom with grains from another bloom so fruit can form.
Stop giving pleasure once the novelty has worn off.
Pound hard in the chest after a fright or a burst of effort.

senses.definition: Bring a sick person relief from pain or other symptoms while the disease itself goes on.

mnemonics: Palliate comes from Latin pallium, "cloak": to palliate a fault is to throw a cloak over it so it looks less bad.

senses.definition: A treatment or plan hailed as able to fix everything, a claim that rarely survives testing.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A magic fix for everything, which nearly always turns out to be too good to be true.

examples.text: A fresh coat of paint was no panacea for a house with a cracked foundation and rotting beams.
Grandpa treated duct tape as a panacea, using it on leaky hoses, torn jackets and even a cracked windshield.
Some parents see banning phones at school as a panacea, but teachers say bullying and boredom will not vanish with the screens.
The startup pitched its app as a panacea for loneliness, poor sleep and bad diets all at once.

distractors.lemma: A gland tucked behind the stomach that helps control blood sugar and digest meals.
A scene so broad that the eye must sweep across it to take it all in.
A contagious illness at large on several continents in the same period.
A dummy treatment whose only power lies in the patient's belief in it.
The full roster of gods in one culture's myths and worship.

mnemonics: Panacea comes from Greek pan, "all", and akos, "cure": a panacea is a cure for all.

senses.definition: Someone or something so excellent in one respect that others are measured against it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A person or thing others are told to copy because it gets something just right.

examples.text: Never late, never rude and always prepared, she was a paragon of professionalism in a chaotic office.
The coach held up the quiet goalkeeper, who had never once argued with a referee, as a paragon of sportsmanship.
He saw his grandfather, who returned every lost wallet he ever found, as a paragon of honesty.
The restaurant was hailed as a paragon of good service, where waiters remembered every regular's order.

distractors.lemma: Something that runs against common sense and still turns out to be so.
The partner in a love affair kept hidden from a husband or wife.
A person no one will invite, hire or be seen with.
A freeloader who takes from friends or family and never pulls their weight.

mnemonics: Paragon comes from Italian paragone, a touchstone used to test gold: a paragon is the standard others are tested against.

senses.definition: Extreme care in spending money; reluctance to spend money unnecessarily.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being very careful with money and refusing to spend it unless totally necessary.

examples.text: His legendary parsimony meant that he reused even the smallest scraps of wrapping paper.
The corporate office enforced strict parsimony regarding travel expenses and office supplies.
Despite his great wealth, a streak of parsimony prevented him from ever tipping generously.
Her parsimony allowed her to save enough money to buy a house by age twenty-five.

distractors.lemma: Marriage, especially when seen as a formal or religious bond.
Wealth or traditions handed down from a father or earlier forebears.
A balance in which neither side stands above the other.
A sour hostility that lingers between people who have clashed.
A preachy air of being more virtuous than everyone else.

senses.definition: The preference, in science or argument, for the simplest explanation that accounts for the facts.

mnemonics: Parsimony comes from Latin parcere, "to spare": a person known for parsimony spares every coin.

senses.definition: A supply or count too small to meet what is needed.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: When there just isn't enough of something to go around.

examples.text: After the dry summer, the paucity of grass forced ranchers to start buying hay for their herds in October.
The village library's paucity of books meant children read the same twelve titles over and over.
Due to the paucity of applicants, the university extended the deadline for the scholarship.
A paucity of women in the engineering department led the dean to rethink how it recruited students.

distractors.lemma: The condition of two rivals being dead even, with no gap between them.
The state of being clean all the way through, with nothing added.
The spongy, hole-riddled quality that lets water soak into stone or soil.
The murkiness of glass or prose that will not let you see what lies behind it.

mnemonics: Paucity comes from Latin paucus, "few": a paucity of anything means there are too few of them.

senses.definition: Treating minor points of rule or fact as if they mattered most, often to display one's learning.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Always correcting people on small points that hardly matter, like a fussy know-it-all.

examples.text: At trivia night, the pedantic host refused to accept 'Holland' because the card said 'the Netherlands.'
Every time someone said 'less people' at dinner, my pedantic cousin cut in to say 'fewer people.'
In his pedantic review, the critic spent three paragraphs on the novel's use of the word 'decimate' and one sentence on its plot.
Instead of enjoying the film, he made pedantic notes about historical inaccuracies in the costumes.

distractors.lemma: Devoted to the medical care of infants and growing children.
Concerned with how lessons are planned and delivered in a classroom.
Dull and run-of-the-mill, the kind of thing nobody remembers.
Given to roaming from post to post, never staying long at any one.

mnemonics: Pedantic comes from pedant, which came into English through French from Italian pedante, a schoolmaster: a pedantic person corrects everyone like a fussy teacher.

senses.definition: A settled taste for something, or a natural pull toward doing it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A strong liking for something that you keep coming back to.

examples.text: Her penchant for gothic novels means every birthday brings another book about haunted castles.
Given his penchant for fiery food, nobody was surprised when he ordered the curry marked with five chili peppers.
The painter's penchant for deep blues shows up in nearly every canvas, from harbor scenes to portraits of her sisters.
His penchant for telling elaborate jokes made him popular at social gatherings.

distractors.lemma: Effort or discomfort a wrongdoer accepts in order to clear their conscience.
An income a retired worker draws from a fund built up during their working years.
Theatrical flair, the knack of turning an ordinary act into a little show.
The fine, ban or lost point handed out when a rule is broken.

mnemonics: Penchant comes from French pencher, "to lean": a penchant is a natural leaning toward something.

senses.definition: Poverty so severe that even food, heat and shelter are out of reach.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being so poor that you struggle to pay for the basics of life.

examples.text: Years of drought and failed harvests drove the valley's farmers into penury, and many sold their land for a few coins.
He grew up in such penury that he owned one pair of shoes and often went to bed hungry.
The poet's letters from that winter describe her penury: a room without heat, a single candle and bread bought on credit.
A generous pension spared the old soldier from the penury that awaited many of his comrades.

distractors.lemma: Knowingly breaking a sworn promise to be truthful when giving evidence.
A set of prayers or duties given after confession as a way of making amends.
The softer grey band at a shadow's edge, lighter than its dark core.
A habit of being drawn again and again to one kind of thing.

mnemonics: Penury sounds like penniless, meaning having no money at all.

senses.definition: Given to breaking faith with those who depend on one's loyalty.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Likely to turn on the friends or partners who trusted you.

examples.text: The perfidious steward smiled at the king each morning while selling his private letters to a rival court.
She could not forgive her perfidious business partner, who had secretly sold their client list to a rival.
History remembers the general as perfidious because he switched sides in the middle of the battle.
Tell a perfidious friend your secret, and you will soon hear it repeated all over the office.

distractors.lemma: Done only to tick a box, with no real effort behind it.
Set on doing the unreasonable thing, often just to be difficult.
Fussy about neatness and detail, and quick to notice any small flaw.
Sure to stir up envy or hard feelings by favoring some people over others.

mnemonics: Perfidious holds fid, from Latin fides (faith), as in fidelity. The per- here means astray, as in perjury, so a perfidious person strays from faith.

senses.definition: Carried out as a mere formality, with the least effort that will pass.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Done just to get it over with, without real care.

examples.text: The inspector gave the machinery a perfunctory glance before signing off.
She offered a perfunctory apology and rushed out of the room.
His perfunctory review of the manuscript missed several major errors.
The doctor's perfunctory checkup lasted two minutes, and she never asked about his symptoms.

distractors.lemma: Curt and bossy, cutting off any chance to argue back.
Shut down for good and now only a thing of the past.
Useful to the discussion because it speaks to the very issue in question.
Lasting with no break or end in sight.

mnemonics: Perfunctory comes from Latin perfungi, to get through a duty: a perfunctory job is done just to be finished with it.

senses.definition: Doing serious damage by degrees, often before anyone realizes the danger.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Slowly and secretly doing a great deal of harm.

examples.text: Lead in old water pipes is pernicious because the damage builds up quietly over many years.
The pernicious idea that girls are bad at math kept many talented students out of science classes.
Skipping sleep is a pernicious habit, because the toll on memory and mood builds so slowly that people blame everything else first.
The leak behind the bathroom tiles proved pernicious, rotting the beams for years before the floor finally sagged.

distractors.lemma: Hard to satisfy because of an endless focus on trivial things.
Showing grown-up talent or manners while still a small child.
Slow to set limits and quick to let others do as they please.
Returning season after season without ever quite going away.

mnemonics: Pernicious comes from Latin pernicies, ruin, built on nex, violent death, the same root found in internecine.

senses.definition: Gifted with sharp insight, so that one grasps the heart of a matter quickly.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Good at seeing the truth of a situation that most people miss.

examples.text: The perspicacious nurse noticed that the patient's cheerful answers did not match his trembling hands.
She was far too perspicacious to be fooled by such a flimsy argument.
A perspicacious teacher can tell at a glance which student has not done the reading.
His perspicacious review pointed out the flaw in the study that the authors themselves had missed.

distractors.lemma: Laid out in clear language that any reader can follow.
Unwilling to give up, pressing on long after others would have stopped.
Persuasive in form while resting on a hidden flaw.
Always spoiling for a quarrel or a fight.

mnemonics: Perspicacious comes from Latin perspicere, to see through, the same root as perspective: a perspicacious person sees through to the truth.

senses.definition: Felt in every corner of a setting, leaving almost nothing untouched by it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Showing up in every part of something, with no place free of it.

examples.text: Corruption was so pervasive that even the clerks expected a bribe to stamp a form.
Sugar is so pervasive in packaged food that it turns up in bread, soup and even salad dressing.
In the drought year, dust was pervasive, settling on plates, pillows and the keys of the piano.
The slang from one video game became so pervasive that teachers heard it in every hallway.

distractors.lemma: Able to bring a doubter around to one's own side of an argument.
Prying into matters that people would rather keep to themselves.
Slippery under questioning, steering around anything one would rather not admit.
Wrapped up in one's own thoughts, often gazing into the distance.

mnemonics: Pervasive comes from Latin per (through) and vadere (to go), as in invade: something pervasive goes through everything.

senses.definition: Prone to pouting and snapping over minor letdowns, in a way that seems childish.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Acting like a spoiled kid who sulks when things go wrong.

examples.text: Told he could not have dessert until he finished his peas, the boy turned petulant, folding his arms and kicking the table leg.
She grew petulant whenever her idea was not picked first, sighing loudly and refusing to help with anyone else's.
When the committee rejected her proposal, she gave a petulant shrug and would not speak for the rest of the meeting.
The star grew petulant when the director cut his favorite scene, and he sulked in his trailer for an hour.

distractors.lemma: Full of remorse and eager to set right what one did wrong.
Fussing over small points of learning to show how much one knows.
Perfectly clear, letting light or meaning through without any haze.
Small and slender in build, used mostly of women.

mnemonics: Petulant starts with pet: picture a spoiled pet that sulks and snaps whenever it does not get its treat.

senses.definition: Short and sharp, yet packed with substance.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Said in a few words that carry a lot of meaning.

examples.text: The CEO delivered a pithy remark that captured the entire strategy in one sentence.
Franklin packed his advice into pithy sayings of six or seven words, which is why people still quote them.
Asked to sum up the novel in one line, she gave a pithy reply: greed wins, then loses.
The editor welcomed her pithy comments, which fit on a single sticky note.

distractors.lemma: Bad enough to make onlookers wince with sorrow or scorn.
Strict about prayer and religious duty.
Turning down most of what is offered until something suits exactly.
Small-minded and spiteful over things that hardly matter.

mnemonics: Pithy comes from pith, the soft core of a plant stem; a pithy remark gets straight to the core of the matter.

senses.definition: Soothe an upset person, typically by offering something that takes the edge off their grievance.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To calm down someone who is upset, often by giving in a little.

examples.text: The airline handed out meal vouchers to placate passengers stuck overnight at the gate.
To placate her neighbors after the late, noisy party, she baked them a tray of lemon bars.
The chef sent out a free dessert to placate the diner whose steak had arrived cold.
Neither an apology nor a full refund could placate the customer, who left a one-star review anyway.

distractors.lemma: Drag someone into suspicion by tying them to a wrongdoing.
Plead from a position of weakness with someone who holds one's fate.
Cover walls or fences with printed notices to spread a message.
Make a duplicate so faithful that no one can tell it from the first.

mnemonics: Placate comes from Latin placare, to calm, a cousin of placid: you placate someone to make them placid again.

senses.definition: A familiar, safe remark that fills a silence without adding any thought.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A tired saying people repeat when they have nothing fresh to add.

examples.text: The coach's halftime talk was one platitude after another about giving it your all.
When I lost my job, my uncle offered the platitude that every cloud has a silver lining, then changed the subject.
Readers mocked the editorial as a string of platitudes about coming together and believing in the future.
At the funeral he heard the same platitude again and again, that everything happens for a reason.

distractors.lemma: The slack an employer or rule-maker allows for doing things one's own way.
A knack that makes a certain kind of task come easily.
A store of something so ample that it never seems to run low.
Warm public praise for an achievement.

mnemonics: Platitude comes from French plat, flat: a platitude is a flat remark with nothing fresh in it.

senses.definition: An oversupply of something, with far more on hand than the situation calls for.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Far more of something than anyone needs.

examples.text: The hotel bathroom held a plethora of tiny soaps and lotions, far more than two guests could use in a week.
Faced with a plethora of nearly identical cereals, he stood in the aisle for ten minutes and left with none.
The new phone came with a plethora of settings, most of which nobody ever opens.
With a plethora of streaming services to choose from, he spent more time scrolling than watching.

distractors.lemma: A ballot that puts a single yes-or-no question to all of a nation's voters.
A chest illness in which the lungs' outer wrapping becomes inflamed and rubs as you breathe.
A session of a council or party that every member is expected to attend.
A point where a rising number stops climbing and holds steady for a while.

mnemonics: Plethora comes from Greek plethein, to be full, a distant cousin of plenty: a plethora is plenty and then some.

senses.definition: An all-out attack in words, usually in print, meant to demolish an opposing view.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: An angry, one-sided essay or speech that tears into someone else's views.

examples.text: Her pamphlet was a blistering polemic against factory farming, and it named every company she blamed.
The reviewer called the book less a history than a polemic, since it attacked the general on every page and never weighed the evidence.
He wrote a furious polemic against modern architecture, mocking glass towers as soulless boxes.
Readers who expected a balanced study found a two-hundred-page polemic aimed squarely at the city's planning board.

distractors.lemma: A community whose members share one government and one set of public rules.
An organization's settled line on an issue, which its staff are expected to follow.
A showy, self-important manner of speaking or behaving.
The finish of work that has been refined until no rough edges show.

senses.definition: A heated public dispute, often over religious or political teaching.
Someone who makes a habit of attacking other people's doctrines in print, especially in religion.

mnemonics: Polemic comes from Greek polemos, war: a polemic wages war on someone's ideas with words.

senses.definition: Heavy and slow-moving, so that every motion seems to take great effort.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Big, heavy and slow, so each move looks like hard work.

examples.text: The old freight train made its ponderous way up the grade, barely faster than a man walking.
The ponderous old elevator groaned upward, pausing at each floor as if to catch its breath.
Loaded with marble, the barge was so ponderous that the tugboat needed an hour to turn it.
The sumo wrestler's charge looked ponderous, but once that much weight got moving nobody could stop it.

distractors.lemma: Letting water or air seep in through a mass of pinholes.
Touching the heart in a way that brings a quiet ache of sorrow.
Too far-fetched or unreasonable for anyone to take seriously.
Full of omens that make people brace for trouble.

senses.definition: Of a speech or book, plodding and heavy-handed, with no lightness of touch.

mnemonics: Ponderous comes from Latin pondus, weight, the same root as pound and ponder (to weigh in the mind): a ponderous thing moves under its own weight.

senses.definition: Judging plans and ideas by how well they work in practice rather than by theory or principle.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Focused on practical solutions and real-world results rather than theory.

examples.text: With a week until the wedding and no caterer, the couple made the pragmatic choice of ordering pizza for all ninety guests.
Engineers have to be pragmatic, because a bridge that is elegant on paper but too costly to build helps nobody.
Too pragmatic to wait for the perfect apartment, she signed a lease on a decent one near the train.
Her pragmatic father said she could study poetry as long as she also learned a trade that would pay the rent.

distractors.lemma: Splitting light into rainbow colors, or shining with many colors.
Raising snags or doubts that stand in the way of a clean answer.
Taking good news and bad news with the same unbothered face.
Serving as the textbook case that others of its type are measured against.

senses.definition: Relating to the school of philosophy that tests the truth of an idea by its practical effects.
Relating to how context and a speaker's purpose shape the meaning of language.

mnemonics: Pragmatic comes from Greek pragma, a deed or thing done: a pragmatic person cares about what can actually be done.

senses.definition: A steady stream of empty words that carry no point or weight.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Endless silly chatter with nothing worth hearing in it.

examples.text: I left the party early, worn out by an hour of prattle about other people's vacations and lawn care.
The toddler's happy prattle about dinosaurs and juice boxes filled the back seat for the whole drive.
She switched off the morning show, unable to stand the hosts' cheerful prattle about celebrity diets.
Between sips of tea, the two neighbors kept up a stream of prattle about the weather, the price of eggs and nothing much at all.

distractors.lemma: A story told in place of an argument, so that listeners draw the lesson themselves.
A cover story offered so that nobody sees why you really acted.
A playful trick meant to fool or tease someone.
A lead-in at the top of a formal text, set before its actual rules or terms begin.

mnemonics: Prattle sounds like rattle, as in a baby's rattle making endless meaningless noise.

senses.definition: Be the spark that makes a looming trouble break out sooner than it otherwise would.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make something bad happen suddenly, before its time.

examples.text: Her offhand joke at the wedding precipitated the family quarrel that everyone knew was coming eventually.
The leaked memo precipitated the chief executive's exit, which had been planned quietly for the spring.
Doctors feared the stress of the move would precipitate the heart failure they had hoped to hold off for years.
A sudden drop in milk prices precipitated a wave of farm sales that might otherwise have been spread over a decade.

distractors.lemma: Treat a future event as likely and plan around it.
Join in with others in something they are doing.
Spread out and melt away over time.
Throb out of rhythm, with the heart racing and skipping.

mnemonics: Precipitate comes from the Latin praeceps, "headlong": to precipitate an event is to send it rushing forward headfirst.

senses.definition: Shut off a possibility ahead of time, so that it can never come about.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To prevent something from happening before it can even start.

examples.text: The bridge's low clearance precludes double-decker buses from using that route.
Not having a law degree precludes her from arguing a client's case in court.
Heavy fog may preclude a landing, so the pilot always carries enough fuel to reach another airport.
Taking the job in Tokyo would preclude any chance of finishing her degree in Boston.

distractors.lemma: Take place earlier, so that something else follows after it.
Work out from the evidence that something must be so.
Tuck someone away out of sight and out of company.
Steer a listener's mind toward a topic with a veiled reference.

mnemonics: Preclude shares its root with close and closet, Latin claudere, to shut: to preclude something is to shut the door on it in advance.

senses.definition: Ahead of the normal timetable in talent, knowledge or maturity, especially as a child.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Doing things far beyond what is normal for their age, especially as a young child.

examples.text: At nine he was a precocious reader who argued with his teachers about Dickens.
Her precocious questions about death and taxes startled the adults at the dinner table.
The coach knew the precocious ten-year-old was special when she started correcting the older players' footwork.
Her letters from summer camp, written at eight, were so precocious that her parents suspected a counselor had helped.

distractors.lemma: Shaky and liable to give way at any moment, leaving whoever relies on it exposed.
Worth a great deal and treasured by its owner, often because it cannot be replaced.
Plunging or climbing at so sharp an angle that a single misstep could mean a long fall.
Measured or stated with such care that nothing in it is even slightly off.

senses.definition: Of a plant, blooming or bearing fruit ahead of the usual season.

mnemonics: Precocious comes from Latin praecox, ripened early (prae, before, and coquere, to cook or ripen): a precocious child is ready before the usual time.

senses.definition: A long-standing taste for a certain kind of thing, which shows in the choices a person keeps making.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A thing you always lean toward and pick when you can.

examples.text: Knowing his predilection for window seats, the travel agent booked him row 12A on every flight.
A predilection for short sentences led the editor to cut half of every draft that reached her desk.
His predilection for loud ties was famous; colleagues could spot him across any conference hall.
Because of her predilection for long walks, she booked a hotel beside the park trails rather than the shopping district.

distractors.lemma: A claim made now about how some future event will turn out.
A difficult spot where every choice seems to make things worse.
The act of walking away from an obligation one was bound to meet.
The doctrine that every soul's fate was fixed by divine decree before birth.

mnemonics: Predilection holds Latin diligere, to single out and love, the root of diligent: a predilection is what you single out ahead of everything else.

senses.definition: Perceiving the significance of events before they occur.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Seeing what is coming before others do.

examples.text: Her prescient call to sell before the housing bubble burst saved her clients millions.
Written in 1949, the novel now seems prescient, since it imagined screens that watch the people watching them.
Investors admired his prescient knack for backing small technology firms years before they became giants.
Packing rain gear turned out to be prescient, because the storm arrived a day earlier than forecast.

distractors.lemma: Laying down rules for how things ought to be done.
Acting with more confidence or familiarity than your place allows.
So urgent that it cannot wait.
Being in the same place as someone or something, rather than away.

mnemonics: Prescient comes from Latin prae, before, and scire, to know, the root of science: knowing what will happen before it does.

senses.definition: Be deliberately ambiguous or unclear in order to mislead or withhold information.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To talk around the truth on purpose, giving vague answers that mislead.

examples.text: When her mother asked where the car had been all night, the teenager prevaricated with a hazy story about driving around with friends.
The witness kept prevaricating, answering each yes-or-no question with a long speech about something else.
Asked whether the product had been tested on children, the spokesman prevaricated, saying only that safety was always their top priority.
Rather than prevaricate about the delay, the pilot told passengers plainly that a part had failed and the flight was canceled.

distractors.lemma: Be the side still standing when a contest is over.
Read the clues of today and announce what tomorrow will bring.
Turn out ready-made building parts that are trucked to the site and bolted together.
Speak against something as wrong or unwise.

mnemonics: Prevaricate comes from Latin praevaricari, to walk crookedly: someone who prevaricates will not walk a straight line to the truth.

senses.definition: Completely free from dirt or contamination.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Completely pure and untouched by dirt or pollution.

examples.text: Fresh snow covered the park in a pristine white sheet before the first dog walkers left their tracks.
After three hours of scrubbing, the kitchen floor was pristine enough to eat from.
The surgeon's gloves must stay pristine, so she touches nothing outside the sterile field.
Workers keep the chip factory's clean room pristine, since a single speck of dust can ruin a wafer.

distractors.lemma: Looked up to because of high standing and a fine reputation.
Showing no interest in or respect for the arts and serious ideas.
So fussy about manners and neatness that other people find it tiresome.
Costing more than most people want to pay.

senses.definition: Existing in the earliest, original form, before later changes.

mnemonics: Pristine comes from Latin pristinus, former or original: a pristine thing is still as it first was.

senses.definition: Strict and reliable honesty in the way a person carries out a position of trust.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being so honest that people trust you with money or power.

examples.text: Known for her probity, the judge once stepped aside from a case because her cousin's firm was involved.
His reputation for probity made him the obvious choice to count the votes.
The new treasurer showed her probity by returning a donor's gift card instead of keeping it.
The museum trusted his probity: for thirty years he had refused dealers' bribes to call a fake painting genuine.

distractors.lemma: The expected share of tries in which a certain outcome turns up.
Wordiness that drags a speech or text out far past its point.
A short gap between where one thing is and where another is.
Plenty of money and success, whether for a family or a whole country.

mnemonics: Probity comes from Latin probus, upright or honest, which also gave us prove: a person of probity proves honest every time.

senses.definition: A pull in a person's character that they give in to again and again, frequently to their cost.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: An urge you keep giving in to, often for something that is bad for you.

examples.text: Her proclivity for gossip made coworkers careful about what they said near her desk.
Because of his proclivity for cutting corners, the bookshelf he built was leaning within a week.
The historian noted the king's proclivity for picking quarrels with neighbors he could not defeat.
Dogs bred for herding have a proclivity to circle and nip at anything that moves, even children.

distractors.lemma: An order or notice read out or posted in the name of a ruler.
Getting more finished work out of the same staff and hours.
The level a learner reaches when a skill no longer takes effort.
The quality of a remark that rewards long reflection.

mnemonics: Proclivity comes from Latin pro, forward, and clivus, a slope: a proclivity tilts you toward a habit, like ground that leans downhill.

senses.definition: Careless with money or goods to the point of throwing a fortune away.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Spending money so freely on fun that you end up broke.

examples.text: The startup's prodigal founders spent their first round of funding on a rooftop office and catered lunches, and had nothing left to pay engineers.
She was prodigal with her paychecks, ordering takeout every night and replacing her phone whenever a new model came out.
He tipped every waiter fifty dollars and bought rounds for strangers, a prodigal streak that emptied his savings in a few months.
Like the son in the parable, she came home broke after a prodigal year abroad.

distractors.lemma: Large enough or strong enough to seem a marvel.
Getting a lot done with the time and effort put in.
Belonging to a familiar old saying that everyone can quote.
Going on for months or years when it should have taken weeks.

mnemonics: Prodigal comes from Latin prodigere, to drive away or squander. The prodigal son in the parable squandered his whole inheritance.

senses.definition: Squandering wealth freely and shamelessly, with no thought of limits.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Throwing away money or supplies as if they would never run out.

examples.text: The team's profligate owner paid a backup goalie more than the whole coaching staff, then wondered why the club was broke.
Running sprinklers at noon in the middle of a drought struck the neighbors as profligate.
Donors stopped giving once they learned how profligate the charity's board had been, spending a third of every gift on galas.
A profligate kitchen throws out a third of the food it buys, while a careful one turns the scraps into soup.

distractors.lemma: Skilled enough at a craft or subject to be trusted with it.
Constantly turning out new work or new young.
Leaving money in hand once all the bills are paid.
Timed or placed so that an undertaking has every chance of going well.

senses.definition: Unrestrained by convention or morality.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Living in a way that ignores all moral rules and social standards.

examples.text: The novel depicts the profligate behavior of the aristocracy in the eighteenth century.
He lived a notoriously profligate life of late-night parties and scandals.
The community rejected his profligate lifestyle and barred him from local events.
She sought to reform her profligate brother before he ruined the family name.
