distractors.lemma: Profoundly religious and devoted to daily prayer.
Professional in demeanor and respectful of tradition.
Prone to anxiety and excessive worrying about details.
Productive and hardworking in professional pursuits.
Protected from external influences by isolation.

mnemonics: Profligate comes from Latin profligare, to strike down or ruin: profligate spending ruins a fortune.

senses.definition: Producing new work again and again, so that the total output is very large.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Making a lot of something, such as books, songs or ideas.

examples.text: Thomas Edison was a prolific inventor, with more than a thousand patents to his name.
A prolific letter writer, my grandmother sent each grandchild a card every week for twenty years.
Agatha Christie was so prolific that she wrote more than sixty detective novels.
The prolific podcaster has released a new episode every weekday for six years.

distractors.lemma: Earning its owners more than they put in.
At ease with a skill and able to use it without errors.
Touching on the hardest questions and saying something wise about them.
Padded with far more words than the point needs.
Spending far beyond reason and feeling no shame about it.

senses.definition: Breeding fast and often, so that numbers grow quickly.

mnemonics: Prolific shares the Latin root proles, "offspring", with proliferate: both are about producing a lot.

senses.definition: A lasting, built-in lean toward behaving one particular way.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Something you tend to do, often without even deciding to.

examples.text: The office printer's propensity to jam on the last page made everyone print a spare copy.
Toddlers have a propensity to put everything in their mouths, so parents learn to keep coins out of reach.
His propensity to say yes to every request left him on three committees with no free evenings.
Voters' propensity to blame whoever holds office for a bad economy worries every president seeking a second term.

distractors.lemma: A time of rising wealth, when business is good and money is easy to come by.
Care to behave in the way polite society expects.
The things that belong to someone and that others may not take.
Showy behavior meant to impress, with nothing real behind it.

mnemonics: Propensity comes from Latin propendere, to hang or lean forward: a propensity is a lean toward some kind of behavior.

senses.definition: Matter-of-fact and plain, with none of the color or lift of poetry.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So everyday that nobody would bother to write a poem about it.

examples.text: After a week of wedding plans, it was almost a relief to talk about prosaic things like the water bill.
After the thrilling trailer, the film itself felt prosaic, with a predictable plot and flat dialogue.
The rock star's diary turned out to be prosaic: dentist appointments, grocery lists and notes about the weather.
Some poets find beauty in prosaic objects, such as a wheelbarrow or a plum left in the icebox.

distractors.lemma: Well off, with a growing business or bank balance.
Taking steps early so that a problem never gets the chance to start.
Turning out later to have foretold the future.
Concerning where the stresses and pauses fall when a line is spoken.

mnemonics: Prosaic grows from prose, the kind of writing that does not rhyme or scan: something prosaic has no poetry in it.

senses.definition: Capable of shifting easily from one form, role, or style to another.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Changing easily into many different shapes, jobs or styles.

examples.text: The actor's protean range let him play a king, a clown, and a killer in the same season.
A protean cook, he could turn the same bag of rice into sushi one night and pudding the next.
The virus proved protean, mutating into new forms faster than vaccines could follow.
Jazz is a protean art, reshaping itself every decade to absorb new styles.

distractors.lemma: Showing all the textbook features of its type.
Dull and everyday, without a spark of flair.
Made of protein or containing a great deal of it.
Keeping watch so that those in one's care come to no harm.

mnemonics: Protean comes from Proteus, a Greek sea god who kept changing his shape so that no one could hold him.

senses.definition: Weighing what could go wrong and choosing the safer, wiser course.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Using good sense so you don't end up in trouble later.

examples.text: The general made the prudent decision to retreat rather than risk his entire army.
It seemed prudent to read the lease twice before signing, and she was glad she did when she found the hidden fee.
A prudent driver slows down before the curve, not halfway through it.
Leaving a spare key with a neighbor proved prudent the night he locked himself out.

distractors.lemma: Quick to take offense at talk of sex or the sight of bare skin.
Right on topic for the question being discussed.
Hard to miss, because it sits up front or sticks out.
Correcting others on tiny points of grammar or fact that hardly matter.

mnemonics: Prudent is a shortened form of Latin providens, foreseeing. A prudent person sees trouble coming and plans for it.

senses.definition: Foolish in a juvenile way that an adult ought to have outgrown.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Acting like a ten-year-old when you are well past that age.

examples.text: The grown man threw a puerile tantrum when his favorite meal was sold out.
The fifty-year-old executives spent the company retreat on puerile pranks, hiding each other's shoes and short-sheeting the beds.
His colleagues grew tired of his puerile habit of drawing silly faces on the whiteboard during budget meetings.
Instead of answering the question, the senator fell back on puerile name-calling, like a boy on a playground.

distractors.lemma: Keeping every appointment and formality to the minute and the letter.
So short of nerve that one backs down from every challenge.
Seeping pus from an infection.
Too small and frail to put up much of a fight.

senses.definition: Having to do with children or the early years of life.

mnemonics: Puerile comes from Latin puer, boy: puerile humor is the kind a schoolboy finds hilarious.

senses.definition: Eager for a clash, and ready to turn any disagreement into a fight.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Always looking for a fight or an argument.

examples.text: The pugnacious senator answered every question with an insult and dared reporters to print it.
Even as a small child he was pugnacious, shoving any kid who took his place in line.
The terrier's pugnacious temperament meant it barked and lunged at dogs three times its size.
After two drinks the pugnacious fan would challenge anyone in a rival jersey to step outside.

distractors.lemma: So foul that people turn away from it.
Sticking with a plan or belief long after others would quit.
Carrying a little soft extra weight.
Having a short nose that looks pressed flat against the face.

mnemonics: Pugnacious comes from Latin pugnare, to fight, from pugnus, fist. Picture a pugnacious person with fists always raised.

senses.definition: Giving off a smell or flavor so intense it seems to sting the nose or tongue.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Having a very sharp and powerful smell or taste that hits you hard.

examples.text: Grating fresh horseradish releases fumes so pungent that the cook's eyes start to stream.
A pungent whiff of ammonia rose from the janitor's bucket and sent us coughing into the hall.
Durian is banned on some trains because its pungent smell fills a carriage in minutes.
A skunk had passed under the porch in the night, and its pungent spray still hung in the air at breakfast.

distractors.lemma: Stirring a tender sadness that lingers after the moment has passed.
Booming and reverberating, with a low, mournful ring.
Designed to make someone pay a penalty for wrongdoing.
Making sure no formality, however small, is ever left out.

senses.definition: Sharply critical or witty in a way that stings.

mnemonics: Pungent comes from Latin pungere, to prick, the root of puncture: a pungent smell seems to prick your nose.

senses.definition: Lying dormant during a pause in activity rather than finished for good.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Resting quietly for a while instead of being over for good.

examples.text: Seeds sealed in a clay jar can stay quiescent for centuries, and a few still sprout once they are planted and watered.
Queen bumblebees spend the winter quiescent in the soil, then dig their way out in spring to start new colonies.
The malicious code sat quiescent on the server for months before it woke up and began copying files.
The old feud between the two clans lay quiescent for a generation, then flared up again over a disputed well.

distractors.lemma: Tending to yield and let others settle matters without argument.
Giving a look that wonders, half amused, what someone means.
Always finding some small thing to grumble about.
Showing every defining trait of its type in its purest form.

mnemonics: Quiescent comes from Latin quiescere, to rest, the same root as quiet: a quiescent seed is resting quietly until conditions change.

senses.definition: Driven by a noble vision that ignores the hard limits of the real world.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Chasing grand dreams that make no practical sense.

examples.text: She set out on a quixotic quest to clean up every park in the state single-handedly.
Fighting a global oil company with nothing but a pen and a blog felt noble but quixotic.
His quixotic dream of reviving the village with a hand-built opera house ignored the fact that only forty people lived there.
He spent his savings on a quixotic campaign to bring back the horse-drawn mail coach, sure that the whole country would follow his lead.

distractors.lemma: Eyeing something with a teasing doubt about what it means.
Fast at catching on and firing back a sharp retort.
Pleasantly behind the times in a way that charms visitors.
Having odd little habits or features that make it stand out.

mnemonics: Quixotic comes from Don Quixote, the hero of Cervantes's novel, who charged at windmills he believed were giants.

senses.definition: Part of the daily routine, too familiar to draw notice.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Plain and everyday, the kind of thing that fills a normal day.

examples.text: Checking the morning mail is a quotidian ritual for the retired professor.
The novel captures the quotidian struggles of working-class families: rent, bus fares, and long shifts.
After months of hospital stays, she found comfort in the quotidian tasks of cooking and folding laundry.
His poetry turns quotidian objects like spoons and doorknobs into works of art.

distractors.lemma: Phrased so neatly that others will want to cite it word for word.
Having to do with noon, when the sun stands highest.
Recurring on a fixed three-month cycle.
Describing what someone used to be but no longer is.

mnemonics: Quotidian comes from Latin quotidie, every day, built from dies, day. Something quotidian turns up every day.

senses.definition: Marked by a grudge that has hardened and soured over time.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Holding on to old anger so long that it turns nasty.

examples.text: Fifteen years after the band split up, the former bandmates still traded rancorous jabs about who really wrote their hit song.
The neighbors' rancorous feud over a fallen fence outlasted both of their marriages.
His memoir is so rancorous toward his old coach that reviewers wondered what had happened between them decades ago.
Long after the merger, a rancorous divide remained between staff from the two old companies, who still blamed each other for the layoffs.

distractors.lemma: Hoarse and clamorous, with a din that scrapes at the nerves.
Too far gone to eat, with a bitter, off taste.
Desperate for food after going a long time without it.
Held to exacting standards so that no shortcut slips through.

mnemonics: Rancorous is built on rancor, an old grudge left to fester: rancorous words come from anger that never healed.

senses.definition: Thin out a gas or other substance so that its particles spread further apart.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To thin out something, like air, so less of it fills the same space.

examples.text: As the pump rarefies the air in the bell jar, the ringing of the bell inside grows fainter.
Letting the gas expand into a larger tank rarefies it, since the same molecules now fill more space.
Engineers rarefy the air inside the tube so the test pod meets almost no drag as it speeds along.
Exhaust fans rarefy the air in the sealed lab slightly, so that any leak draws air in rather than letting germs out.

distractors.lemma: Vote to accept an agreement that negotiators have already drafted.
Repair an error or injustice once it has come to light.
Mistake a mental label for an object that exists out in the world.
Fork again and again into smaller and smaller offshoots.

senses.definition: Make a style or idea loftier and more delicate, further from the everyday.

mnemonics: Rarefy comes from Latin rarus, thin or scattered, plus facere, to make: to rarefy air is to make it thin.

senses.definition: Balking at commands and pushing back against whoever gives them.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Openly stubborn with anyone who gives you orders.

examples.text: Ordered to clear the sidewalk, the recalcitrant protesters linked arms and sat down where they stood.
The recalcitrant soldier was jailed after he refused, for the third time, to report for guard duty.
Told for the fifth time to sit down, the recalcitrant passenger stayed standing in the aisle and kept shouting at the crew.
Two recalcitrant states refused to hand over their voting records, even after the court ordered them to.

distractors.lemma: Stretched out at rest rather than sitting or standing.
Sparing with words about private matters, even among friends.
Showing up once more each time it seemed gone.
Returned in kind, so that both parties give and receive alike.
Coolly weighing every move by what it will win for oneself.

mnemonics: Recalcitrant comes from Latin recalcitrare, to kick back with the heels (calx, heel): a recalcitrant person kicks back at every order.

senses.definition: Unmanageable and quick to rebel against whoever is in charge.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Fighting back against rules and the people who set them.

examples.text: The refractory crew ignored the captain's orders and steered the ship back toward port on their own.
A refractory group of senators defied the party leaders and blocked every compromise they offered.
Even after three warnings from the referee, the refractory striker kept arguing and was finally sent off.
Medieval kings often stripped the lands of refractory nobles who refused to pay their taxes.

distractors.lemma: Causing light to change course as it moves into the material.
Small to the point of being nearly negligible.
Reaching back to cover what happened before the rule was even made.
Inclined to turn things over in the mind before speaking.

senses.definition: Of an illness, failing to improve with the usual medicines.
Of a nerve or muscle, briefly unable to react again just after firing.
Of a brick or ceramic, fit for lining furnaces because heat barely affects it.

mnemonics: Refractory comes from Latin refringere, to break back, the same root as fracture: a refractory person breaks every rule you set.

senses.definition: Defeat a statement by producing facts it cannot survive.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To prove that a claim is wrong, not just say that it is.

examples.text: A single photo from the archive was enough to refute the senator's claim that he had never met the lobbyist.
Scholars found shipping logs that refute the old story that the captain abandoned his crew.
Simply calling a theory silly does not refute it; you need evidence that shows it is false.
The new tree-ring data refuted the long-held belief that the drought had lasted only two years.

distractors.lemma: Pump fresh gas into a tank that has nearly gone dry.
Hand someone a stern dressing-down for a misstep.
Bring something shabby back to a smart, usable state.
Look back on an event and weigh what it meant.

mnemonics: Refute comes from Latin refutare, to drive back: you refute a claim by driving it back with proof.

senses.definition: Shift someone or something aside into a lesser place where it gets less notice.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To put someone or something on the sidelines, below where it was before.

examples.text: When the new phone came out, the old one was relegated to a kitchen drawer full of tangled chargers.
After the scandal, the senator was relegated to a minor committee that rarely met.
When the square was redesigned, the town relegated the old statue to a corner of the parking lot.
Busy parents often relegate their own health to the bottom of the to-do list.

distractors.lemma: Oversee an activity through rules that keep it within limits.
Hold a table's attention with one lively tale after another.
Ease up on a hard stance and let the other side have its way.
Turn a proposal into law by formal vote.

senses.definition: Hand a matter over to someone else to settle.
Order someone to leave the country and stay away.

mnemonics: Relegate comes from Latin relegare, to send away: when you relegate something, you send it away to a lesser place.

senses.definition: Press objections on someone directly, laying out reasons against what they are doing.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To complain to someone directly and argue that they should change course.

examples.text: Several parents went to remonstrate with the principal about the cancelled field trip, arguing that the students had earned it.
The neighbors went over to remonstrate with the builder, pointing out that his new wall blocked the shared driveway.
Her doctor tried to remonstrate with her about the long night shifts, listing the risks to her heart.
Friends who remonstrated with him over his reckless spending got only a shrug.

distractors.lemma: Walk an audience through a product or method step by step.
Reward someone with a fee or wage for their labor.
Restore a fired worker or official to their old post.
Order a suspect held in custody while the case waits for trial.

mnemonics: Remonstrate comes from Latin re-, again, plus monstrare, to show: you remonstrate by showing someone, point by point, why they are wrong.

senses.definition: A person given over to vice who no longer cares what decent people think.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A person with bad habits and no shame about them.

examples.text: Her grandmother called the charming lodger a reprobate the day he pawned the family silver to pay his bar tab.
The notorious swindler lived out his final years as an unrepentant reprobate.
The novel's hero begins as a reprobate who steals from his own mother and ends as a man worth admiring.
The town gossips dismissed him as a reprobate after he drank away his wages and left his children to beg from the neighbors.

distractors.lemma: A recent hire still in the test months of a new post.
A churchman senior enough to be addressed as Your Grace or Your Eminence.
Someone who has come home from abroad to live in their native land.
A newcomer to a faith or movement, won over from another.

mnemonics: Reprobate comes from Latin reprobare, to reject after testing: a reprobate is someone who failed the test of decent behavior.

senses.definition: Publicly reject an idea, claim, or person and disown any link to it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To reject something completely and say you want nothing to do with it.

examples.text: Late in life, the general repudiated the war he had once led, calling it a mistake built on lies.
The senator was quick to repudiate the endorsement from the extremist group, saying he shared none of its views.
Years after leaving the sect, she publicly repudiated its teachings and now helps other members walk away.
The author publicly repudiated the biography, saying it was full of invented quotes.

distractors.lemma: Arrange for people stranded abroad to go home to their own nation.
Strike back at an attacker with a blow of one's own.
Buy back the good graces of someone you have offended.
Hold forth on a topic at great length, adding point after point.

senses.definition: Refuse to honor a debt or a contract.

mnemonics: Repudiate comes from Latin repudium, a formal divorce: to repudiate a belief is to divorce yourself from it.

senses.definition: Formally take back a ruling or an offer, cancelling its effect.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To officially cancel something, such as a rule or an offer.

examples.text: After the lab tests came back clean, health officials rescinded the boil-water notice for the eastern districts.
The university had to rescind the scholarship offer after discovering an error in the transcripts.
Under pressure from farmers, the senate voted to rescind the trade embargo.
The league rescinded the red card after video replay showed the defender never touched the striker.

distractors.lemma: Pull someone free from a fire, a flood, or other peril.
Nurse a sore feeling toward someone over a past wrong.
Step down from a job or role and hand over its duties.
Make a booming sound that carries and bounces back from walls.

mnemonics: Rescind comes from Latin rescindere, to cut off: rescinding an order cuts it off so it no longer counts.

senses.definition: Saying little, especially about private matters, and keeping one's views in reserve.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Quiet about yourself and slow to share your private thoughts.

examples.text: Despite persistent questioning by the reporters, the author remained notably reticent about her upcoming novel.
He was naturally reticent in large social gatherings, preferring to observe from a quiet corner.
The usually reticent diplomat surprised everyone with a passionate speech at the summit.
Teachers often find it difficult to draw out answers from students who are exceptionally reticent.

distractors.lemma: Feeling remorse for a misdeed and wanting to make amends.
Tough enough to come through hardship and return to normal.
Full of awe and humility before something held sacred.
Openly defiant of those in charge and hard to bring under control.

senses.definition: Cool and formal in manner.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Someone who is reticent acts in a very formal, detached, and emotionally distant way.

examples.text: Her reticent demeanor during the negotiation prevented the other party from gauging her true intentions.
The aristocrat maintained a cool and reticent posture throughout the entire formal banquet.
His reticent response to the compliment left the guests feeling slightly uncomfortable.
She adopted a distinctly reticent approach when dealing with unfamiliar colleagues.

distractors.lemma: Excessively warm and enthusiastic in greeting others.
Lacking proper manners or social etiquette.
Prone to emotional outbursts in public.
Displaying vibrant and colorful personal style.
Quick to form close personal attachments.

senses.definition: Reluctant to draw attention to yourself.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Someone who is reticent tries to avoid being noticed by others.

examples.text: He was a reticent scholar who preferred dusty archives to the spotlight of academic conferences.
Her reticent nature ensured that she slipped out of the crowded party unnoticed.
Despite her immense talent, she remained reticent and rarely sought public applause.
The reticent artist avoided giving interviews about her award-winning paintings.

distractors.lemma: Constantly seeking the center of attention in every room.
Boasting loudly about personal achievements.
Wearing flashy clothes to attract the gaze of passersby.
Demanding immediate praise for minor tasks.
Eager to lead every public demonstration.

mnemonics: Reticent comes from the Latin reticere, "to keep silent", built on tacere, the same root as tacit.

senses.definition: Feeling or showing profound respect or veneration.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Showing deep, quiet respect, as people do in a place of worship or at a memorial.

examples.text: The young chef watched with reverent attention as the old master folded the dumplings, afraid to miss a single movement.
She turned the pages of the medieval manuscript with reverent care, as if each one were sacred.
Out of reverent regard for the villagers' beliefs, the climbers stopped a few steps short of the sacred summit.
Visitors to the war memorial stood with bowed heads, reverent and silent, as the names were read aloud.

distractors.lemma: Connected to the question being asked, and so useful in answering it.
Holding back from speaking up, especially about private matters.
Burning with eager passion for a cause.
Full of regret for past misdeeds and ready to make amends.

mnemonics: Reverent and revere share a Latin root, revereri, to stand in awe: a reverent person reveres what is before them.

senses.definition: Permission from a body that has the power to allow or forbid an action.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: An official yes from the people in charge, letting something go ahead.

examples.text: The archaeologists dug only after winning the sanction of the tribal elders, who chose which graves could be disturbed.
The club could not change its name without the sanction of the league, so the request went to a vote of all twenty owners.
The rebels claimed to act with the sanction of the church, but the bishop denied ever giving it.
With the sanction of her surgeon, the marathon runner went back to training two weeks after the operation.

distractors.lemma: A protected spot that pursuers are not allowed to enter.
The holiness that makes it unthinkable to harm or profane a thing.
Put-on holiness used to look down on other people.
The handling of a community's waste so that it does not spread disease.

senses.definition: An economic or diplomatic penalty aimed at pressuring a state or group to change course.

mnemonics: Sanction comes from Latin sancire, to make sacred or decree: a sanction is a decree, which can approve an act or punish one.

senses.definition: Parading one's own goodness in a preachy way while judging others.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Showing off how good you are and looking down on others for falling short.

examples.text: His sanctimonious lectures on charity annoyed everyone who knew he never gave a dime.
She adopted a sanctimonious tone while judging her neighbors for missing church.
She left sanctimonious notes on the office fridge about wasted food, though half the moldy containers inside were hers.
Instead of offering genuine sympathy, he delivered a sanctimonious sermon on personal responsibility.
Fresh from his first week without meat, he gave a sanctimonious speech about the evils of hamburgers to his neighbors at their barbecue.

distractors.lemma: Guarded from all change by the deep reverence people feel for it.
Inclined to expect the best, with little worry about setbacks.
Delighting in slaughter, or involving heavy loss of life.
Officially allowed, with the blessing of those in charge.
Soured by quarrels in which both sides trade cutting remarks.

mnemonics: Sanctimonious comes from Latin sanctus, 'holy', as in saint and sanctuary: a sanctimonious person puts on a show of holiness.

senses.definition: Grimly amused by the folly of others and quick to sneer at it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Smirking at what you find foolish, with a bite in your words.

examples.text: When the train was canceled for the third time that week, a sardonic voice in the crowd thanked the railway for the free exercise.
Watching the candidate promise lower taxes and more spending in one breath, the old reporter gave a sardonic snort.
Asked how he liked the new open-plan office, he gave a sardonic smile and said he loved being watched all day.
When the boss announced a pizza party instead of raises, Maya gave a sardonic laugh and muttered, "How generous."

distractors.lemma: Concerning the cut and style of the clothes someone wears.
Morally squalid, the kind of thing people hide out of shame.
Sickly sweet in tone, with gushing, sugary sentiment.
Wicked enough to seem the Devil's own work.

mnemonics: Sardonic goes back to a Greek tale of a Sardinian plant whose poison twisted the face into a grim grin: a sardonic smile is bitter, not merry.

senses.definition: Feed an appetite or craving until there is no room left for more.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To completely satisfy a desire or hunger.

examples.text: After three helpings of stew, even the hungriest farmhand was satiated and pushed his bowl away.
No amount of information could ever fully satiate her relentless curiosity.
Six seasons in one week did not satiate her appetite for the show; she started again from the first episode.
Toddlers who graze on crackers all afternoon come to dinner already satiated and refuse their peas.

distractors.lemma: Mock a person or idea by exaggerating its faults for comic effect.
Choose where something will stand and set it there.
Make a surface safe to touch by killing the germs on it.
Have one's mouth water in hungry expectation.

senses.definition: Eat much more than one needs.

mnemonics: Satiate comes from Latin satis, 'enough', the same root as satisfy: once you are satiated, you have had enough.

senses.definition: Habitually gloomy and sullen, with a dark, forbidding look.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Gloomy, moody and quiet, with a grim look.

examples.text: Her saturnine uncle sat silent through the whole dinner, frowning at his plate.
The detective was a saturnine man with heavy brows who rarely smiled and spoke even less.
Even at parties his saturnine face made him look as if he were attending a funeral.
The composer's saturnine moods grew worse during the long, grey winters.

distractors.lemma: Soaked through, so that no more liquid can be taken in.
Twisting this way and that in long, looping curves.
Briny all through, from the salt mixed into it.
Resting with the spine against the ground or a bed, gazing upward.

senses.definition: Bitter or scornful.

mnemonics: Saturnine comes from Saturn: astrologers held that people born under that slow, distant planet were gloomy and sullen.

senses.definition: A scholar whose knowledge runs so deep that others treat them as an authority.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Someone who knows a huge amount, often more than anyone else about their subject.

examples.text: A savant of medieval law, she could quote obscure twelfth-century statutes from memory.
Napoleon brought more than a hundred savants to Egypt to study its ruins, plants and languages.
The old professor was a true savant, as comfortable explaining Sanskrit grammar as quantum theory.
Reporters sought out the economic savant whenever markets crashed, hoping he could explain why.

distractors.lemma: A household worker who answers to the family that employs them.
A person credited with pulling a group or cause back from the brink.
A person whose cruelty knows no limits.
Someone whose goodness was so complete that believers now pray to them.

senses.definition: A person with autism or a brain injury who shows a single astonishing gift, far beyond their other skills.

mnemonics: Savant comes from French savoir, 'to know': a savant is someone who knows a great deal.

senses.definition: Meekly obeying and flattering whoever holds power over one.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Always bowing and saying yes to the people above you, with no pride left.

examples.text: He laughed at every one of the director's jokes, fetched her coffee unasked and agreed before she finished speaking; his servile manner embarrassed the whole team.
Every editorial in the state newspaper praised the dictator in the same servile tone, hailing each decree as an act of genius.
The new intern's servile habit of agreeing with whoever spoke last made it hard to know what she really thought.
Courtiers who had been servile to the old king turned on him the day he lost his throne.

distractors.lemma: Treated so that nothing alive remains on it to infect a wound.
Growing forgetful and muddled in very old age.
Plain yet fit for everyday use.
Peaceful inside and unshaken by trouble.

senses.definition: Belonging to the lowly work or status of an enslaved person or a domestic worker.

mnemonics: Servile shares its Latin root with servant and serve: a servile person serves anyone in power too eagerly.

senses.definition: Able to lull a person toward sleep or heavy drowsiness.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So dull or calming that it makes you want to nap.

examples.text: The slow rocking of the hammock proved soporific, and within minutes the book slid from his chest.
Night-shift nurses avoid heavy meals, which can be soporific at three in the morning.
A warm bath, dim lights and a page of tax law made up her soporific routine, and it never failed to put her out by ten.
The documentary's endless shots of drifting clouds were soporific; by the halfway mark the cinema was full of nodding heads.

distractors.lemma: Full and booming in sound, with a deep ring to it.
Causing the skin to break out in sweat.
Serving to pay tribute to the person it is used for.
Built on clever-sounding reasoning meant to mislead.

mnemonics: Soporific comes from Latin sopor, 'deep sleep', plus -fic, 'making': something soporific makes you sleep.

senses.definition: Fake or unsound, however convincing it may look.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Not what it claims to be; a fake or a mistake dressed up as the real thing.

examples.text: Experts proved the 'lost' Lincoln letter was spurious; its paper had not been made until the 1920s.
The certificate looked official, but it was spurious: the gallery it named had closed ten years before the painting was supposedly bought there.
The ad's claim that the cream was "clinically proven" turned out to be spurious, since no clinic had ever tested it.
The fortune teller's proof of her powers was exposed as spurious when her assistant admitted feeding her the guests' names.

distractors.lemma: Cropping up only now and then, in scattered bursts.
Large inside, with room to stretch out.
Making loans at crushing rates that exploit the borrower.
Stripped of every luxury, by choice or by hardship.

senses.definition: Born out of wedlock.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Born to parents who are not married to each other.

examples.text: In older legal codes, a spurious child faced significant restrictions on inheritance.
The historical record noted the lineage of the spurious heir to the estate.
Parish registers often recorded the baptism of spurious infants with specific notations.
Social customs of the era strictly stigmatized anyone born with a spurious status.
The dominions of both rulers passed away to their spurious or doubtful offspring

distractors.lemma: Lacking proper manners or social etiquette.
Originating from a foreign country or culture.
Exhibiting unusual physical strength or resilience.
Possessing a bright and cheerful disposition.

mnemonics: Spurious comes from Latin spurius, 'illegitimate child': like a false heir, a spurious claim has no true right to what it claims.

senses.definition: Spend something valuable carelessly, so that it is gone with little to show for it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To use up something precious carelessly and have nothing to show for it.

examples.text: The campers squandered their water on splash fights the first week and spent the rest of the trip hauling jugs from town.
She squandered her one question to the famous author by asking where he bought his jacket.
Granted a rare free week in Paris, he squandered it asleep in his hotel room with the curtains shut.
Their grandfather squandered his pension on mail-order cures that did nothing for his knees.

distractors.lemma: Keep up a petty fight over a point too minor to matter.
Peer at something through eyelids pressed nearly shut.
Crush an objection or rumor so thoroughly that nobody raises it again.
Move into a vacant house uninvited and make it a home.

mnemonics: Squander ends in a sound like wander: squandered money wanders off and never comes home.

senses.definition: Respectable and set in long habit, with a steadiness that livelier people find dull.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Calm, proper and fixed in old habits, never up for anything wild or new.

examples.text: Her staid parents, who ate dinner at six and were in bed by nine, never understood her punk band.
Even at the office party the staid accountant kept his tie knotted and sipped only water.
Nobody expected the staid headmaster, who wore a three-piece suit even in July, to arrive at the costume party dressed as a pirate.
Beside her sister, who dyed her hair purple and hitchhiked across Mexico, she seemed staid in her gray cardigan and sensible shoes.

distractors.lemma: Past its prime after sitting out too long, so that it tastes off or crumbles.
Unshakable in allegiance, still backing a side when backing it costs something.
Grimly empty, offering the eye nothing warm to rest on.
Spotted by spills that left their color behind.

mnemonics: Staid began as an old spelling of stayed: a staid person has stayed in the same sober habits for years.

senses.definition: Jarringly harsh in sound, or pushy and combative in the way views are voiced.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So harsh and pushy, in sound or in argument, that it sets people's teeth on edge.

examples.text: Through the thin wall came the strident squeal of a beginner's violin, the same scale over and over.
In the group chat she grew more strident with each message, typing in all capitals and ordering everyone to agree.
The coach's strident pep talk, all shouting and fist-pounding, left the young players more rattled than inspired.

distractors.lemma: Setting a bar so exacting that most attempts fall short of it.
Calling for so much muscle and stamina that only the fit should try it.
Hit hard by some misfortune and still reeling from the blow.
Tense and uneasy, with ill feeling just under the surface.

mnemonics: Strident comes from Latin stridere, to creak or screech: a strident voice screeches at you.

senses.definition: Bring an effort to a standstill by putting something in its way that it cannot get past.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To block someone's progress so that they get stuck.

examples.text: Layers of permits and sign-offs often stymie small inventors who cannot afford lawyers.
The defenders managed to stymie every attack, and the visitors never got a clean shot on goal.
The locked gate stymied the delivery driver, who circled the block three times looking for another way in.
The childproof latch stymied Grandpa for a good ten minutes before a four-year-old opened it for him.

distractors.lemma: Dull someone's wits until they can only sit and gape.
Hold someone up to lasting public dishonor over a trait or past event.
Talk in jerky bursts, catching on certain sounds and saying them several times.
Write a firm requirement into the terms of a deal.

mnemonics: Stymie began as a golf word: your putt was stymied when another ball lay between yours and the hole.

senses.definition: Grand or excellent far beyond the ordinary, enough to stir awe or rapt delight.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Amazingly good or grand, the kind of thing that leaves you lost for words.

examples.text: Standing beneath the roaring falls, soaked in spray, she found the scene sublime rather than merely pretty.
After a week of camp food, the plain bowl of noodles tasted sublime, better than any restaurant meal she could remember.
The goalkeeper's sublime save, a full-stretch dive to tip the ball over the bar, is still replayed on television.
Astronauts often describe the view of Earth from orbit as sublime, a beauty so vast that it makes their own worries seem tiny.

distractors.lemma: Acting on a person from beneath the level of what they consciously notice.
Finely shaded and understated, easy to overlook at a glance.
Free of stiffness in the joints and muscles.
Meek toward those in power and slow to object to their commands.

senses.definition: Worthy of adoration or reverence.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Extremely worthy of deep respect and honor.

examples.text: Generations of scholars have studied the sublime teachings of the ancient philosopher.
She approached the sacred altar with a sense of sublime reverence.
The saintly leader exhibited a sublime dedication to helping the poor.
Historians marveled at the sublime integrity of the whistle blower.

distractors.lemma: Inspiring intense fear and dread in onlookers.
Marked by petty selfishness and greed.
Relating to underground subterranean structures.
Describing a sound that is barely audible.
Pertaining to common everyday tasks.

mnemonics: Sublime comes from Latin sublimis, raised high: sublime things lift you up.

senses.definition: Turn a claim from mere assertion into something proven, by producing evidence for it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To show with proof that what someone claims actually holds up.

examples.text: The hiker said she had reached the summit, and her time-stamped photos of the marker substantiated it.
The reporter held the story until two more sources could substantiate the senator's account.
The insurer would not pay until a mechanic's report substantiated that hail, not the driver, had dented the car.
Neighbors said the factory dumped waste at night, but no one could substantiate it until a teenager filmed the trucks.

distractors.lemma: Use one item where another was meant to go.
Survive on meager resources from week to week.
Hold a conquered people down and deny them any say in their own affairs.
Put the energy of an impulse one cannot act on into something admired instead.

senses.definition: Represent in bodily form.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To give physical form or shape to an abstract idea.

examples.text: The sculptor sought to substantiate his internal grief in marble and stone.
Ancient myths often try to substantiate natural forces as living deities.
The director managed to substantiate complex philosophical themes through compelling characters.
Architects help to substantiate dreams of a new city into concrete blueprints.
The painting substantiates the feelings of the artist

distractors.lemma: Provide factual evidence to support a legal claim.
Dissolve a solid object into a liquid solution.
Erase all traces of a past civilization.
Translate a text from one language into another.
Measure the exact dimensions of a physical object.

mnemonics: Substantiate contains substance: you give a claim substance by backing it with proof.

senses.definition: Added on top of what the job requires, so that leaving it out would lose nothing.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Not needed at all; you could cut it and nobody would miss it.

examples.text: The editor cut every superfluous adjective, and the essay shrank by a third.
With the bill already passed, any further lobbying seemed superfluous.
Once the car had a working GPS, the stack of paper maps in the glove box became superfluous.
A second warning label would be superfluous when the first one is printed in bright red.

distractors.lemma: Skimming the top of a subject and never getting into its depths.
Coolly scornful, acting as though others rank far below oneself.
So excellent that it sits at the very peak of its field.
Rich and soothing to listen to, with every syllable running into the next.

mnemonics: Superfluous comes from Latin super, over, and fluere, to flow: what is superfluous overflows what is needed.

senses.definition: An oversized helping or stock of something, past the point where more is welcome.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So much of something that it stops being a treat and becomes a burden.

examples.text: With a surfeit of zucchini from the garden, she left bags of it on every neighbor's porch.
The town has a surfeit of coffee shops, three on a single block and most of them half empty.
A surfeit of footnotes can bury the one fact a reader actually needs.
A surfeit of meetings left the team with no hours for actual work.

distractors.lemma: A thing given up as the price of breaking a rule or a promise.
A forgery made well enough to slip past a cashier or customs officer.
A settled freedom from doubt about how things stand.
The act of laying down arms and yielding to the other side.

senses.definition: Eating until excessively full.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The act of eating or drinking way too much.

examples.text: His stomach ached after a long evening of festive surfeit.
Medieval feasts often resulted in severe illness caused by sheer surfeit.
The physician blamed his patient's ailments on a chronic surfeit of heavy foods.
Moderation in diet helps prevent the discomforts of sudden surfeit.

distractors.lemma: Surrendering to fatigue during a strenuous hike.
Supporting a heavy weight with structural beams.
Suppressing an appetite through medication.
Surpassing nutritional standards recommended by experts.
Succeeding in a competitive eating contest.

mnemonics: Surfeit comes from Old French surfait, overdone: sur, over, plus fait, done. A surfeit is too much.

senses.definition: Marked by quiet and caution and secrecy; taking pains to avoid being observed.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Sneaky and kept out of sight, so that others will not catch you at it.

examples.text: During the sermon she kept up a surreptitious text conversation, her phone tucked inside the hymnal.
The spies exchanged surreptitious whispers in the crowded railway station.
He made a surreptitious exit from the boring gala through the garden doors.
While his mother's back was turned, the boy slipped a surreptitious second cookie into his pocket.

distractors.lemma: Tiresome because the same points or steps keep coming back again.
Ruled by irrational fears of bad omens and faith in lucky charms.
Dreamlike and bizarre, so that one half expects to wake up.
Sour and grudging in manner, quick to snap at anyone who speaks to them.

mnemonics: Surreptitious comes from Latin surripere, to snatch from under: a surreptitious act is done under cover.

senses.definition: A hanger-on who fawns over powerful people and echoes their views for what it may bring.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A person who acts overly nice to important people just to get ahead.

examples.text: The new intern quickly became a sycophant, praising the director's every tie and fetching her coffee unasked.
Only a sycophant would tell the chef that the burned soup was the best he had ever tasted.
Fresh from her election win, the governor found her inbox full of gushing notes from every sycophant hoping for a job.
Off the field the star player was a sycophant, agreeing with the owner's every opinion even when he reversed it the next day.

distractors.lemma: Someone who treats soft living and indulgence as the whole point of existence.
Someone who expects a hidden selfish reason behind every kind deed.
Someone who claims to read minds or foresee events, often for a paying client.
Someone who dresses up faulty reasoning so that it passes for wisdom.

mnemonics: Sycophant comes from Greek sykophantes, literally fig-shower. Picture a fawning courtier forever showing the king a basket of figs.

senses.definition: Disposed by nature to keep talk to a minimum, even where others would chat.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Saying as few words as possible, by habit, even among friends.

examples.text: On the long drive, her taciturn uncle spoke exactly twice: once to ask for gas money and once to say goodbye.
Being taciturn served the old sheriff well, because suspects often filled his long silences by confessing.
Their taciturn new neighbor had lived next door for a year before anyone learned his first name.
She was taciturn in meetings, rarely saying a word, yet her written reports ran to twenty pages.

distractors.lemma: Gifted at voicing unwelcome truths gently enough that they are heard without resentment.
Sensed by touch rather than by sight or hearing.
Aimed at winning a particular battle or step rather than the whole campaign.
Garish and flimsy at once, enough to make people of taste wince.

mnemonics: Taciturn comes from Latin tacere, to be silent, the same root as tacit.

senses.definition: Bearing on the matter at hand only at its edges, so that following it leaves the real question behind.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Off to the side of the main point and not really about it.

examples.text: The professor's lengthy anecdote about his dog was tangential, and students stopped taking notes.
The witness's answers were so tangential that the judge reminded her the question was about the night of the fire, not her cousin's wedding.
Footnote 14 is tangential to the study; you can skip it without missing anything about the vaccine trial.
Asked about the budget shortfall, the treasurer gave a tangential reply about the town's coat of arms and never mentioned the missing money.

distractors.lemma: Present in solid form, so that it could be held in the hand or set on a scale.
Differing in name only from some other act, since the result comes out the same.
Good only if some other event comes to pass, and void if it does not.
Teasing with a glimpse of a pleasure that never quite arrives.

senses.definition: In geometry, lying along or pointing the same way as a tangent line.

mnemonics: Tangential comes from tangent, a line that touches a circle at one point and heads off; a tangential remark touches the topic and drifts away.

senses.definition: Held up by so little that a light push or a pointed question could bring it down.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Weak and shaky, barely holding together.

examples.text: The museum's claim that the sword belonged to a Viking king rests on a tenuous clue: one smudged letter on the hilt.
The film's tie to the true story is tenuous; apart from the hero's name, almost nothing matches the real events.
Their friendship had grown tenuous, kept alive by one birthday text a year.
The climber kept a tenuous hold on the ledge with two fingers until the rope tightened.

distractors.lemma: So dull and drawn out that every minute seems to drag.
Prone to sudden outbursts, with calm never lasting long.
Written or argued with a built-in slant toward one side of a dispute.
Twisting this way and that, so that it never takes the direct route.

senses.definition: Very thin in gauge or diameter.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Extremely thin in width or diameter.

examples.text: The jeweler worked with tenuous strands of gold wire to create the delicate filigree.
Spider silk is renowned for being exceptionally strong despite its tenuous fibers.
The artisan wove the fabric using tenuous threads of raw silk.
Microscopic cracks appeared along the tenuous beams of the suspension bridge.
A tenuous thread

distractors.lemma: Built with heavy and robust structural timbers.
Wide and expansive in overall surface area.
Shaped into a flat rectangular block of metal.
Coated with a thick layer of protective enamel.
Consisting of multiple braided ropes of hemp.

senses.definition: Of a gas or fluid, spread so thin that it is barely there.

mnemonics: Tenuous comes from Latin tenuis, thin: a tenuous link is a thin thread that could snap.

senses.definition: Stripped down to the fewest words that will do, often with an edge of impatience.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Short and clipped, with no extra words and often no warmth.

examples.text: The coach's halftime speech was terse: "Run harder. Stop fouling." Then he walked out.
Her terse email said only that the proposal was rejected, with no reason given.
Telegrams were terse because senders paid for every word.
The novelist is known for terse sentences that rarely run past a dozen words.

distractors.lemma: Stiff with nerves while waiting for something to go wrong.
Heard so often before that it lands with no effect.
Neither hot nor cold, with just a little warmth left.
Marking the point past which nothing further comes.

mnemonics: Terse comes from Latin tersus, wiped clean: a terse reply has every extra word wiped away.

senses.definition: Looping through needless complications before it finally gets where it is going.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Winding and complicated, so it takes a long time to get through.

examples.text: Her tortuous reasoning ran through six separate "if" clauses before arriving at a simple yes.
The bill took a tortuous path through Congress, rewritten in three committees and stalled twice before it passed.
The novel's tortuous plot, with three narrators and four timelines, left the book club drawing diagrams.
The contract's tortuous wording buried a clause that let the gym keep charging members after they cancelled.

distractors.lemma: Painful enough to feel like a punishment handed out on purpose.
Giving another person grounds to sue for harm done to them.
Turning up by a lucky accident rather than by anyone's design.
Pouring down in great sheets, with no break for hours on end.

senses.definition: Of a road or river, curving back and forth many times along its course.

mnemonics: Tortuous comes from Latin torquere, 'to twist', the root of contort and torque: a tortuous path keeps twisting back on itself.

senses.definition: Giving way readily to direction, so that handling it takes little effort.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Easy to lead and quick to go along with what you want.

examples.text: The new recruits were tractable for the first week, but by the third they were arguing with every order.
Unlike his stubborn older brother, the younger boy was tractable and did whatever his tutors asked.
The dictator wanted a tractable press that would print his speeches without a single question.
Once the fever broke, the toddler was tractable again and let us dress him without a fuss.

distractors.lemma: Leaving enough of a trail that its source can be found.
Possible to take back after it has been said or promised.
Concerned with how things feel, as opposed to how they look or sound.
Worked out for the move in front of you, not the campaign as a whole.

senses.definition: Simple enough to solve or work through with a reasonable amount of effort.

mnemonics: Tractable comes from Latin tractare, 'to handle': a tractable horse is easy to handle.

senses.definition: Sharp enough in criticism to find the weak point at once and lay it bare.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Sharp and direct in a way that goes right to the weak spot.

examples.text: The critic's trenchant review pointed out, in one paragraph, every flaw the author had tried to hide.
In two trenchant sentences, the referee's report showed that the paper's main result rested on a math error.
He expected vague praise, but his mentor gave him trenchant notes that found the exact weakness in his argument.
Orwell's trenchant essays name a political lie and then take it apart line by line.

distractors.lemma: Dug in so deep that rooting it out would take a long fight.
Present for a brief spell and then gone.
Quaking so that a voice catches or a hand will not keep still.
So great in size or force that it dwarfs whatever stands beside it.

senses.definition: Marking a clean, unmistakable line between one thing and another.

mnemonics: Trenchant comes from Old French trenchier, 'to cut', the same source as trench: trenchant remarks cut deep.

senses.definition: Inclined to treat any disagreement as a cue to fight.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Hostile and rough, the sort of person who picks quarrels.

examples.text: The truculent neighbor met every friendly wave with a scowl and a threat to call the police.
After three beers, the truculent fan in row twelve was daring anyone who cheered for the other team to step outside.
The witness was truculent on the stand, snapping at the lawyer and refusing to answer simple questions.
When the referee called the foul, the truculent striker shoved him and demanded a replay.

distractors.lemma: Loyal on the surface but quick to sell out a friend.
Off somewhere else when one should be at a desk or post.
Swallowing any tale, however unlikely, without asking for proof.
Faking papers or claims to get something one is not owed.

mnemonics: Truculent comes from Latin trux, 'fierce': a truculent person is fierce and ready for a fight.

senses.definition: Overblown and self-important in style, so each sentence feels heavier than it should.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Written in a puffed-up, wordy way that is a chore to read.

examples.text: The museum's wall labels were so turgid, wrapping every simple point in academic phrases like "liminal materiality", that visitors walked past them unread.
The wedding toast turned turgid when the best man began quoting Milton and calling the couple "twin celestial orbs".
The court's opinion was turgid, taking four pages of grand clauses to say that the fence could stay.
The senator mocked her rival's turgid oratory, which called a pothole "an infrastructural lacuna of grave consequence".

distractors.lemma: Dwelling on gore or scandal in order to shock the reader.
Burning with a romantic passion that runs hot from the start.
Repeated so often over the years that nothing fresh is left in it.
Lukewarm in feeling, with barely a spark of eagerness.

senses.definition: Of a body part or plant cell, stretched taut from within by built-up pressure.

mnemonics: Turgid comes from Latin turgere, 'to swell': turgid writing is swollen with more words than it needs.

senses.definition: Encountered on every side, so widespread that hardly any place is without it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So common that you see it almost anywhere you go.

examples.text: Within a year of its launch, the cartoon frog was ubiquitous: on lunchboxes, billboards, cereal boxes and pajamas.
Dandelions are ubiquitous in North America, popping up in lawns, sidewalk cracks and highway medians.
In the 1990s the jingle was ubiquitous, playing on every radio station and in every mall.
Plastic is now ubiquitous, turning up in deep-sea fish, Arctic ice and even rainwater.

distractors.lemma: Wicked in a way that wrongs people who cannot defend themselves.
Flattering and submissive toward anyone who might reward it.
Set on a slant, at a tilt to whatever it crosses.
Leaving its meaning in doubt, since the words point two ways at once.

mnemonics: Ubiquitous comes from Latin ubique, 'everywhere': ubiquitous things turn up everywhere you look.

senses.definition: A feeling of anger caused by being offended.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The sore, prickly feeling you get when you think someone has slighted you.

examples.text: The chef took umbrage when a diner asked for ketchup to put on his steak.
Taking umbrage at a joke about his country, the diplomat walked out of the dinner.
There was no need to take umbrage when your sister said your haircut looked a little short.
The novelist took umbrage at being called a "beach-read writer" and cancelled the interview.

distractors.lemma: A tribute paid to a person or work that one admires.
A government's refusal to let goods cross its border to or from a rival nation.
The mood that hangs over a place and greets anyone who walks in.
A wholehearted taking up of a cause, belief or change.

mnemonics: Umbrage comes from Latin umbra, shade, the root of umbrella. Picture someone stalking off into the shade to sulk after a slight.

senses.definition: Swell up and sink back again and again in a smooth, even rhythm.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Move in slow, smooth ups and downs, over and over.

examples.text: As the first big wave passed under the dock, the floating walkway began to undulate beneath our feet.
The eel seemed to undulate through the water, its whole body rippling from head to tail.
When the dancers underneath raised and lowered their poles in turn, the long paper dragon began to undulate down the street.
On the old waterbed, every movement made the mattress undulate for several seconds.

distractors.lemma: Swamp someone with far more than they could ever get through.
Cry out at length in a shrill howl, whether mourning or cheering.
Follow in a role model's footsteps with the aim of catching up to them.
Heap worship on a person as though they could do no wrong.

senses.definition: Curve gently up and down along its length.
Disturb the surface of water so that small ripples spread across it.

mnemonics: Undulate comes from Latin unda, a wave: things that undulate move or curve the way waves do.

senses.definition: Take someone harshly to task for a fault or misdeed.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To tell someone off harshly for a mistake.

examples.text: The coach upbraided the players at halftime, listing every missed tackle in a voice the whole stand could hear.
Grandpa upbraided the boys for leaving the gate open, then sent them across three fields to round up the goats.
The judge upbraided the lawyer for arriving late and unprepared for the third time that week.
Rather than upbraid the nervous intern for the typo, the editor quietly fixed it and explained the rule.

distractors.lemma: Pay extra to go from a basic seat or plan to a better one.
Rule on appeal that a lower court got its decision right.
Make people abandon a settled life and start over somewhere far away.
Wear a surface thin through steady grinding or scraping.
Tip an object over until it rests on its top.

mnemonics: Upbraid is built from up and the Old English verb that also gave us braid. It first meant to bring up a fault against someone.

senses.definition: Assured and gracious among people, with the ease that comes from years spent in cultivated company.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Smooth, worldly and charming with people, never awkward in company.

examples.text: Even when a guest spilled red wine on his rug, the urbane host simply laughed and refilled her glass.
On the late-night show, the urbane novelist traded jokes with the host in three languages without missing a beat.
He envied his urbane roommate, who could chat with a duke or a doorman with the same easy charm and never once looked out of place.
Next to his urbane older brother, who knew every wine list and every head waiter in Paris, Tom felt like a clumsy schoolboy.

distractors.lemma: Located in a built-up city area, among dense streets and tall buildings.
Belonging to the residential districts that ring a city's center.
Careful to spare those in one's power from needless pain.
Ordinary and routine, of the everyday sort that draws no notice.

mnemonics: Urbane comes from Latin urbanus, of the city, like urban. City manners were thought more polished than country ones, so the word came to mean smooth and refined.

senses.definition: Lean one way on a decision, then the other, then back again, without ever committing.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Say yes, then no, then yes again, because you cannot decide.

examples.text: My sister vacillated over the paint color for a month, so the living room wall still has six test patches on it.
The senator vacillated on the bill, praising it on Monday and attacking it by Friday.
Offered the red bike or the blue one, my niece vacillated for twenty minutes, pointing first at one and then at the other.
The referee vacillated, first signaling a goal, then waving it off, then signaling it again, until both benches were shouting.

distractors.lemma: Inject a weakened or harmless form of a germ so the body builds defenses against it.
Move out of a room or home and hand back the keys.
Clear obstacles out of a plan's path so that it can go ahead.
Clear smoke or fumes from a room by keeping air flowing through it.

senses.definition: Tip first to one side and then the other without quite falling over.

mnemonics: Vacillate comes from Latin vacillare, to sway or totter: a person who vacillates sways between choices like a wobbly table.

senses.definition: Lacking any real ideas or spirit, so that it says nothing worth hearing.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Dull and shallow, with no real thought behind it.

examples.text: The pop song's vapid lyrics repeated the same two words over the same four chords.
The dinner guests traded vapid compliments about each other's shoes all night, and nobody said one thing she remembered the next day.
The company's new mission statement was so vapid, promising to "deliver excellence" and "empower people", that the staff made a game of mocking it.
The magazine's vapid advice column told every reader with a problem to simply be themselves.

distractors.lemma: Resting on sound grounds, so that it holds up when someone checks or challenges it.
Burning with keen interest in a pursuit and eager for more of it.
Fast enough that it is over almost before it starts.
Serene and slow to react, with almost nothing able to ruffle it.

senses.definition: Weak and dull to the taste, with no tang left.

mnemonics: Vapid comes from Latin vapidus, used of wine that had gone flat, and is probably related to vapor. Vapid talk has lost its spirit the same way.

senses.definition: Hold a person or thing in awe and show it the kind of honor usually kept for the holy.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Respect someone or something so much that it is close to worship.

examples.text: Pilgrims who venerate the saint walk hundreds of miles to kneel at her tomb.
Collectors venerate the novel's first printing, handling their copies with gloves and speaking of them in near whispers.
Jazz musicians still venerate Louis Armstrong, and his photo hangs on the wall of nearly every club.
Fans in Naples venerate Maradona so deeply that his face is painted on walls across the city.

distractors.lemma: Leave a person limp and sluggish, without the will to move.
Free a suspect from a charge once the evidence points elsewhere.
Turn the motion of wind or water into electric power.
Modernize a run-down building with new wiring, plumbing and floors.

mnemonics: Venerate shares its Latin root with Venus, the goddess: to venerate is to honor something almost as people honored a god.

senses.definition: Truthfulness, whether in a person who does not lie or in a report that matches what really happened.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: How truthful a person is, or how true a story is.

examples.text: The insurance adjuster doubted the veracity of the burglary claim once she found the "stolen" television in the man's own vacation photos.
Hikers doubted the veracity of the guide's claim that the trail took one hour, and they were right: it took four.
Nobody challenged the veracity of the old fisherman's account, since every detail matched the harbor log.
Many courts reject lie-detector results because the machines cannot reliably measure a witness's veracity.

distractors.lemma: An appetite so huge that a person keeps eating long past the point of hunger.
A spirited liveliness that makes a person fun to be around.
A moving object's speed, taken together with its heading.
Savage fierceness in an attack or a fight.

mnemonics: Veracity comes from Latin verus, true, the same root as verify and verdict: veracity is truthfulness.

senses.definition: Stretching a message out with words that add nothing to it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Talking or writing much longer than needed.

examples.text: The verbose memo took four pages to say that the office would close early on Friday.
The app's verbose error message ran to three screens yet never said which button to press.
The lease's verbose clauses, each a paragraph thick with "heretofore" and "notwithstanding", hid one simple rule: pay by the first of the month.
A verbose recipe blog makes you scroll past the author's life story before you reach the list of ingredients.

distractors.lemma: Agreed or delivered by speech alone, with nothing written or signed.
Matching the original wording down to the last word.
Lush with growing things and green all over.
Handy in a wide range of roles rather than only one.

mnemonics: Verbose comes from Latin verbum, word, as in verbal: a verbose speaker hands out words by the bucketful.

senses.definition: Make someone cross, so that the matter keeps nagging at them.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make someone annoyed or fed up.

examples.text: The squeaky office chair vexed Priya so much that she finally oiled it herself during lunch.
Small delays vex him more than big disasters, and a slow elevator can spoil his whole morning.
It vexed her that her brother borrowed her charger every day and never once put it back.
A fly buzzing around his head vexed him through the entire exam.

distractors.lemma: Lay a curse on a person through magic or witchcraft.
Screen a job applicant or nominee for hidden problems before saying yes.
Send a bill back to lawmakers unsigned, refusing to let it become law.
Settle a legal right on someone so that it is fully theirs.

senses.definition: Leave someone stumped, as a hard problem does.

mnemonics: Vex comes from Latin vexare, 'to shake or harass': a vexing habit shakes your calm.

senses.definition: Paint a person or group as wicked through a stream of abuse and smears.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Talk about someone as if they were a villain, to turn others against them.

examples.text: In his memoir, the former coach vilifies his old assistant, blaming him for every loss and hinting that he sold team secrets.
Tudor writers vilified Richard III, giving him a twisted body and a list of murders that many historians now doubt.
Wartime posters vilified the enemy as snarling beasts with blood on their claws.
Family counselors warn divorcing parents not to vilify each other in front of the children, who hear every insult.

distractors.lemma: Confirm a fact by checking it against a trusted source.
Make a dull scene or story spring to life again.
Strip a law or deal of any power to bind anyone.
Ease an upset person's temper with apologies or favors.

mnemonics: Vilify contains vile, from Latin vilis, cheap or worthless: to vilify someone is to paint them as vile.

senses.definition: Show to be right by providing justification or proof.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To prove that a person or idea others doubted was right after all.

examples.text: The chef insisted the old recipe needed no sugar, and the judges' first prize vindicated her stubbornness.
When the market crashed in October, the investors who had sold everything in the spring felt vindicated.
Historians had dismissed the old map as a fake, but tests on its ink vindicated the collector who had defended it.
Mocked for carrying an umbrella on a cloudless morning, Raj felt vindicated when the afternoon storm soaked everyone else.

distractors.lemma: Taint an agreement or argument so that it no longer holds.
Rent out a hit show's reruns to local stations across the country.
Fail to commit, drifting from one option to its rival and back.
Hand over a crown and stop being the ruler.

senses.definition: Insist on a right or claim and argue in its defense.

mnemonics: Vindicate comes from Latin vindex, a champion who stepped forward to defend a claim: when the facts vindicate you, they step forward on your side.

senses.definition: Bursting with spite and hate aimed at a chosen target.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Bitterly hateful and eager to hurt.

examples.text: The two brothers' feud grew so virulent that they hired separate lawyers just to divide their mother's teacups.
The letters to the editor were so virulent, some wishing harm on the mayor's family, that the paper stopped printing them.
The pamphlet spread a virulent hatred of immigrants that later fed riots in three cities.
Her review was so virulent that readers wondered whether she held a personal grudge against the author.

distractors.lemma: Brimming with the vigor of a grown man in his prime.
Living by a strict sense of right and wrong.
Never letting one's guard down against possible threats.
Built out of software, with no physical substance to touch.

senses.definition: Able to make its victims very sick very fast, said of a germ.

mnemonics: Virulent comes from Latin virus, which meant poison or venom: a virulent attack is written to poison its target.

senses.definition: Thick in body, so that it moves sluggishly when tipped or stirred.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Thick and slow to drip or spread.

examples.text: Pancake batter left overnight turns viscous, so add a splash of milk before you pour it.
The new paint was too viscous for the sprayer, which kept clogging until we thinned it with water.
Engineers chose a more viscous oil for the gearbox because thinner oil drained off the hot gears too quickly.
Blood grows more viscous when a person is badly dehydrated, so the heart has to work harder to push it around.

distractors.lemma: Cruel and quick to attack or cause pain.
Springing straight from gut feeling.
Showing a blank mind behind the words or the face.
Tasted only by following what happens to somebody else.

senses.definition: Gluey enough to cling to whatever touches it.

mnemonics: Viscous comes from Latin viscum, mistletoe, whose berries were boiled into a sticky paste for trapping birds.

senses.definition: Ready to flare or swing at any moment, so its calm can never be trusted.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Calm one minute and swinging wildly the next.

examples.text: Oil prices have been so volatile this year that airlines cannot plan their fares more than a month ahead.
His volatile temper meant a joke at breakfast could end with a slammed door by lunch.
The meeting between the landlord and the tenants turned volatile once the new rent figures went up on the screen, and two people walked out.
Spring weather in the mountains is volatile, with sunshine at noon and hail an hour later.

distractors.lemma: Never short of words, and quick to let them spill out.
Offered by someone who was free to say no.
Cut so roomy that it billows around the body.
Lush and indulgent enough to make the body sigh with pleasure.

senses.definition: Quick to turn into vapor when left in open air.

mnemonics: Volatile comes from Latin volare, to fly: a volatile mood or market can fly off in any direction at any moment.

senses.definition: Hungry for huge amounts, and quick to gulp down whatever is on offer.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Wanting a lot of something, like food or books, and taking it in fast.

examples.text: A voracious reader of history, he kept library cards in three different towns.
The voracious caterpillars stripped every leaf from the young tomato plants in two days.
The startup's voracious appetite for cash meant it had to find new investors every six months.
Sharks are voracious hunters that will swallow almost anything that fits in their jaws.

distractors.lemma: Faithful to the facts in everything one says or writes.
Sparkling with cheerful energy whenever other people are around.
Grating on one's patience over and over until it wears thin.
Making one's views known by shouting them for all to hear.

mnemonics: Voracious comes from Latin vorare, to swallow up, the root also found in devour and carnivore.

senses.definition: Shift between options without settling, or let a firm resolve slacken.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To be unable to settle on a choice, or to start doubting one you made.

examples.text: At the paint store he wavered between the gray and the green for so long that the clerk went on break.
Even when the crowd booed, the referee did not waver from his call.
Her support for the plan began to waver once she saw how much it would cost.
The witness began to waver under cross-examination, unsure now whether the car had been blue or black.

distractors.lemma: Let someone off a fee or rule one could have held them to.
Lay down money on how a match or a vote will turn out.
Run a crosswise yarn back and forth to build up a length of cloth.
Flap a hand in the air to say hello or goodbye.

senses.definition: Sway or totter as though about to collapse.
Shimmer or quaver instead of holding steady.

mnemonics: Waver is wave with an r added. Like a flag waving in shifting wind, a wavering mind swings one way and then the other.

senses.definition: Skilled at outfoxing others with ruses and sly maneuvers.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Full of sneaky tricks for staying a step ahead of others.

examples.text: The wily fox doubled back and waded down a stream so the hounds would lose its scent.
The wily prisoner faked a fever, then slipped out the door while the guard went to fetch the doctor.
Only a wily negotiator would pretend to walk away from a deal she badly wanted, just to win a lower price.
The wily old attorney let the witness ramble on until he contradicted his own alibi.

distractors.lemma: Lean, with hard, ropy muscle.
Deaf to advice and contemptuous of rules.
Quick with a funny turn of phrase.
Thin, faint and loosely scattered.

mnemonics: Wily is wile plus -y: a wile is a trick or lure, so a wily person is full of tricks.

senses.definition: Devoted to a cause or task with fierce, tireless energy, sometimes to excess.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Working hard and eagerly for a cause you care about a great deal.

examples.text: The zealous volunteers knocked on every door in the district twice before the election.
The zealous young prosecutor stayed at the office past midnight for months, determined to bring the fraud case to trial.
A zealous new convert, he spent every weekend handing out pamphlets on street corners.
The zealous hall monitor wrote up classmates for arriving even a minute late to lunch.

distractors.lemma: Bitter that a rival has won the luck or reward one wanted.
Grabbing the biggest share and leaving others to make do.
Treating anyone with a foreign accent or passport as a threat.
Staying single and steering clear of all romance and sex.

mnemonics: Zealous means full of zeal, from Greek zelos, ardor. Jealous comes from the same Greek word, which is why the two look so alike.

senses.definition: The crowning stage of a rise, beyond which a career or empire climbs no further.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The top of something's success, before things start to slide.

examples.text: The old mill town was at its zenith in 1910, when its looms ran day and night and its population topped forty thousand.
The bakery reached its zenith the year a food magazine named its croissants the best in the state, and the lines have been shorter ever since.
At the zenith of disco in the late 1970s, it seemed every radio station played nothing else.
Most sprinters reach their zenith in their mid-twenties and spend the following years trying to hold on to it.

distractors.lemma: The circle of star signs that a horoscope is read from.
A light, pleasant breath of wind on a warm day.
A lively delight that a person brings to whatever they take on.
Single-minded, burning commitment to a mission that one will not let go of.

senses.definition: The point overhead where a plumb line, extended upward, would meet the sky.

mnemonics: Zenith comes from Arabic samt ar-ra's, the path over the head: the zenith is the point straight above you, so anything at its zenith can climb no higher.

senses.definition: Advancing by small, unseen steps, so that the harm is done before anyone looks.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Hurting things little by little while staying out of sight.

examples.text: Hearing loss from loud headphones is insidious, since each day's damage is too small to notice.
Inflation can be insidious, shaving a little off a family's savings each year until the retirement plan no longer adds up.
