Small daily shortcuts had an insidious effect on the crew, and by spring no one followed the safety rules at all.
The malware was insidious, copying a few files at a time so the network's alarms never went off.

distractors.lemma: Sure to breed grudges by setting some people above others.
So bland that it leaves no impression at all.
Cheeky and scornful toward those one ought to respect.
Repeating a demand until it is met.

senses.definition: Pleasant to give in to, yet quietly ruinous.
Laid like a snare to catch someone off guard.

mnemonics: Insidious comes from Latin insidiae, an ambush, from sitting in wait: an insidious threat lies hidden until it strikes.

senses.definition: Formally reject or disavow a formerly held belief or allegiance.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To swear off a cause or belief you once held and promise to be done with it.

examples.text: Threatened by the court, the old astronomer agreed to abjure the idea that the earth circles the sun.
New citizens must abjure loyalty to any foreign ruler before they take the oath.
Once the new data came in, the scientist abjured her earlier support for the theory and published a full retraction.
Years after leaving the cult, she publicly abjured its teachings in a book about her escape.

distractors.lemma: Urge someone to act by calling on a higher power as witness.
Commit a crime by giving false evidence on the stand.
Flee out of reach of those one owes or answers to.
Wipe someone's record clean of a sin or a charge.

mnemonics: Abjure comes from Latin ab, away, and jurare, to swear: to abjure a belief is to swear it away.

senses.definition: A public salute to someone's excellence, whether spoken or handed over.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: An award or a public sign of praise for something done well.

examples.text: The rescue dog received an accolade from the city council, along with a year's supply of treats.
The app's design won industry accolades, yet users still complained that they could not find the settings menu.
The chef shrugged off the accolades of food critics and said the real test was whether regulars came back.
Winning the county science fair was the first accolade of a career that would later include a Nobel Prize.

distractors.lemma: A peace deal or treaty that rival sides sign after long talks.
The passing of a crown to its next wearer.
A buildup made of many small additions over a long time.
The jury's word that sends a defendant home free.

senses.definition: The rite in which a monarch dubs someone a knight.

mnemonics: Accolade comes from French accoler, to hug around the neck (Latin ad, to, and collum, neck), from the embrace once given to a new knight.

senses.definition: Stinging and mocking in the way it finds fault.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Saying critical things in a sharp, sour way that hurts.

examples.text: Her acerbic toast at the wedding, which listed the groom's many former girlfriends, left the room in uneasy silence.
The coach's acerbic halftime remarks, such as asking whether his defenders had ever been introduced, stung more than any shouting.
She dropped her acerbic tone when she saw that the intern was close to tears.
Readers loved the editor's acerbic replies to complaint letters, each one a polite but biting put-down.

distractors.lemma: Done at a pace that keeps the breath going hard for a long stretch.
Choosing a bare, comfortless life for the sake of the soul.
Twisting and tumbling through the air with a gymnast's control.
Living mostly in one's head, where thinking outranks feeling.

senses.definition: Tasting tart enough to make the mouth pucker.

mnemonics: Acerbic comes from Latin acerbus, harsh or sour, related to acer, sharp: an acerbic remark has a sharp, sour bite.

senses.definition: Shrewdness shown by keen insight.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The knack of sizing up a situation fast and seeing what will pay off.

examples.text: Her business acumen turned a single food truck into a chain of twelve restaurants within five years.
Investors trusted his financial acumen after he sold every bank stock months before the crash.
The coach lacked the tactical acumen to adjust when the other team switched to a zone defense.
Political acumen told the governor that the bill would pass only if farmers were on board first.

distractors.lemma: The highest level or degree attainable.
A rough and bitter manner.
Exactness in aim, measurement or reporting.
The pursuit of common ground among rival Christian traditions.

senses.definition: A narrow, pointed tip at the end of a leaf or other plant part.

mnemonics: Acumen is a Latin word for a point, from acuere, to sharpen: a person with acumen has a sharp mind.

senses.definition: Quick or skillful or adept in action or thought.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Able to handle tools, people or tricky moments smoothly and well.

examples.text: The adroit negotiator got both unions to sign before either realized how much it had given up.
With a few adroit cuts, the tailor turned the baggy jacket into one that fit perfectly.
The press secretary was adroit at turning hostile questions into a chance to talk about the budget.
An adroit juggler, he kept five flaming torches in the air while chatting with the crowd.

distractors.lemma: Afloat and drifting with no aim or direction.
Impervious to pleas, persuasion, requests, reason.
Having the requisite qualities or resources to meet a task.
Full of strong, eager feeling for a cause or a person.

mnemonics: Adroit comes from French à droit, properly, from droit, right. Droit also names the right side, the hand long tied to skill, as in dexterous.

senses.definition: Showing a relaxed, cheerful courtesy that invites conversation.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Smiling, cheerful and quick to make others feel welcome.

examples.text: The affable landlord always stopped to ask about our kids and remembered every one of their names.
Despite his fame, the actor was affable with fans, chatting and posing for photos after every show.
The hotel put its most affable clerk at the front desk, where every guest would meet him first.
New students found the dean surprisingly affable; she joined them for lunch and laughed at their jokes.

distractors.lemma: So vast or sacred that no words can describe it fully.
Prosperous enough to afford far more than life's basics.
Showy and unnatural, adopted for effect rather than truly felt.
Able to get things wrong now and then, since no person or method is perfect.

mnemonics: Affable comes from Latin affabilis, easy to speak to, from ad, to, and fari, to speak.

senses.definition: Whatever a person or group rejects outright as hateful or forbidden.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A thing you hate so much that you will have nothing to do with it.

examples.text: Raising taxes of any kind was anathema to the party, so the budget relied on cuts alone.
Open-plan offices are anathema to writers who need silence to think.
The idea of retiring was anathema to the eighty-year-old surgeon, who still operated three days a week.
To the purist chef, a bottle of ketchup on the table was anathema, and he banned it from the restaurant.

distractors.lemma: A thing out of step with its time, placed in an era where it does not fit.
Whatever stands at the opposite pole from a given idea or thing.
A loss of feeling, produced by drugs so that surgery causes no pain.
A solemn song, often of a nation, that a crowd sings together on formal occasions.

senses.definition: A formal church curse that casts a person out of the faith.

mnemonics: In Greek, anathema meant an offering set apart for a god; the early church used it for a person cursed and cut off, so an anathema is something cast out.

senses.definition: Free of anything sharp, bold or challenging, and so unlikely to stir any reaction.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So bland and harmless that it bothers no one and excites no one.

examples.text: The company's anodyne statement expressed deep concern but said nothing about who was to blame.
Hoping to offend no one, the best man filled his toast with anodyne remarks about teamwork and the weather.
Critics found the band's new album anodyne, all smooth melodies and none of the anger that made them famous.
Hotel lobbies are hung with anodyne paintings of beaches and flowers that no guest will remember.

distractors.lemma: Without a known name, so others cannot tell who did it or wrote it.
Showing a blend of traits seen as typical of both men and women.
Similar or equivalent in some respects though otherwise dissimilar.
Belonging to a different era from the one it appears in.

senses.definition: Able to ease or dull pain.

mnemonics: Anodyne comes from Greek an, without, and odyne, pain: first a painkiller, and now anything so mild it could not hurt anyone.

senses.definition: Commonly repeated as fact, though probably made up or impossible to trace to a real source.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Passed from person to person as fact, with nothing to back it up.

examples.text: The tale of young George Washington and the cherry tree is apocryphal; a biographer invented it after his death.
Every office has an apocryphal story about an intern who emailed the whole company, though no one can ever name the intern.
Historians treat the quote as apocryphal, since no record of it appears until fifty years after the speech.
The coach's apocryphal claim that he once struck out Babe Ruth fell apart when a reporter checked the dates.

distractors.lemma: Warning of total ruin, or of the world coming to an end.
Claiming beliefs or virtues that one's own conduct does not show.
Not caring at all, even about matters that should stir a person.
So angry that one can hardly speak.

mnemonics: Apocryphal comes from Greek apokryphos, hidden away, the name given to books kept out of the Bible because their origin was in doubt.

senses.definition: A favorable verdict on someone or their work, expressed as approval or praise.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Approval and praise from others.

examples.text: The young cellist glanced at her teacher in the front row, hoping for a nod of approbation.
The developer added a public park to the plan, and only then did it earn the council's approbation.
He craved his father's approbation, but the old man never once told him he had done well.
The novel met with little approbation from critics but still sold millions of copies.

distractors.lemma: A set time in which a new worker or released offender is closely watched for good conduct.
The act of claiming another's property or idea and treating it as one's own.
Firm honesty that holds even when cheating would go unseen.
A label someone or something goes by, often a formal or official one.

mnemonics: Approbation shares its Latin root with approve: probare, to test and find good. Approbation is the approval something earns.

senses.definition: Obscure enough that only a few insiders can follow it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Strange and hard to understand unless you have special knowledge.

examples.text: The arcane rules for salvage claims at sea are known to so few lawyers that clients fly in from abroad to consult them.
The game's arcane scoring system, with bonus points for left-handed throws, baffled every new player.
The tax code is so arcane that even accountants call each other for help with its stranger sections.
Fans traded arcane trivia, such as the jersey number of every backup goalie since 1970.

distractors.lemma: So extremely old as seeming to belong to an earlier period.
Suggesting the calm of an imagined golden age in the countryside.
Lacking sufficient water or rainfall.
Plainly and wholly bad, with no doubt about it.

mnemonics: Arcane comes from Latin arcanus, secret, related to arca, a chest: arcane knowledge is locked away where few can reach it.

senses.definition: Marked by care and persistent effort.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Sticking with a task patiently and doing every part of it with care.

examples.text: Thanks to her assiduous notes from every lecture, the whole study group passed the final.
The museum's assiduous restorers spent four years removing grime from the ceiling, inch by inch.
An assiduous gardener, he checked every tomato plant for pests each morning before work.
After months of assiduous practice, the boy could play the whole sonata without a single mistake.

distractors.lemma: Requiring sitting or little activity.
Disposed to venture or take risks.
Quick to speak up for oneself and press one's case.
Of trees and shrubs, standing bare through the winter months.

mnemonics: Assiduous comes from Latin assidere, to sit down to: an assiduous worker sits down to a task and stays until it is done.

senses.definition: A greedy, endless urge to pile up wealth.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Strong greed for money or things.

examples.text: Driven by avarice, the landlord raised the rent three times in one year while the heat stayed broken.
In the myth, the king's avarice is punished when everything he touches turns to gold, even his food.
The banker's avarice led him to hide losses from clients so that his own bonus would grow.
Scrooge's avarice is so complete that he begrudges his clerk a single extra lump of coal.

distractors.lemma: A deep dislike that makes one want to stay away from something.
A crafty trick, or the skill of devising one.
A statement asserting the existence or the truth of something.
A pursuit that fills spare hours but earns no living.

mnemonics: Avarice comes from Latin avarus, greedy, from avere, to crave: avarice is a craving for wealth that is never satisfied.

senses.definition: Having or showing a ready disposition to fight.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Always itching for a fight or a war.

examples.text: The general's bellicose speech called for an immediate invasion of the neighboring province.
After two drinks he turned bellicose, shoving anyone who bumped into his table.
The prime minister's bellicose threat to sink any ship entering the strait sent oil prices soaring.
Her bellicose letters to the neighbors about a shared fence ended, predictably, in a lawsuit.

distractors.lemma: Offered only once its proper occasion is over.
Left in ignorance and cut off from learning or progress.
Moving with the smooth, controlled grace of trained dance.
Talking down another person's worth or achievements.

mnemonics: Bellicose comes from Latin bellum, 'war', which also gives belligerent and antebellum: a bellicose person is always ready for war.

senses.definition: Lacking or showing a lack of due concern.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Not worried about something that you really should worry about.

examples.text: He drove through the school zone at fifty miles an hour with a blithe smile, as if no child had ever crossed there.
Investors' blithe assumption that house prices could only rise left them unprepared for the crash.
She brushed off the doctor's warnings with a blithe remark that her grandfather had smoked until ninety.
The company answered the data breach with a blithe two-line note telling customers they had nothing to worry about.

distractors.lemma: Slim and flexible in body, with easy, flowing movements.
Mild and dull, with nothing to excite the taste or the mind.
Innocent of any wrong, with nothing to answer for.
Plain for all to see, with no effort made to hide a wrong.

senses.definition: Cheerful and untroubled in spirit.

mnemonics: Blithe meant simply 'joyful' in Old English. A blithe attitude stays happy-go-lucky even when something deserves worry.

senses.definition: Short and sharp with people, without the usual politeness.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Cold and abrupt when talking to people, as if they are a bother.

examples.text: The receptionist's brusque "Sit down and wait" made the nervous patients feel unwelcome.
When I asked a follow-up question, the senator gave a brusque "No comment" and turned his back on me.
His emails were so brusque, often a single word with no greeting, that new staff assumed he was angry with them.
She apologized for her brusque manner during the call, admitting that she had cut her mother off mid-sentence and hung up without a goodbye.

distractors.lemma: Moving or acting at a quick, lively pace.
Sunk in gloomy thought about one's troubles.
Bright and airy in mood, untouched by worry.
Relying on tired, worn-out sayings.

mnemonics: Brusque came into English through French from Italian brusco, 'rough' or 'tart': a brusque reply leaves a tart taste.

senses.definition: Charming and peaceful in the way country life is often pictured.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Calm and pretty, like farms and open fields far from the city.

examples.text: The painting shows a bucolic scene of cows grazing beside a stone bridge over a slow stream.
Tired of traffic and sirens, they traded their city apartment for a bucolic life of orchards, hens and quiet mornings.
The brochure promised a bucolic retreat among meadows, but the farmhouse sat beside a six-lane highway.
Each summer the village festival offers a bucolic afternoon of hayrides, fiddle music and homemade pie.

distractors.lemma: Marked by swollen glands, as in one deadly form of plague.
Swelling out into a fat, round shape.
Pushy and full of oneself in an irritating way.
Queasy in the stomach, or sour and irritable in mood.

senses.definition: Having to do with shepherds or the herding of animals.

mnemonics: Bucolic comes from Greek boukolos, 'herdsman', built on bous, 'ox': a bucolic scene is the herdsman's world of fields and grazing cattle.

senses.definition: Young and inexperienced.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Young and still new to how the world works.

examples.text: As a callow nineteen-year-old, he signed the first lease he was shown without reading a word of it.
The veteran editor had seen many callow reporters arrive convinced that a single story would make them famous.
Looking back at her callow first speeches, the senator winced at how sure she had been about things she barely understood.
The coach worried that such a callow squad, fresh out of high school and untested in big games, would crumble under playoff pressure.

distractors.lemma: Cold toward others' suffering.
Having a dull, yellow-tinged skin tone.
Always plotting quietly for personal advantage.
Giving vague replies so as to hide what one intends.

mnemonics: Callow meant 'bald' in Old English and was later used of young birds that had not grown their feathers. A callow youth has not grown his feathers yet either.

senses.definition: A deliberately misleading fabrication.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A lie about someone or something that gets passed around as if it were true.

examples.text: The old canard that vaccines cause autism has been disproved by study after study.
A rival spread the canard that the bakery reused stale bread, and sales fell for months before the rumor was traced.
The historian traced the canard to a forged letter that a newspaper printed in 1903 without checking.
Fact-checkers labeled the viral claim a canard, noting that the quoted speech was never given.

distractors.lemma: The body of writings that a field treats as its central classics.
A chapter-like part of a book-length poem.
A survey of people's views or voting plans.
A short sung text drawn from Scripture for use in worship.

mnemonics: Canard is French for 'duck'. Picture a duck quacking a made-up story until the whole pond believes it.

senses.definition: Surrender to an opponent, or stop resisting and accept terms one had refused.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To give in and stop fighting or arguing.

examples.text: After a six-week siege with no food left, the garrison capitulated and opened the city gates.
The landlord finally capitulated to the tenants' demands and replaced the broken boiler.
My parents swore they would never get a dog, but they capitulated after a year of begging.
With every train idle and losses mounting, the rail company was forced to capitulate within a week of the strike.

distractors.lemma: Go back over the main points briefly.
Turn a situation into a gain for oneself.
Delight someone so much that they are spellbound.
Tip over and end up upside down in the water.

mnemonics: Capitulate comes from Medieval Latin capitulare, 'to draw up under headings' (caput means 'head'). It first meant to set out the terms of an agreement and later narrowed to agreeing to surrender.

senses.definition: Strong disapproval or blame, often stated formally by an official body.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Strong blame or criticism, often from someone in charge.

examples.text: The senator faced censure from her own party after leaking the committee's private report.
The medical board issued a formal censure against the surgeon for operating without the patient's consent.
Despite public censure of his remarks from fans, players and sponsors, the coach refused to apologize.
A vote of censure is a rare and serious rebuke, though it does not remove the official from office.

distractors.lemma: Official control over what may be printed, shown or broadcast.
A government count of every resident of a country, repeated at set intervals.
Broad agreement reached among the members of a group.
An office that brings income or status while asking for almost no effort.

mnemonics: Censure comes from Latin censere, 'to judge or assess', the job of the Roman censor: a censure is a judgment against someone's conduct.

senses.definition: Holding back out of caution or distrust.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Careful, and slow to trust someone or take a risk.

examples.text: Having been cheated by a business partner once, she was chary of signing anything without a lawyer.
Chary investors pulled their money out of the startup after its third change of chief executive in a year.
The cat stayed chary of the visitors, watching from under the sofa until they had left.
Villagers remained chary of the new well until an inspector confirmed that the water was safe to drink.

distractors.lemma: Full of good spirits and quick to smile.
Quick to fill quiet moments with small talk.
Sexually pure, or free of showy decoration.
Lightly mocking toward people one should respect.

mnemonics: Chary grew from the same Old English root as care: a chary person takes great care before trusting or acting.

senses.definition: A dream or plan so far-fetched that it has no chance of becoming real.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A wild hope or idea that will never come true.

examples.text: The promise of cheap, endless energy from the device proved a chimera that cost investors millions.
For decades a cure for the common cold has remained a chimera, always said to be a few years away.
She stopped chasing the chimera of a flawless house and bought one that was simply good enough.
Perfect security on the internet is a chimera, since every system can eventually be broken into.

distractors.lemma: Sly, dishonest maneuvering meant to cheat or mislead others.
A rare gift for drawing devoted followers.
The instant sense of connection two people can have when they meet.
The sting of embarrassment that follows a failure or a mistake.

mnemonics: In Greek myth the Chimera was a monster made from a lion, a goat and a snake. A hope as impossible as that beast is a chimera.

senses.definition: Heedful of potential consequences.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Careful to think about the risks before you act or speak.

examples.text: Physicians are now more circumspect about recommending the drug, prescribing it only after other treatments fail.
Knowing that every word would be quoted, the spokesperson was circumspect and confirmed only what had already been announced.
A circumspect hiker checks the forecast, tells a friend her route and packs extra water before setting out.
Be circumspect about what you post online, since employers often look before they hire.

distractors.lemma: Held within fixed, narrow limits.
Taking a long, winding route.
Suggestive of a fact but falling short of proving it.
Given to examining one's own feelings.

mnemonics: Circumspect joins Latin circum, 'around' (as in circle), and specere, 'to look' (as in inspect): a circumspect person looks all around before acting.

senses.definition: Conducted with or marked by hidden aims or methods.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Done in secret, out of sight of anyone who might stop it.

examples.text: Forbidden to see each other, the couple arranged clandestine meetings in the back room of the library.
Agents ran a clandestine operation to smuggle the defector out of the country under a false name.
During Prohibition, clandestine bars hid behind barbershops and laundries, admitting only those who knew the password.
Police uncovered a clandestine lab in the basement, where the drug had been made for months without the neighbors' knowledge.

distractors.lemma: Sticking closely to one's own group and keeping outsiders away.
Full of loud shouting and noisy demands.
Mild in weather, or merciful in judgment.
Said to perceive what lies ahead through some sixth sense.

mnemonics: Clandestine comes from Latin clam, 'secretly': a clandestine plan is one that is kept out of sight.

senses.definition: Treat separate things or ideas as one, often blurring an important difference.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To blur two ideas together so the difference between them gets lost.

examples.text: Students often conflate weather with climate, citing one cold week as proof that the planet is not warming.
The article conflates correlation with causation, assuming that because two trends rose together, one must have caused the other.
Don't conflate being busy with being productive; a full calendar can still get nothing done.
Early biographers conflated two men with the same name, so the book credits one with the other's inventions.

distractors.lemma: Swell something by pumping it full of air.
Gather loose pages and stack them so each copy runs from first page to last.
Unburden oneself by sharing private worries with someone close.
Show with evidence that a claim or its maker is mistaken.

mnemonics: Conflate comes from Latin conflare, 'to blow together', which was used for fusing metals in a fire: to conflate two ideas is to fuse them into one lump.

senses.definition: Dismay so sudden that it leaves people unsure what to think or do.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The upset, confused feeling of being caught off guard by bad news.

examples.text: To the consternation of the wedding guests, the groom never arrived at the church.
News that the bridge would close for a year caused consternation among commuters who had no other way into the city.
There was consternation in the control room when every screen went dark at once.
Her parents listened in consternation as she announced she was leaving law school a month before graduation.

distractors.lemma: Heartfelt sadness at having done wrong, joined by a resolve to put it right.
The act of turning a matter over in one's mind at length, without hurry.
A manner that treats other people as less important or less clever than oneself.
Something that makes a loss or a letdown easier to bear.
A ceremony that makes a place or object holy and sets it apart for worship.

mnemonics: Consternation has stern in the middle: picture a stern boss's sudden frown throwing the whole office into alarmed confusion.

senses.definition: Deserving blame or censure as being wrong or evil or injurious.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: At fault for something bad, so that blaming you is fair.

examples.text: The inquiry found the airline culpable for the crash because it had skipped required engine checks.
A driver who knowingly texts at the wheel is more culpable than one who skids on a patch of black ice.
Nobody on the committee wanted to look culpable, so each member blamed the others for the budget mess.
The court held the landlord culpable for ignoring years of complaints about the broken smoke alarms.

distractors.lemma: Good enough at a task to handle it well.
Felt so clearly in a room that nobody can deny it is there.
Belonging to the art and trade of the cook.
Nice to eat, or mild enough that people can go along with it.

mnemonics: Culpable comes from Latin culpa, fault, as in mea culpa (my fault): a culpable person is the one at fault.

senses.definition: Extreme greed for material wealth.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Wanting more and more money and things, no matter how much you already have.

examples.text: Never satisfied with his millions, the tycoon let his cupidity push him into one shady deal after another.
Driven by cupidity, the heir began selling his grandmother's silver before she had even moved out.
The novel's villain is a banker whose cupidity grows with every fortune he squeezes out of his clients.
Each new tax break for the rich only fed the cupidity of men who already owned more than they could ever spend.

distractors.lemma: Foolishness that comes from failing to think things through.
The urge to poke into, ask about and explore whatever is new or hidden.
How finely the eyes, ears or mind can pick out detail.
The know-how and means to carry out a given task.

mnemonics: Cupidity comes from Latin cupere, to desire, the root of Cupid's name, but this desire is for money rather than love.

senses.definition: Raise one's voice in public against something, branding it a wrong.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Say loudly and in public that something is bad.

examples.text: Doctors have long decried the sugary drinks sold in school vending machines.
Critics decried the new tower as an ugly glass box that ruined the city's skyline.
Fishermen decried the new quotas at a noisy meeting on the docks, saying the limits would put them out of work.
At every rally, union leaders decry the pay gap between managers and workers as an insult to the people who do the work.

distractors.lemma: Manage to spot something far off or faint.
Settle a matter by an official order that others must obey.
Unscramble a coded message to reveal what it says.
Slowly spoil and fall apart as time passes.

mnemonics: Decry comes through French from crier, to cry out: to decry something is to cry it down in public.

senses.definition: Hold back from going along with a request, giving polite reasons why not.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Pause and politely push back when asked to do or accept something.

examples.text: Asked to cut the last chapter, many authors would demur, insisting the story makes no sense without it.
He always offers to pay for dinner, and she always demurs for a moment before letting him.
When a seller names a sky-high price, a careful buyer will demur and ask to see the accounts first.
The retired judge has been asked to run for mayor many times, but she always demurs, saying she has no taste for campaigning.

distractors.lemma: Take away someone's rank and put them in a less senior post.
Strip someone of dignity or of the respect of others.
Cast an opponent as a villain so that hatred of them feels justified.
Set the boundary between two pieces of land or two fields of work.

mnemonics: Demur comes from Latin demorari, to linger or delay: someone who demurs holds back before saying yes.

senses.definition: Describe someone or something as worthless or bad, usually unfairly.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Put down a person or thing by saying they are no good.

examples.text: Instead of debating her ideas, his campaign ads denigrated her, calling her a lightweight who had never held a real job.
Some older musicians denigrate hip-hop, claiming it takes no talent to make.
Fans of the old team still denigrate the new coach, mocking his record at every game.
The memoir denigrates her former business partner at every turn, painting him as lazy and dishonest.

distractors.lemma: Spread a manager's workload among the staff below.
Lose soundness bit by bit through age, wear or neglect.
Wipe out the effect of an action or result.
Give up living in one's native land and make a permanent home abroad.

mnemonics: Denigrate comes from Latin denigrare, to blacken: to denigrate people is to try to blacken their name.

senses.definition: Express strong disapproval of; deplore.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Say plainly that you strongly dislike or object to something.

examples.text: The report deprecates the practice of hiring relatives, though it stops short of banning it.
Most style guides deprecate long strings of nouns, which make sentences hard to follow.
The bishop deprecated the decision to hold the festival on a Sunday morning, calling it thoughtless.
Teachers' groups have long deprecated phones in classrooms, warning that the constant alerts ruin concentration.

distractors.lemma: Fetch a lower price than before, through age or wear.
Spoil a sacred site through vandalism, theft or misuse.
Push a pedal, key or button downward.
Name a building, book or song in honor of someone.

senses.definition: Mark a software feature as outdated and likely to be removed in a later version.

mnemonics: Deprecate comes from Latin deprecari, to pray against: you deprecate what you would like to see go away.

senses.definition: An amateur who engages in an activity without serious intentions and who pretends to have knowledge.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Someone who dabbles in a subject for fun but never learns it deeply.

examples.text: The full-time painters in the colony regarded him as a mere dilettante, since he turned up only on sunny weekends.
She was no dilettante: she had studied wine for twenty years and could name a vineyard from a single sip.
The hiring panel worried that a dilettante who had tried six careers in ten years would not stay long.
He reads a chapter of philosophy here and a page of physics there, a dilettante who never finishes anything.

distractors.lemma: A teenage girl for whom a formal ball is held to launch her into elite social life.
A member of the team that a union or party sends to a conference.
A person who is one of the sides in a court case.
A minor with a record of petty crimes.

mnemonics: Dilettante comes from Italian dilettare, to delight: a dilettante studies a subject for the delight of it, not to master it.

senses.definition: Cause to lose one's composure.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Make someone feel awkward and flustered so they lose their calm.

examples.text: The senator was visibly discomfited, shifting in his seat and stammering, when the reporter read his old statements back to him.
Her steady stare discomfited the job candidate, who began to stumble over his answers.
Good comedians are not discomfited by hecklers; they simply turn the interruption into a joke.
The surprise question discomfited the usually smooth speaker, who lost his place and fumbled with his notes.

distractors.lemma: Set aside a rumor or warning instead of acting on it.
Expose a witness, theory or source as unreliable.
Come upon a fact or place that was unknown until then.
Let others in on something that had been kept secret.

mnemonics: Discomfit sounds like discomfort, though the roots differ: to discomfit someone is to leave them flustered and ill at ease.

senses.definition: Not straightforward or candid; giving a false appearance of frankness.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Putting on a show of honesty to cover up the truth.

examples.text: The company's claim that the price rise was meant to help customers was disingenuous; its own emails showed it was about profit.
The minister's claim that she had never heard of the report was disingenuous, since her initials were on the cover.
Her friends called his excuse disingenuous, since he had posted the photo precisely to embarrass her.
Claiming you were only asking questions is disingenuous when the questions were meant to spread a rumor.

distractors.lemma: Inventive and quick to find new answers to hard problems.
Neutral because one has nothing to gain or lose either way.
First found in a region and never introduced there by outsiders.
Lacking any wish to do something.

mnemonics: Disingenuous is dis- (not) plus ingenuous (innocent and open): a disingenuous person only plays at being innocent.

senses.definition: Given over to drink, sex, gambling and other vices, with no moral restraint.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Living a wild, careless life of parties and bad habits.

examples.text: After inheriting his father's fortune, he wasted a dissolute decade in casinos and nightclubs and came home with nothing.
The film's hero is a dissolute prince who sleeps until noon and spends his nights in gaming houses.
Her parents blamed his dissolute friends for the nights he came home drunk at dawn.
Years of dissolute living, with endless parties and heavy drinking, had ruined the once-famous actor's health.

distractors.lemma: Sunk in grief that no kind word can lift.
Abandoned and bleak, the sort of place few would choose to visit.
Unshaken in one's aims and hard to talk out of a decision.
Left with no money or means of support, and dependent on charity.

mnemonics: Dissolute comes from Latin dissolutus, loosened: a dissolute person's morals have come loose.

senses.definition: Deliberate deceit in which a person says one thing and secretly does another.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Fooling people by pretending to be on their side while working against them.

examples.text: The double agent's duplicity went unnoticed for years, as she swore loyalty to one government while reporting to another.
Tenants were stunned by the duplicity of a landlord who promised their homes were safe while secretly selling the building.
Her partner had smiled through every meeting while keeping a second set of books, and his duplicity cost her the business.
The play's villain charms everyone to his face while plotting against them, and the audience sees his duplicity long before the other characters do.

distractors.lemma: Needless overlap, with the same task or record made twice.
The state of being many and of many different kinds.
The shared guilt of someone who helped others do wrong or quietly let it happen.
Coverage in the news that makes the public aware of someone or something.

mnemonics: Duplicity comes from Latin duplex, double: a person of duplicity wears a double face, one honest and one false.

senses.definition: Conspicuously and outrageously bad or reprehensible.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So bad that it seems hard to believe or excuse.

examples.text: The referee made an egregious call, awarding a goal even though replays showed the ball never crossed the line.
Charging a sick patient four hundred dollars for a box of tissues is an egregious case of hospital overbilling.
The report lists dozens of safety lapses, the most egregious being a fire exit that had been chained shut.
Even by the standards of the tabloids, printing the grieving family's home address was egregious.

distractors.lemma: Restless when alone and at ease in a crowd.
Taken up with oneself and keen to boast about one's own worth.
Opposed to ranking people by birth, wealth or class.
Lovely enough to make people stop and stare.

mnemonics: Egregious comes from Latin e- (out of) and grex (flock): an egregious error stands out from the herd.

senses.definition: Steady calm of mind that holds firm under stress or hardship.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The ability to keep a cool, steady head when things go badly.

examples.text: When the bank turned down her loan, she simply folded the letter and started on a new plan, with an equanimity her partners envied.
After forty years at sea, the old captain met every squall with the same equanimity.
The coach asked his young players to accept bad calls with equanimity instead of shouting at the referee.
Years of meditation gave him an equanimity that even a canceled flight and a lost suitcase could not shake.

distractors.lemma: Bigness of heart that lets a person give freely and hold no grudges.
Agreement so complete that no one in the group objects.
Lasting ill will that one person or group holds against another.
A timid, small-spirited habit of backing down whenever courage is called for.
Talk that keeps two meanings open so the speaker can never be pinned down.

mnemonics: Equanimity joins Latin aequus, 'even' (as in equal), and animus, 'mind': an even mind that stays level under pressure.

senses.definition: Avoid something by deliberate choice, often on principle.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To stay away from something by choice, and to stick with that choice.

examples.text: The author eschews adverbs, believing that strong verbs do the work better.
Many monks eschew meat entirely, living on rice, beans and vegetables.
The new mayor promised to eschew the backroom deals that had disgraced her predecessor.
Although he could afford a driver, he eschewed such luxuries and took the bus to work.

distractors.lemma: Hand out or publish something on behalf of an authority.
Look up to someone and think well of them.
Climb by stages to a higher or fiercer level.
Go along with someone to guide, guard or keep them company.
Distort information so that it gives a slanted or unfair picture.

mnemonics: Eschew comes from an Old French word related to English shy: when you eschew something, you shy away from it on purpose.

senses.definition: Call on someone, with earnest and impassioned words, to do something.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To push someone hard, with serious words, to do something.

examples.text: The coach exhorted his exhausted players to give everything they had in the final quarter.
In her farewell sermon, the minister exhorted the congregation to forgive their enemies.
Posters across the city exhort residents to save water during the drought.
His doctor had exhorted him for years to quit smoking, and he finally listened.

distractors.lemma: Bring a buried coffin back to the surface, often for a fresh autopsy.
Breathe out, emptying air from the chest.
Rid a haunted house or a possessed person of a demon through ritual.
Fire back a quick, cutting reply to something someone said.

mnemonics: Exhort comes from Latin hortari, 'to urge', the root also found in hortatory: to exhort is to urge someone hard.

senses.definition: Clear the guilt of a wrong or sin by paying a penalty or making up for it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To pay for a wrong you did, by suffering or by doing good.

examples.text: He spent ten years volunteering at the shelter, trying to expiate the drunk-driving crash that had killed a neighbor.
In the legend, the knight walks barefoot to Rome to expiate his betrayal of the king.
No apology could expiate the company's decades of dumping waste into the river, the judge said.
Each spring the villagers sacrificed a goat, hoping to expiate whatever wrongs had brought on the drought.

distractors.lemma: Go on at length about a subject in speech or writing.
Speed up a task or process so it finishes sooner.
Stop being valid when its time limit runs out.
Seize land or goods from their owner by official order.
Wipe something out completely, down to its roots.

mnemonics: Expiate shares a root with pious: Latin piare, 'to make holy or appease'. To expiate a sin is to make yourself clean of it again.

senses.definition: Very particular about detail, neatness or cleanliness, and hard to satisfy.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very fussy about getting every detail right or keeping things clean.

examples.text: A fastidious editor, she once held up a book's release to fix a single misplaced comma.
He was so fastidious about his kitchen that he wiped the counter after cutting each slice of bread.
The fastidious cat refused to eat from any bowl that had been rinsed but not scrubbed.
Even on camping trips, my fastidious uncle ironed his shirts and folded his socks in pairs.

distractors.lemma: Prone to flippant wisecracks when a straight answer is called for.
So empty-headed that it borders on the idiotic.
Always ready to bicker, rebel or throw a tantrum.
Wearisome because it drags on and never varies.

senses.definition: In biology, needing special nutrients or conditions in order to grow, as some bacteria do.

mnemonics: Fastidious comes from Latin fastidium, 'disgust': a fastidious person is put off by the smallest smudge or mistake.

senses.definition: Weak-willed and ineffective, without the drive to handle tasks or responsibilities.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Lazy and unreliable, unable to get useful things done.

examples.text: Her feckless brother borrowed money every month and never once looked for a job.
The feckless committee met for two years without producing a single recommendation.
Residents blamed feckless city officials, who let the snow pile up for a week before sending out plows.
He was charming but feckless, forgetting his rent, his bills and even his own birthday party.

distractors.lemma: Rushing into danger with no thought for what might go wrong.
Changing loyalties or opinions often and without warning.
Showing no sign of being afraid, even in danger.
Living wild, though descended from tame animals.
Uneasy and fidgety, often whining or unable to settle.

mnemonics: Feckless comes from Scots feck, a shortened form of effect: a feckless person is without effect and gets nothing done.

senses.definition: Very fertile, with a great capacity to breed or to grow plants.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Bursting with life, so that it breeds or grows a great deal.

examples.text: The fecund river delta has fed farming villages for thousands of years.
Rabbits are famously fecund, and a single pair can produce dozens of young in a year.
Each fecund salmon lays thousands of eggs, so the river teems with young fish every spring.
Farmers prized the fecund black soil of the valley, where almost anything they planted grew.

distractors.lemma: Merry and full of good cheer.
Red-cheeked and ruddy in the face.
Stinking of rot or decay.
Without the backbone to take charge of one's own life.

senses.definition: Rich in new ideas and creative work.

mnemonics: Fecund shares its Latin start, fe-, with fetus: fecund herds and fields keep bringing forth new life.

senses.definition: Heavily decorated, especially with showy and elaborate language.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Full of too many fancy details, especially in writing or speech.

examples.text: The senator's florid speech, packed with quotations and grand metaphors, lasted an hour and said almost nothing.
Her editor cut the florid descriptions of sunsets, leaving short and simple sentences.
The architect stripped the old bank's florid facade of its gilded scrolls, cherubs and carved trumpets.
Victorian love letters often sound florid to modern readers, full of sighs, vows and lavish compliments.

distractors.lemma: Relating to flowers or showing a flower pattern.
Flowing smoothly and easily, without stops or awkward breaks.
Droopy and slack where it should be firm.
Going from strength to strength, with steady growth and success.
Giving off a glow while ultraviolet or other rays strike it.

senses.definition: Of a person's face, pink or red, as from drink or poor health.

mnemonics: Florid comes from Latin floridus, 'covered in flowers': florid prose is so flowery that the meaning gets lost in the blooms.

senses.definition: A harmless quirk in someone's personality that friends learn to live with.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A little fault in a person that is easy to put up with.

examples.text: Her habit of humming while she typed was a foible her coworkers came to find charming.
The biography is honest about the president's foibles, from his vanity about his hair to his love of bad puns.
Grandpa's one foible was telling the same fishing story at every holiday dinner.
Good comedies poke gentle fun at human foibles such as vanity, nosiness and stubbornness.

distractors.lemma: A short invented story, often about talking beasts, that ends with a moral.
A character whose contrasting traits make another character's qualities stand out.
The choice to let an offense pass when one has every right to respond.
A pretend attack meant to draw an opponent's guard away.

senses.definition: In fencing, the outer half of a blade, nearer the tip and easier to deflect.

mnemonics: Foible comes from an old French word for weak, the same word that gave us feeble: a foible is a small weak spot in someone's character.

senses.definition: Say flatly that a claim is wrong, or argue against it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To argue that a claim is false.

examples.text: No one could gainsay her results, since three other labs had repeated them.
The general was brave, but few historians would gainsay that his strategy failed.
Several witnesses tried to gainsay the officer's account, but the dashboard camera backed him up.
The data were so clear that even the drug company's own scientists could not gainsay the link to heart damage.

distractors.lemma: Run tests on ore or metal to find out what it contains.
Make a first, tentative try at a task.
Add to what one already has, whether weight, speed or money.
Read off a size, level or pressure, or make a careful estimate of one.

mnemonics: Gainsay is built from an old prefix gain-, 'against' (as in against), plus say: to gainsay is to say against.

senses.definition: So bright, loud or flashy that it looks cheap and lacks taste.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Too bright or flashy, in a way that looks cheap.

examples.text: The diner's garish neon sign, flashing pink and green, could be seen from a mile away.
She painted over the garish orange walls with a soft gray as soon as she moved in.
His garish suit, purple with gold buttons, drew stares at the quiet funeral.
The once-elegant hotel lobby now had garish plastic palm trees and a blinking slot machine in every corner.

distractors.lemma: Inclined to talk so much that no one else can get a word in.
Mixed up and confusing, so the message is hard to follow.
Lanky and ungainly, with limbs that seem hard to manage.
So vast that ordinary measures seem tiny beside it.
Holding back one's real thoughts, wary of saying too much.

mnemonics: Garish sounds a bit like glare: garish colors glare at you, bright and cheap.

senses.definition: Bearing directly on the topic at hand and therefore worth considering.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Closely connected to what is being discussed.

examples.text: The judge struck the question about old parking tickets, saying it was not germane to a robbery trial.
Please keep your questions germane, since we have only ten minutes to discuss the budget.
Her years as a nurse were germane to her new job writing health policy.
He kept bringing up his vacation, a story hardly germane to a meeting about software bugs.

distractors.lemma: At a very early phase, holding the seeds of what comes later.
Able to kill bacteria and other harmful microbes.
Gentle and merciful, careful not to cause needless suffering.
Real rather than copied or pretended.
Concerned with old people and the treatment of their illnesses.

mnemonics: Germane comes from Latin germanus, 'having the same parents': a germane point is closely related to the topic, like a brother or sister.

senses.definition: Puffed up and lofty in style, using words far grander than the subject calls for.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Showing off with big, fancy words.

examples.text: The mayor's grandiloquent speech compared a new parking garage to the pyramids of Egypt.
Students often turn grandiloquent in essays, writing 'utilize the aforementioned methodology' instead of 'use this method'.
The grandiloquent waiter called the soup 'a symphony of autumn's harvest' before admitting it was just carrot.
Stripped of its grandiloquent phrases, the letter simply said the company was cutting jobs.

distractors.lemma: Moving and persuasive in the way one speaks or writes.
Fond of talking and hard to stop once started.
Made up of small grains or particles.
Brought on by an earlier event or decision, as its outcome.

mnemonics: Grandiloquent joins Latin grandis, 'great', and loqui, 'to speak' (as in eloquent): grandiloquent people speak in grand, puffed-up words.

senses.definition: Uncalled for, with nothing in the situation to justify it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Not needed or asked for, and often unkind or over the top.

examples.text: The film's gratuitous violence added nothing to the story and drove many viewers out of the theater.
She had already won the argument, so her gratuitous jab at his haircut only made her look petty.
Nobody had asked about his salary, and his gratuitous mention of it at dinner struck everyone as bragging.
The editor cut every gratuitous adjective, keeping only the words each sentence truly needed.

distractors.lemma: Courteous and generous in manner, even toward those one has no need to impress.
Wanting to repay a kindness, or at least to say thank you for it.
Satisfying to see or learn, because it rewards one's hopes or effort.
Coming about by accident, and usually turning out well.

senses.definition: Provided free, with nothing asked in return.

mnemonics: Gratuitous shares its Latin root with gratis, 'free': a gratuitous remark is thrown in for free, though nobody wanted it.

senses.definition: Something that precedes and indicates the approach of something or someone.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A first hint that some event or change is on the way.

examples.text: The first robins hopping across the frozen lawn are a cheerful harbinger of spring.
Economists read the sudden fall in factory orders as a harbinger of the recession that arrived a year later.
That scratchy throat turned out to be the harbinger of a flu that kept her in bed for a week.
In the old ballad, a raven tapping at the window is a harbinger of death in the house.

distractors.lemma: A stretch of sheltered water where boats can tie up safely.
A long, loud speech that lectures or scolds its listeners.
A merchant whose shop sells men's suits, shirts and hats.
A masked clown of old Italian comedy, dressed in a costume of colored diamonds.

mnemonics: Harbinger once named an officer who rode ahead of a royal party to arrange its lodgings. A harbinger still goes before what is coming.

senses.definition: Pride and overconfidence so great that a person ignores limits and risks, often bringing about their own fall.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being so proud and sure of yourself that you take foolish risks.

examples.text: It was pure hubris to plan the victory party before a single vote had been counted.
The company's hubris led it to laugh off its small rivals until they had taken half its customers.
In the myth, Icarus's hubris carries him so close to the sun that the wax in his wings melts.
After three easy championships, the coach admitted that hubris had made his players stop training hard.

distractors.lemma: The confused din of many voices and much activity at once.
Pretense and empty talk meant to fool people.
A mix produced by crossing one breed, design or kind with another.
A list of criteria used to score or grade a piece of work.

mnemonics: Hubris is the Greek hybris, 'outrageous insolence'. In Greek tragedy it is the pride that makes a hero defy the gods, and it always ends in a fall.

senses.definition: A behavioral attribute that is distinctive and peculiar to an individual.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A strange little habit that is typical of one particular person.

examples.text: One of the professor's idiosyncrasies was lecturing to the chalkboard with his back to the class.
Her habit of eating dessert before dinner is an idiosyncrasy her friends stopped remarking on years ago.
The biographer listed the poet's idiosyncrasies: green ink, no chairs in the study and a tortoise named Horace.
A good actor studies the small idiosyncrasies of a real person, such as how he blinks or holds a cup.

distractors.lemma: A fixed phrase that means something other than what its words say one by one.
Great foolishness, or an act that shows it.
The shared body of beliefs behind a political movement or way of governing.
A stretch of untroubled bliss in a simple, unspoiled setting.

mnemonics: Idiosyncrasy joins Greek idios, 'one's own' (as in idiom), with krasis, 'a mixing': a person's own particular mix of habits.

senses.definition: Bringing disgrace and a loss of respect, especially through a humiliating failure.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So embarrassing that it makes people lose respect for you.

examples.text: After promising a landslide, the senator suffered an ignominious defeat, losing even his home county.
The champion's reign came to an ignominious end when she was caught using a banned drug.
The army made an ignominious retreat, leaving its flags and supplies behind in the mud.
After a rat was filmed in its kitchen, health inspectors shut the famous restaurant, an ignominious end to fifty years of business.

distractors.lemma: Warning, by its look or feel, of trouble to come.
Knowing little, either in general or about a given matter.
Made of rock that was once molten and then turned solid.
Inventive, with a knack for clever solutions.

mnemonics: Ignominious holds Latin nomen, 'name' (as in nominate): an ignominious act costs you your good name.

senses.definition: Characterized by undue haste and lack of thought or deliberation.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Acting fast on a sudden feeling, without stopping to think first.

examples.text: In an impetuous moment, he proposed on their second date, then spent a week wondering what he had done.
The general's impetuous charge, launched before the scouts returned, ran straight into the enemy's cannons.
She regretted the impetuous email she had fired off to her boss at midnight.
Teenagers are often called impetuous, but the study found that adults made just as many snap decisions.

distractors.lemma: Commanding in a proud manner that leaves no room for argument.
Sealed so that no liquid or gas can get through it.
Irreverent toward religion and what believers hold sacred.
Short of money and often unable to pay one's way.

senses.definition: Marked by violent force.

examples.text: Impetuous heaving waves

mnemonics: Impetuous comes from Latin impetus, 'a rush or attack': an impetuous person rushes ahead before thinking.

senses.definition: Beg persistently and urgently.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Keep asking someone for something in a pushy, tiresome way.

examples.text: Street vendors importuned every tourist who stepped off the ferry, waving postcards and refusing to take no for an answer.
She had importuned the city council for months before it finally repaired the broken streetlight.
Too proud to importune his wealthy uncle for a loan, he took a second job instead.
Fans importuned the actor for autographs all the way from the stage door to his car.

distractors.lemma: Bring in goods from another country to be sold or used locally.
Attack a person's motives or a statement as false or dishonest.
Lay the blame or credit for something on a particular person or cause.
Take a car, animal or goods into official custody until a matter is settled.

mnemonics: Importune comes from Latin importunus, 'ill-timed' or 'troublesome', the opposite of opportune: someone who importunes asks at every bad moment.

senses.definition: Too set in bad habits or wrongdoing to be reformed, however often corrected.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So stuck in a bad habit that nothing will ever change it.

examples.text: My incorrigible uncle still tells the same awful jokes at every family dinner, however often my aunt kicks him under the table.
The school expelled him as incorrigible after a fourth suspension for fighting changed nothing.
She is an incorrigible optimist who packs sunglasses even when the forecast promises a week of rain.
Fines did nothing to stop the incorrigible litterbug, who simply paid them and kept tossing cans from his car.

distractors.lemma: Staying honest no matter what bribe or temptation is offered.
Grieving so deeply that no comfort helps.
Clashing with its setting or with what one would expect.
Expressed so confusedly that it cannot be followed.

mnemonics: Incorrigible is in-, 'not', plus Latin corrigere, 'to correct': an incorrigible person cannot be corrected.

senses.definition: Showing sustained enthusiastic action with unflagging vitality.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Able to keep working hard for hours or days without getting tired.

examples.text: The indefatigable volunteer knocked on four hundred doors in a single weekend before the election.
Even at ninety, my grandmother was indefatigable, gardening all morning and baking all afternoon.
Thanks to one indefatigable researcher who read every letter in the archive, the poet's lost diary was finally found.
The rescue dogs seemed indefatigable, searching the rubble for twelve hours without a rest.

distractors.lemma: So wrong that no argument can justify it.
Too subtle to be put precisely into words.
Permanent, so that no washing or time can erase it.
Open-ended, with no limit or end date set in advance.

mnemonics: Indefatigable is in-, 'not', plus Latin defatigare, 'to tire out', from the same root as fatigue: someone who never gets fatigued.

senses.definition: Calmly carefree and untroubled, often when others would be worried.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Relaxed and not worried, even when there might be good reason to be.

examples.text: With the plane already boarding, he strolled to the gate with an insouciant smile and a coffee in hand.
Her insouciant approach to deadlines drove her more anxious coworkers to distraction.
When the stage lights failed mid-joke, the comedian's insouciant shrug won over the whole crowd.
Investors stayed strangely insouciant about the rising debt, buying more shares as the warnings piled up.

distractors.lemma: Talking back to a superior with open, deliberate disrespect.
Having debts greater than all one's assets.
Causing damage gradually and out of sight, so it is noticed too late.
So flat and dull that it leaves no impression on the tongue or the mind.

mnemonics: Insouciant is French: in-, 'not', plus soucier, 'to worry'. An insouciant person has no souci, no worry at all.

senses.definition: Toughen someone through repeated exposure until a hardship or shock no longer affects them.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Make someone so used to something bad that they barely notice it.

examples.text: Years of night shifts had inured her to the wail of sirens outside the hospital window.
Growing up on a dairy farm inured him to early mornings and hard physical work.
Some worry that a steady stream of violent news inures viewers to real suffering.
The coach held winter practices outdoors to inure the team to playing in the snow.

distractors.lemma: Wound or hurt the body of a person or creature.
Arrange for payment to be made if something is lost, damaged or stolen.
Wall someone in or lock them away from the world.
Draw someone in by appealing to their desires.

mnemonics: Inure comes from the old phrase in ure, 'in use': whatever you are inured to has been put to use on you so often that you stop feeling it.

senses.definition: Abusive or venomous language used to express blame or censure or bitter deep-seated ill will.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Angry, insulting language aimed at hurting or attacking someone.

examples.text: The debate soon turned into a stream of invective, with each candidate calling the other a liar and a coward.
The critic's review was pure invective, mocking the director's talent, his taste and even his haircut.
Anonymous accounts flooded her comments with invective after she criticized the popular singer.
Despite the invective hurled at him from the gallery, the judge calmly finished reading the verdict.

distractors.lemma: A prayer calling on a god or spirit for aid, often said at the start of a ceremony.
A rise or dip in pitch as someone speaks.
A bonus or other gain held out to make people more willing to act.
A message asking someone to join a party, meal or other event.

mnemonics: Invective comes from Latin invehi, 'to attack with words', literally 'to be carried against': invective charges at its target.

senses.definition: Characterized by jokes and good humor.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Joking and playful in a friendly way.

examples.text: Despite the two-hour delay, the pilot's jocular announcements kept the passengers laughing.
Her jocular tone made it clear she wasn't really angry that we had eaten all the cookies.
The best man gave a jocular speech, full of gentle teasing about the groom's hopeless sense of direction.
Even when the news was bad, the old doctor kept his jocular manner, cracking a joke before every injection.

distractors.lemma: Found in the neck or throat, or relating to that part of the body.
Concerned with the eye and how it sees.
Naive and simple, showing little experience of life.
Soured by experience and quick to expect the worst.
Cryptic and weighty, in the manner of a prophecy.

mnemonics: Jocular comes from Latin joculus, a little joke, from jocus, the same root that gave English the word joke.

senses.definition: Marked by the exercise of good judgment or common sense in practical matters.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Careful and sensible in deciding what to do or how to use something.

examples.text: The editor made a few judicious cuts, removing the weakest scenes and leaving the story tighter.
Instead of spending her bonus at once, she made the judicious choice to pay off her highest-interest card first.
A judicious coach knows when to rest an injured star rather than risk losing her for the whole season.
With only enough water for three days, the hikers had to be judicious about when and how much they drank.

distractors.lemma: Belonging to the system of courts and judges that applies the law.
Inclined to condemn other people's choices before hearing their reasons.
Tending to hurt someone's interests or to sway opinion unfairly against them.
Pushy about enforcing petty rules and meddling in other people's business.
So absurd that it invites laughter or disbelief.

mnemonics: Judicious comes from Latin judicium, judgment, a cousin of judge: a judicious person judges a situation well before acting.

senses.definition: Quick to weep and often in tears, even over small things.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Always ready to burst into tears.

examples.text: After two glasses of wine my uncle turns lachrymose and starts weeping over old family photos.
She was a lachrymose bride, sobbing through her vows and again through the first dance.
Reporters expected a defiant speech, but the lachrymose senator had to stop twice to wipe his eyes.
Even a sad commercial would leave my lachrymose roommate reaching for the tissues.

distractors.lemma: Sparing with words, saying little more than is needed.
Dull and flat, without energy or shine.
Half-hearted and sloppy, showing no drive to do things well.
Openly lustful in a way that others find crude.

senses.definition: Sad enough to move listeners or viewers to tears.

mnemonics: Lachrymose comes from Latin lacrima, a tear: a lachrymose person always seems close to tears.

senses.definition: Denounce someone or something in harsh, angry terms.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To criticize someone very harshly and angrily.

examples.text: The reviewer lambasted the sequel, calling its plot lazy, its jokes stale and its stars overpaid.
At the town meeting, residents lambasted the council for ignoring two years of complaints about the flooded road.
The coach lambasted his players at halftime, shouting that not one of them had made a tackle.
Consumer groups lambaste the airline every winter, when storms strand thousands of travelers with no information.

distractors.lemma: Keep roasting meat moist by brushing it with its own drippings.
Mourn openly, or voice sorrow over a loss.
Bond thin layers together, or seal something in clear plastic film.
Waste away, or stay stuck in a bad state with no progress.

senses.definition: Give someone a thrashing with a stick or cane.

mnemonics: Lambaste joins two old verbs, lam and baste, that both once meant to thrash. Today the thrashing is done with words.

senses.definition: Showing little energy and moving in a slow, unhurried way.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Slow and lazy, with little energy.

examples.text: She gave a languid wave from the hammock, too comfortable to sit up and say hello.
By mid-afternoon the heat had made everyone languid, and nobody wanted to leave the shade.
On Sunday mornings the old dog padded around the garden at a languid pace, stopping often to lie down.
After the overnight flight, he stretched out on the sofa and gave languid, one-word answers to our questions.

distractors.lemma: Clear in thought or expression, so that it is simple to follow.
Transparent and unclouded, so that light passes through freely.
Told in gruesome or scandalous detail meant to thrill.
Long-limbed and skinny in an ungainly way.
Racked with deep suffering, in body or mind.

mnemonics: Languid comes from Latin languere, to be faint or weak, the root of languish too: a languid person seems too weak to hurry.

senses.definition: Free and lavish giving of money or gifts, often by a rich or powerful patron.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Generous giving of money or presents by someone who has plenty.

examples.text: The small museum survives on the largesse of a few collectors who cover its losses each year.
Voters grew wary of the governor's sudden largesse, which arrived as tax rebates just weeks before the election.
A tech billionaire's largesse paid for the new library wing, a scholarship fund and free summer concerts.
Tired of living on her uncle's largesse, she took a second job so she could pay her own rent.

distractors.lemma: Great size, or the fact of being bigger than most.
Theft of another person's belongings, treated as a crime.
A heavy tiredness that saps the will to do anything.
Slackness in applying rules, so that standards slip.

senses.definition: Gifts or sums of money handed out by a wealthy giver.

mnemonics: Largesse came into English from French, and its root is Latin largus, generous or plentiful: largesse is giving on a large scale.

senses.definition: Heap public attention and praise on someone, as though they were a star.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Treat someone as a hero and give them lots of attention.

examples.text: After she rescued the trapped miners, the young engineer was lionized on talk shows and magazine covers.
The tenor was lionized in Vienna, where crowds waited outside the opera house just to watch him leave.
The town lionized its quarterback, naming a street after him before he had even finished college.
Critics argue that we lionize tech founders while ignoring the engineers who actually build the products.

distractors.lemma: Give atoms or molecules an electric charge by stripping away or adding electrons.
Settle in another people's land and rule it as one's own.
Address someone in a smug tone that implies they cannot understand much.
Struggle for a long time over a hard decision or a worry.

mnemonics: Lionize comes from an old use of lion for a celebrity whom everyone wanted to see; to lionize someone is to make them that kind of lion.

senses.definition: Heavy with sorrow, in a way that often seems exaggerated.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very sad and gloomy, often more than the moment calls for.

examples.text: The undertaker spoke in a lugubrious murmur even when he was only ordering lunch.
The band followed its upbeat single with a lugubrious ballad, sung at half speed, about a widow at a graveside.
His long, lugubrious face, with drooping eyes and a downturned mouth, made strangers ask what was wrong.
Fans groaned through the coach's lugubrious press conference, where he sighed before every answer as if the season were already lost.

distractors.lemma: Promoting good health, said of air, climate or surroundings.
Slyly lewd and sexually suggestive.
Earning large profits for whoever owns or runs it.
Glowing with its own light.

mnemonics: Lugubrious comes from Latin lugere, to mourn: a lugubrious voice sounds as if it belongs at a funeral.

senses.definition: Wishing or appearing to wish evil to others; arising from intense ill will or hatred.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Wanting to hurt others or to see bad things happen to them.

examples.text: Failure made him malevolent toward his old classmates, and he began spreading rumors to wreck their careers.
In the fairy tale, a malevolent fairy curses the princess to die on her sixteenth birthday.
The outage was no accident but the work of a malevolent former employee who deleted every backup on his way out.
From the doorway the old man watched us with a malevolent grin, as if he hoped we would fall.

distractors.lemma: Workable under a hammer without cracking, or easily swayed by others.
Having a strong, nasty smell.
Awkward and inept, especially in delicate situations.
Torn between two opposite feelings about something.
Weak or unhealthy from not eating enough of the right foods.

senses.definition: Having or exerting a malignant influence.

examples.text: Malevolent stars

mnemonics: Malevolent joins Latin male, badly, and volens, wishing: a malevolent person wishes others harm, while a benevolent one wishes them well.

senses.definition: Effusively or insincerely emotional.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So sentimental that it feels fake or sickly sweet.

examples.text: The film ruins a strong story with a mawkish ending, in which the dying dog wags its tail once more as violins swell.
Her editor cut the mawkish last paragraph, where the narrator weeps at a sunset and calls it her mother's final gift.
The greeting card's mawkish verse about baby angels crying happy teardrops made him cringe.
Some readers love the novel's tender scenes, but I found them mawkish and manipulative.

distractors.lemma: Quick to back war or harsh measures in dealing with other nations.
Stubbornly refusing to change course or give in.
In step with the latest trends and styles.
Scornfully making fun of someone or something.

mnemonics: Mawkish grew out of mawke, an old English word for a maggot, and first meant sickly or nauseating. Now it describes sentiment so sugary it turns the stomach.

senses.definition: Someone who dislikes people in general.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Someone who does not like or trust other people and keeps away from them.

examples.text: A lifelong misanthrope, the old lighthouse keeper said he preferred gulls to people because gulls never asked questions.
Her neighbors called her a misanthrope because she never answered the door and scowled at anyone who waved.
The sitcom's hero is a misanthrope who moves to a remote island so he never has to speak to another human being.
Years of reading online comment sections can turn even a cheerful person into a misanthrope.

distractors.lemma: Someone who stockpiles money and begrudges every cent spent.
Someone who holds women in contempt.
Someone who studies how human cultures and societies developed.
Someone sent abroad by a church to spread its faith.

mnemonics: Misanthrope joins Greek misein, to hate, and anthropos, human being: a misanthrope hates humankind.

senses.definition: A small or moderate or token amount.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Just a little of something, often barely enough.

examples.text: If he had shown even a modicum of remorse, the judge might have given him a lighter sentence.
The report adds only a modicum of new data; most of it repeats last year's findings.
With a modicum of planning, you can avoid most of the stress of moving house.
The climbers set off without even a modicum of caution, ignoring the storm warning posted at the trailhead.

distractors.lemma: A separate unit that can be fitted together with others to build something larger.
The habit of playing down one's own talents or achievements.
An official pause on some activity, ordered for a set time.
The force a moving thing gathers that keeps it going.

mnemonics: Modicum comes from modicus, the Latin for moderate, which is built on modus, a measure: a modicum is a modest measure of something.

senses.definition: Sharp and stinging in a way meant to wound, especially in humor or criticism.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Funny or critical in a harsh, biting way that hurts.

examples.text: Chefs dreaded her mordant reviews, which could empty a new restaurant within a week.
The play's mordant take on office life had the audience laughing and wincing at the same time.
Even in his last letters, Twain kept his mordant wit, mocking the greed and hypocrisy he saw around him.
Her mordant remark that the committee had finally achieved nothing at record speed stung everyone in the room.

distractors.lemma: Preoccupied with dying, disease and decay in a way that seems unwholesome.
Fading toward its end, with little life or energy left.
Quietly at rest for a period, with its activity paused rather than ended.
Full of guilt and sorrow over your own past wrongdoing.

mnemonics: Mordant comes from Latin mordere, "to bite": mordant humor bites. Dyers use the same word for a chemical that makes color bite into cloth.

senses.definition: Head off a difficulty in advance, so that some later action is no longer required.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make something unneeded by dealing with the problem ahead of time.

examples.text: A second backup drive would obviate the need to rebuild every file by hand after a crash.
Writing a clear contract at the start can obviate months of argument later on.
The new bridge obviated the long ferry ride that commuters had made for decades.
She packed snacks and games for the children to obviate any meltdowns on the long drive.

distractors.lemma: Cloud the meaning of something on purpose, often to hide the truth.
Make someone answerable for doing something, through a law, contract or promise.
Turn aside from the expected path, plan or standard.
Cut a written word down to a few of its letters.

mnemonics: Obviate shares Latin via, "way," with obvious: you meet a problem in the road ahead and clear it, so no fix is needed later.

senses.definition: So hateful or offensive that it fills people with disgust.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Horrible in a way that makes people feel disgust and hate.

examples.text: Charging grieving families double for funeral flowers struck everyone as an odious way to make money.
The regime's odious policy of jailing children along with their parents drew protests around the world.
Most voters found the candidate's jokes about wounded veterans odious and punished him at the polls.
Slavery was defended for centuries, though we now see it as one of the most odious institutions in history.

distractors.lemma: Having a scent strong enough to notice.
So dull and slow that time seems to drag.
Pleasant to hear because of its tuneful sound.
Hinting that bad things lie ahead.

mnemonics: Odious comes from Latin odium, "hatred," which English also uses for strong public dislike. Odious things earn odium.

senses.definition: Harden into a fixed state that no longer changes or lets in new ideas.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To get stuck in old ways and stop changing or growing.

examples.text: Without new members, the club's traditions ossified, and every meeting followed the same script for thirty years.
Critics warned that the party had ossified into a circle of aging leaders who no longer listened to voters.
Some novelists ossify after an early success and write the same book again and again.
