senses.definition: In rhetoric, an appeal to the listeners' feelings rather than to logic or to the speaker's character.

mnemonics: Pathos is Greek for suffering or feeling, the root of sympathy and pathetic: pathos makes you feel for someone who suffers.

senses.definition: A thin coloring or sheen that slowly builds up on old metal or wood through weather, use and handling.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The thin colored film that old metal or wood takes on as it ages.

examples.text: After a century of rain, the bronze statue in the square has a green patina.
Collectors pay more for old copper pots that keep their original patina than for ones polished to a bright shine.
Years of hands resting on the oak banister have given it a warm, dark patina.
Architects often choose copper roofs knowing the metal will weather to a blue-green patina within a decade.

distractors.lemma: A thin film of nerve cells inside the eyeball that converts incoming light into signals for the brain.
A woven cloth, often silk, with a slick, lustrous front and a matte back.
A dense, pale gray metal prized for jewelry because it never tarnishes.
A gel-forming compound found in apples and citrus peel that helps jam set.

senses.definition: A surface look or air that something has gained over time, which may hide what lies beneath.

mnemonics: Patina comes through Italian from Latin patina, a shallow dish: picture an old bronze dish dug up green with age.

senses.definition: Read or inspect something closely, taking in the details.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To go over a text or document slowly and with care.

examples.text: She spent an hour perusing the contract, checking every clause before she signed.
Before the auction, buyers perused the catalog and marked the lots they meant to bid on.
He liked to peruse the old maps slowly, tracing each river with a finger.
The committee will peruse every application in detail before inviting anyone to an interview.

distractors.lemma: Follow hard on someone's heels in an effort to catch them.
Seep into and fill every corner of a place, group or atmosphere.
Bring someone round to your view or plan through reasoning and appeal.
Shake someone's calm, leaving them uneasy and on edge.

mnemonics: Peruse is probably built from per-, thoroughly, and use: it first meant to use something up, and now means to go through a text thoroughly.

senses.definition: A person who scorns or shrugs off art, literature and serious ideas, valuing only practical or material things.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A person with no interest in art, books or ideas, who may even sneer at them.

examples.text: Only a philistine would tear down a beautiful old theater to build a parking garage.
He cheerfully admits to being a philistine who would rather watch football than sit through an opera.
The new minister, a philistine who called museums a waste of money, cut the arts budget in half.
Don't be such a philistine; the painting is worth a look even if you can't name the artist.

distractors.lemma: A wealthy person who funds schools, hospitals and other good works.
A person who hunts down rare postmarks, misprints and old issues of stamps to fill an album.
A feudal lord who held a king's powers within his own territory.
A person who parades strict virtue and judges others while failing to live by it.

senses.definition: A member of an ancient people who lived on the coast of what is now southern Israel and Gaza.

mnemonics: Philistine comes from the Philistines, the Bible's foes of Israel; German students used Philister for dull townsfolk, and Matthew Arnold brought the insult into English.

senses.definition: A flash of hurt, sulky anger in someone whose vanity has just been bruised.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A short burst of anger or sulking because someone has hurt your pride.

examples.text: Left off the guest list, he skipped the wedding in a fit of pique.
In a moment of pique, she deleted the whole chapter after her editor called it merely fine.
The senator voted against the bill out of pique, stung that nobody had asked for his support.
When a critic called his soup bland, the offended chef took it off the menu in a fit of pique.

distractors.lemma: A tangy, spicy sharpness that makes food or talk lively and interesting.
A sorrowful concern felt on seeing someone else suffer.
A deep devotion to God shown in faithful prayer and worship.
A brief, sneaky glance at something not meant to be seen yet.

senses.definition: A cotton cloth with a textured weave of fine cords or small diamonds, used for polo shirts.

mnemonics: Pique comes from French piquer, to prick or sting: a fit of pique is the sting of hurt pride.

senses.definition: Belonging to or typical of ordinary working people, and so seen by snobs as lacking refinement.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Ordinary and common, lacking the polish that upper-class people prize.

examples.text: The duchess sniffed at the buffet, calling the hot dogs and potato salad hopelessly plebeian.
He hid his plebeian taste for cheap thrillers from his friends in the literature department.
Critics called the opera's staging plebeian, full of slapstick and cartoon costumes aimed at the cheap seats.
Despite his fortune, the senator liked to flaunt his plebeian roots by eating diner breakfasts on camera.

distractors.lemma: Held with all of a body's delegates present at one sitting.
Padded with words that repeat what has already been said.
Bloated and overstuffed, holding far beyond a sensible amount.
Endlessly changeable, slipping from one form or role into another with ease.

senses.definition: Belonging to the ordinary citizens of ancient Rome rather than to its noble families.

mnemonics: Plebeian comes from Latin plebs, the mass of ordinary Roman citizens outside the noble patrician families: plebeian tastes are those of the crowd.

senses.definition: Hold forth with lofty self-importance, as if one's opinions were beyond question.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To talk on and on about your opinions as if you were the expert on everything.

examples.text: At every family dinner my uncle pontificates about the economy, though he has never read a budget.
The actor pontificated for twenty minutes on climate science, lecturing the actual scientists on the panel.
Rather than pontificate from the stage, the speaker asked the audience what they thought.
Commentators who pontificate on cable news rarely admit when their confident predictions turn out wrong.

distractors.lemma: Turn a question over slowly and quietly in one's mind.
Dodge a straight answer with vague, slippery talk to avoid the truth.
Break up a stretch of talk or activity at intervals with something different.
Soothe an angry person, often by giving in to part of what they want.

senses.definition: Lead a church service in the role of a bishop or pope.

mnemonics: Pontificate comes from pontifex, the Latin title of Rome's high priests and later of the pope: to pontificate is to speak as if issuing a papal decree.

senses.definition: Serve as an early signal of a coming event, most often a harmful one.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To be an early hint that something, often something bad, lies ahead.

examples.text: Sailors believed that a red sky at dawn portended storms before nightfall.
The sudden resignation of the finance minister may portend deeper trouble in the government.
Economists fear that the steep drop in new orders portends layoffs at the factory next year.
In the play, a flock of crows circling the castle portends the king's death.

distractors.lemma: Present oneself or itself as something, with the claim often open to doubt.
Bring a person or scene to life on canvas, on the page or on stage.
Belong to a subject as one of its relevant concerns.
Ration out food or goods so that each person gets a set amount.

mnemonics: Portend comes from Latin portendere, to stretch forward (por-, forward, and tendere, to stretch): a portent points ahead to what is coming.

senses.definition: Lay down a claim as true for the time being, so that an argument or theory can rest on it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To suggest an idea as true so you can build an argument on it.

examples.text: Astronomers posited an unseen planet to explain the odd wobble in the orbit of Uranus.
The theory posits that people make choices by weighing costs against benefits.
For the sake of argument, let us posit that the witness is telling the truth; what follows?
Some economists posit a link between cheap credit and rising house prices, then test it against the data.

distractors.lemma: Strike attitudes or make showy claims meant to impress rather than inform.
Put off something scheduled until a later day or hour.
Topple a monarch or leader and strip them of office.
Hold something as one's own, whether goods, land or a quality.

senses.definition: Set or place something firmly in a particular spot.

mnemonics: Posit comes from Latin positus, placed, the root of position: to posit an idea is to place it down as the base of an argument.

senses.definition: A principle or instruction that sets out how a person ought to act.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A rule or lesson about the right way to behave.

examples.text: Her grandfather lived by one simple precept: never borrow money you cannot repay within a year.
The ancient medical precept to do no harm applies to teachers as well as doctors.
Buddhist monks follow precepts that forbid killing, stealing and lying.
He taught his apprentices by example rather than by precept, letting them watch him work.

distractors.lemma: A cover story offered to justify an action whose true motive is kept hidden.
A mental picture of a whole class of things, built up by generalizing from cases.
What a person registers through sight, hearing or touch, as opposed to an idea reasoned out.
An outcome that may lie ahead and that people hope for or dread.

senses.definition: A written order from a court or official directing someone to act.

mnemonics: Precept comes from Latin praeceptum, a teaching, built from prae-, before, and capere, to take: precepts are lessons you take in before life tests you.

senses.definition: Spread word of a creed, theory or policy far and wide by preaching or publishing it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To push an idea or a new rule out to the public until nearly everyone has heard of it.

examples.text: Missionaries traveled the trade routes to promulgate their faith in distant ports.
The group used pamphlets, radio talks and summer camps to promulgate its theory that the moon landing was faked.
Through popular lectures and books, the economist promulgated the idea that free trade benefits everyone.
Health officials set out to promulgate the new handwashing guidelines in every school and clinic.

distractors.lemma: Offer gifts or sacrifices to calm an offended power and make it kindly again.
Pledge that one will do something later, staking one's honor on it.
Stroll at an unhurried pace along a public walkway, often to show oneself off.
Spur someone into an action, or set off a reaction.

senses.definition: Bring a statute or decree into force by publishing it in an official notice.

mnemonics: Promulgate comes from Latin promulgare, to make publicly known, which Roman officials did with new laws: to promulgate is to get word out to the public.

senses.definition: Taken by most people to be the case, though never firmly proven.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Believed or said to be true or real, even though nobody has proved it.

examples.text: A DNA test showed that the putative father of the baby had no genetic link to her at all.
The putative benefits of the herbal tea have never been tested in a careful clinical trial.
Police questioned the gang's putative boss, who turned out to be a minor errand runner.

distractors.lemma: Meant as a penalty for someone who has done wrong.
Gone bad and reeking as it breaks down.
Showing a low opinion of the thing it describes.
Making a patient more comfortable without aiming to cure the illness.

mnemonics: Putative comes from Latin putare, to think or suppose, also the root of reputation. A putative fact is one that people suppose is true.

senses.definition: A prick of conscience warning that a planned act may be unfair or dishonest.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A small, uneasy feeling that a choice you are making may be wrong.

examples.text: He felt a qualm of conscience as he signed the expense report he knew was padded.
Despite her qualms about keeping a secret from her sister, she said nothing about the surprise party.
The landlord had no qualms about keeping the entire deposit over a single scuffed wall.

distractors.lemma: An odd habit or trait that sets one person apart.
A clever one-liner tossed off in conversation.
An unsteady trembling heard when someone speaks or sings.
A short, violent spell of wind and rain that blows up without warning.

senses.definition: A passing bout of slight nausea.

mnemonics: Qualm rhymes with calm: a qualm is the small doubt that keeps your conscience from feeling calm.

senses.definition: Hold an audience's attention with a flow of colorful stories or talk.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To delight people with a long run of funny or exciting stories.

examples.text: Over dessert, Uncle Ray regaled the table with fishing stories until everyone was wiping away tears of laughter.
The tour guide regaled us with juicy gossip about the palace's former owners, and the group begged for more.
She regaled her coworkers with tales of lost luggage and missed trains, and the whole office was laughing.

distractors.lemma: Shunt someone or something aside into a minor, less valued role.
Attack someone with harsh, insulting words.
Lose ground and fall back toward an earlier stage of growth.
Set official limits on what a business or process may do.

senses.definition: Serve someone generous helpings of fine food and drink.

mnemonics: Regale contains gale, as in a gale of laughter: a good storyteller regales a table until it roars.

senses.definition: Falling short in one's duties through carelessness or neglect.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Letting slide a job or task that was yours to take care of.

examples.text: The lifeguard was remiss in reading a novel while children splashed in the deep end.
The inspector was remiss in approving wiring he had never actually looked at.
Parents who leave pills within a toddler's reach are remiss in a basic duty of care.

distractors.lemma: Filled with regret over a wrong one has done.
Given as extra help to students who have fallen behind.
Quick to give in and do what others want.
Carrying echoes of an earlier person, place or thing.

mnemonics: Remiss contains miss: someone who is remiss misses a duty they were supposed to carry out.

senses.definition: Break one's word by backing out of a deal or a commitment.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To back out of a promise or deal after giving your word.

examples.text: After winning the election, the mayor reneged on her pledge to cut bus fares.
The buyer reneged on the contract a day before closing, leaving the sellers with no deal and no deposit.
Anyone who reneges on a poker debt at this club is never invited back.

distractors.lemma: Sign up again for a membership or lease when the old term runs out.
Formally walk away from a right or belief one used to hold.
Strip out and rebuild the worn parts of a house.
Work out new terms for a deal that is already in place.

mnemonics: Renege shares its root with renegade: both come from Latin negare, to deny. To renege is to deny a promise you once made.

senses.definition: Thoroughly filled or richly stocked with something.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Full of something, or having a great deal of it.

examples.text: The museum's new guidebook is replete with maps, photographs and floor plans.
Her memoir is replete with funny stories about growing up above a busy diner.
By June the garden is replete with roses, lilies and humming bees.

distractors.lemma: Dull from going over the same ground again and again.
Able to be swapped out for another of the same kind.
Crushing dissent and keeping citizens under tight control.
Trusted by the public thanks to a long, clean record.

senses.definition: Having eaten so much that one can hold no more.

mnemonics: Replete comes from Latin replere, to fill up. Its root plere, to fill, also gives us complete.

senses.definition: Brilliant and grand in appearance, glowing with color or light.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Dazzling to look at, in bold colors or fine clothes that make people stare.

examples.text: The bride's mother arrived resplendent in emerald silk and her grandmother's pearls.
After the restoration, the chapel ceiling was resplendent with gold leaf and deep blue paint.
The maple trees stood resplendent in red and orange along the October roadside.

distractors.lemma: Gloomy and ready to give up after a run of bad luck.
Bouncing back fast from trouble without lasting harm.
Holding a grudge over a slight that still stings.
Showing polite regard for others and their feelings.

mnemonics: Resplendent comes from Latin resplendere, to shine brightly, from the same splendere, to shine, that gives us splendid.

senses.definition: Occurring all over a place or group, mostly said of something damaging.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Found nearly everywhere, usually when the thing is bad, like crime or disease.

examples.text: Bribery was rife at the port, where every inspector expected a cut.
Typos were rife in the first draft; the editor found three on the opening page alone.
In the crowded camps, cholera was rife within weeks of the floods.

distractors.lemma: Grown soft and sweet enough to pick and eat.
Showing regret mixed with a wry, self-mocking smile.
Joking about sex or the body in a bawdy, coarse manner.
Worked up into a prickly, short-tempered state.

mnemonics: Rife rhymes with strife: where strife is rife, trouble is everywhere you look.

senses.definition: Churn in a turbulent way, or throw a group or place into turmoil.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To churn or stir up wildly, or to throw something into confusion and unrest.

examples.text: News of the bank's collapse roiled markets around the world for a week.
The plan to close the village school roiled a town that rarely argued about anything.
Months of layoffs roiled the newsroom, and every meeting turned into a shouting match.
Below the dam, brown water roiled and foamed after three days of rain.

distractors.lemma: Block a plan or an attempt so that it comes to nothing.
Labor long and hard at heavy, tiring work.
Damage something until it loses its worth, or let food go bad.
Jump backward with sudden force after being fired or struck.

senses.definition: Make water murky by disturbing the mud beneath it.

mnemonics: Roil sounds like boil, and a roiling crowd or sea churns like a pot at a rolling boil.

senses.definition: Think about something at length, going back to it again and again.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To think about something slowly and deeply, again and again.

examples.text: She spent the long train ride ruminating on whether to accept the job in Denver.
Lying awake, he ruminated over every word he had said at the meeting.
Philosophers have ruminated for centuries on what makes a life well lived.

distractors.lemma: Toss things aside in a bag or cupboard while hunting for something.
Crease and tousle hair or bedclothes.
Brighten a space by shining lamps or rays on it.
Rage and thunder in protest against something.

senses.definition: Chew food that has been brought back up from the stomach.

mnemonics: Ruminate comes from Latin ruminari, to chew the cud. A cow chews the same mouthful again and again, and a person who ruminates chews on the same thought.

senses.definition: Standing out from everything around it as the most striking or significant.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Standing out clearly as the main or most important thing.

examples.text: Her summary covered only the salient points, leaving the details for anyone who wanted them.
The salient detail in the old photo was a red umbrella, the only spot of color in a gray crowd.
In court, the lawyer kept returning to one salient fact: the door had been locked from inside.

distractors.lemma: Holding dissolved salt and tasting sharply of it.
Doing good in the end, even when the lesson is an unpleasant one.
Wise in the way of a sage who has studied and reflected for years.
Pale and yellowish in the face, often from illness or poor sleep.

senses.definition: Pointing out beyond the line of the parts around it.

mnemonics: Salient comes from Latin salire, to leap: a salient fact leaps out at you.

senses.definition: Fold something into a broader group or system as one of its parts.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To take something in as a part of something bigger.

examples.text: When the two companies merged, the small billing team was subsumed into the finance department.
Her early poems on grief were later subsumed into a longer work about her mother's life.
Critics worry that local dialects will be subsumed under one national standard.

distractors.lemma: Take a thing for granted and act on it as fact.
Carry on with something that was halted for a while.
Ease off and grow weaker after reaching a peak.
Pay a yearly fee so a journal keeps arriving in the mail.

senses.definition: Treat a single case as one instance covered by a broader law.

mnemonics: Subsume joins Latin sub, under, and sumere, to take: to subsume is to take something in under a larger heading.

senses.definition: Secret scheming, or a false cover story, that keeps others from seeing what one is really doing.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A sneaky plan or fake excuse that fools people about what you are up to.

examples.text: Posing as a delivery driver, the reporter used subterfuge to get past the guard at the gate.
Rather than resort to subterfuge, she told her boss plainly that she was interviewing elsewhere.
His sudden headache before every family reunion was a subterfuge that fooled nobody.
Wartime spies relied on subterfuge, from forged papers to coded radio chatter, to move secrets across the border.

distractors.lemma: A shelter that keeps people safe from harm or from those chasing them.
A way of living that covers only the basic needs of food and shelter.
A slow sinking of the ground, often over old mines or drained land.
A grant from public funds that lowers what a business or buyer has to pay.
A spinning lab machine that pulls blood or other mixtures apart into layers.

mnemonics: Subterfuge comes from Latin subterfugere, 'to escape in secret' (fugere, to flee, as in fugitive): a trick that lets you slip away unseen.

senses.definition: Arrive at a likely idea of the facts from scant or partial evidence.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make an educated guess when you only have part of the story.

examples.text: From the muddy boots by the door, I surmised that the kids had been playing in the creek.
Reading the curt two-line reply, she surmised that her proposal had not gone over well.
With no plans or records left behind, historians can only surmise how the bridge was built.
Seeing the dark windows and the empty parking lot, he surmised that the shop had closed early.

distractors.lemma: Rise above a hardship or barrier and get past it.
Boil a long text or talk down to its key points.
Preach moral lessons at people who never asked for them.
Startle someone with an event or news they had not foreseen.
Outdo a rival, a record or an earlier result.

mnemonics: Surmise goes back to Old French surmettre, built from sur (on top of) and mettre (place): to surmise is to lay a guess on top of the few facts you have.

senses.definition: Coming down to the same thing as something else, though not openly called by that name.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Really the same as something else, even if nobody calls it that.

examples.text: Refusing to answer the senator's question about the bribe was tantamount to admitting it.
For a small bakery, a month without power is tantamount to closing for good.
Changing the rules after the votes were counted was tantamount to cheating, the losing side said.
In that close-knit village, skipping the harvest festival was seen as tantamount to an insult.

distractors.lemma: Coming first, so that every other matter has to give way to it.
Teasing the senses with a promise that is never quite kept.
Only loosely tied to the main topic under discussion.
Having real substance that a hand could feel.

mnemonics: Tantamount ends in amount: if one thing is tantamount to another, it amounts to the same thing. It comes from Anglo-French tant amunter, 'to amount to as much'.

senses.definition: Strong control that a person or thing has over someone, leaving that person captive or spellbound.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being in someone's power, or so gripped by something that you cannot pull away.

examples.text: For decades the mill town was in thrall to one family, which owned every factory, shop and rented house.
The magician held the children in thrall for a full hour, and not one of them asked for a snack.
Many people admit they are in thrall to their phones, checking them even at the dinner table.
The novel follows a young woman who finally breaks free of the thrall of a controlling cult leader.

distractors.lemma: A quick burst of eager joy that makes the heart race.
A sharp, wrenching pang of pain or struggle.
A habit of spending sparingly and saving where one can.
The central idea that a speech or plan is driving at.

senses.definition: A person owned by or bound to serve a lord or master.

mnemonics: Thrall is the root of enthrall. To be in thrall, like a thrall (an old word for a slave), is to be held captive, whether by a master or by a gripping story.

senses.definition: A stock idea, situation or character that writers and speakers reuse so often that audiences expect it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: An idea or pattern used so often in stories or speeches that people see it coming.

examples.text: The wise old mentor who dies halfway through the film is a trope that audiences have seen a hundred times.
Campaign ads lean on the trope of the plain-spoken outsider who will clean up the capital.
The orphan who learns he is secretly a king is a trope as old as fantasy itself.
Romantic comedies rarely resist the trope of a last-minute dash through the airport.

distractors.lemma: A band of actors or acrobats who go from town to town putting on shows.
A hidden store of valuable things that someone finds.
A bending of a plant's stem or roots as it grows toward light, water or gravity.
A gauge of disorder in a physical system, which tends to rise over time.
A cup, plaque or other prize handed to a winner.

senses.definition: Language that bends a word away from its plain, literal meaning.

mnemonics: Trope comes from Greek tropos, 'a turn': a trope is a familiar turn that stories take again and again.

senses.definition: Unable to hold up under challenge, or impossible to keep going as things stand.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Too weak to defend, or too hard to keep going.

examples.text: Once the lab results came back, the company's claim that its water was safe became untenable.
With three ministers resigning in a single week, the prime minister's position was untenable.
Paying rent on two apartments was an untenable arrangement, so she gave up the lease on one.
The theory that the comet was a spacecraft proved untenable once astronomers measured its orbit.

distractors.lemma: Out of reach no matter how hard one tries.
Put forward as a first try and still open to change.
Gripping hard and slow to let go or give up.
Still wild and never brought under human control.

mnemonics: Untenable contains Latin tenere, 'to hold', as in tenant: an untenable position is one that cannot be held.

senses.definition: Surprising in an unwelcome way, or not fitting what is proper.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Odd in a bad way that nobody planned for, or not quite proper.

examples.text: The flight landed on time, and the crew reported nothing untoward: no turbulence, no sick passengers, no warning lights.
Neighbors noticed nothing untoward until smoke began pouring from the upstairs window.
The coach's untoward remarks about the referee's family earned him a two-game ban.
If anything untoward happens while I am away, such as a burst pipe or a break-in, call me at once.

distractors.lemma: So vast that no one could tally it.
Left in a mess, with things strewn about.
Never yet tested in real use.
Off guard and easy to catch in a trap.
Left whole and unharmed, never handled or used.

mnemonics: Untoward is un- plus toward. Something untoward heads away from what you hoped for or from what is proper.

senses.definition: A surviving scrap of something that has otherwise faded away or come to an end.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The little that is still left of something that has almost vanished.

examples.text: A few crumbling arches are the only vestige of the Roman baths that once stood on this hill.
After twenty years in London, not a vestige of her Texas drawl remained.
Bowing to the judge is a vestige of courtroom customs that date back many centuries.
The tiny hip bones inside a whale's body are a vestige of the legs its ancestors walked on.

distractors.lemma: A high standing earned through success, rank or quality.
A small hall where visitors step in before reaching the main rooms.
A ceremonial garment that clergy put on to lead worship.
A giddy sense that the room is whirling or tipping.

mnemonics: Vestige comes from Latin vestigium, 'footprint': a vestige is the print left behind after something has passed.

senses.definition: The use of one's own will in choosing or deciding what to do.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Choosing for yourself because you want to, not because you were told to.

examples.text: Nobody asked him to stay late; he scrubbed the whole kitchen of his own volition.
The judge had to decide whether the suspect came to the station of her own volition or under pressure.
Reflexes like blinking happen without volition, before you have time to think about them.
The contract is void if either party signed it under threat rather than by free volition.

distractors.lemma: The breach of a law, pact or right.
The work a person feels deeply called to do.
The quality of swinging sharply and unpredictably from one state to another.
The pace at which a moving object covers ground in one direction.
The slow change of living species over many generations.

mnemonics: Volition comes from Latin volo, 'I wish', the same root as voluntary: acting of your own volition means doing what you yourself want.

senses.definition: Meant to harm, though nothing provoked it and nothing could justify it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Cruel or destructive on purpose, with no cause at all.

examples.text: Vandals smashed every window in the empty school in an act of wanton destruction.
The judge called the attack on the sleeping man an act of wanton cruelty that nothing could excuse.
Villagers were angered by the wanton killing of deer that the hunters simply left to rot.
Critics accused the developer of wanton disregard for the historic buildings it tore down overnight.

distractors.lemma: Customary for someone and done out of long habit.
Having a washed-out, sickly face that shows strain.
Lacking something needed, or falling short of a standard.
Shrinking bit by bit in size, force or glow.

mnemonics: Wanton comes from Middle English wantowen, 'badly brought up' (wan-, lacking, plus towen, trained): wanton acts are what an unruly person does for no reason.

senses.definition: A great, disordered mass of things, often too many to sort out.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A big, messy jumble of stuff that is hard to make sense of.

examples.text: Buried in a welter of receipts and bank statements, she could not find the one tax form she needed.
The report's one good idea is lost in a confusing welter of half-explained statistics.
After the storm, the beach was a welter of driftwood, seaweed and broken lobster traps.
Voters faced a welter of conflicting claims about what the new tax would really cost them.

distractors.lemma: A puffy red stripe that rises where a strap or switch has stung.
How well someone is doing in body, money and peace of mind.
A covered place where people can wait out a storm or hide from danger.
The state of the air outdoors on a given day, from heat and wind to cloud and rain.

mnemonics: Welter rhymes with helter-skelter, and a welter is a helter-skelter heap of things. It comes from an old verb meaning 'to roll or toss about'.

senses.definition: Humorous in a dry, quietly mocking way.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Funny in a low-key way that pokes fun a little.

examples.text: Rained in on the first day of his beach holiday, Tom remarked with wry humor that at least he would not get sunburned.
Her memoir is full of wry observations about growing up with six brothers in a two-bedroom flat.
Asked how the rocket launch went, the engineer offered a wry reply: 'Well, it went up.'
The columnist's wry take on office meetings made readers laugh and wince at the same time.

distractors.lemma: Lean and sinewy, with strength hidden in a slight frame.
Watchful and slow to trust, in case of danger.
Worn out after long effort or strain.
Crafty and full of sly schemes.

senses.definition: Crooked or turned askew.

mnemonics: Wry once meant 'twisted', from an Old English verb for 'to turn', and a wry smile twists up at one corner, half amused and half mocking.

senses.definition: Hear the evidence in a dispute or claim and give an official ruling on it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To hear both sides of a dispute and make the formal ruling that ends it.

examples.text: Two chess players disagreed about whether a move was legal, so the tournament director came over to adjudicate.
Our grandmother was always the one to adjudicate when the cousins fought over who got the last slice of pie.
Before the tribunal could adjudicate her claim of unfair dismissal, it heard from six former coworkers.
Because the two neighbors could not agree on where the fence belonged, a court had to adjudicate their claims and fix the boundary.

distractors.lemma: Break off a session and set a later date to pick up where it left off.
Stand against another building, room or field with nothing in between.
Step down as a king or queen and hand over the crown by choice.
Champion a cause or a policy and press others to back it.
Shift or tweak a setting, a fit or a plan a little until it is right.

senses.definition: Judge the entries in a contest and choose the winners.

mnemonics: Adjudicate comes from Latin ad-, to, and judicare, to judge: you adjudicate a dispute by sitting as its judge.

senses.definition: A lasting grudge or bitter dislike aimed at a particular person or group.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A strong dislike of someone that lasts and shapes how you treat them.

examples.text: The senator's animus toward the press was obvious; he called reporters liars at almost every rally.
Years after the lawsuit, there was still real animus between the two brothers, who would not sit at the same table.
The judge found that the firing was driven by personal animus rather than by any problem with her work.
Fans of the rival clubs share an animus that goes back a century, and police line the streets on match days.

distractors.lemma: A faith that treats mountains, beasts and even storms as beings with minds of their own.
Liveliness and spirit shown in a person's voice, face and gestures.
A lack of any dissent, with no one at all taking the other side.
Steady, unshaken calm that holds even when things go badly.
A timid lack of nerve that keeps a person from taking any risk.

senses.definition: The purpose or motive that drives someone's actions.

mnemonics: Animus is Latin for mind or spirit, the same root as animosity: animus is a spirit turned against someone.

senses.definition: Someone or something that stands at the far opposite extreme from another.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The total opposite of something else.

examples.text: Calm, patient and soft-spoken, the new coach is the antithesis of the screaming man he replaced.
Endless forms and two-hour waits are the antithesis of the quick service the agency promised.
For a band known for loud, wild shows, this quiet acoustic album is the antithesis of what fans expected.
She saw the gold-plated mansion, with its fountains and marble lions, as the antithesis of good taste.

distractors.lemma: The result of merging two rival theories or styles into a third.
An idea put forward to explain something, which tests can then check.
A bit of extra comment the sentence could lose without breaking its grammar.
A treatment doctors give after a snakebite or overdose to undo the damage.
A flawed, often selfish lead figure in a novel or film whom readers still root for.

senses.definition: A way of writing that pairs opposed ideas in two phrases built the same way, for effect.

mnemonics: Antithesis joins Greek anti, against, and thesis, a position: it is a position set directly against another.

senses.definition: Repeat a name, figure or label in loose talk, so it gets passed from mouth to mouth.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To keep a word or name going around in casual chat.

examples.text: Wild numbers were bandied about at the meeting, but nobody could say where any of them came from.
His name has been bandied around as a possible candidate, though he has never said he wants the job.
Pundits bandy the word crisis about so freely that many viewers have stopped listening.
Rumors of layoffs were bandied about the office all week before management said anything official.

distractors.lemma: Dress an injured arm or leg by winding cloth snugly around it.
Shake a sword, club or gun in the air to scare people off or to show it off.
Desert a person, pet or project and leave it to fend for itself.
Join with others in a group to work toward a shared goal.
Mark a calf as one's own by searing a symbol into its skin.

senses.definition: Swap sharp words or insults with someone during an argument.

mnemonics: Bandy first meant to knock a ball to and fro in a game: a name that gets bandied about is batted from person to person.

senses.definition: Bound to someone by a debt or favor, and so not free to act against them.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Owing someone a favor, so they can count on you to take their side.

examples.text: The chess champion had coached the principal's son for free, so the principal felt beholden to him and let the club keep the library every Friday.
A singer who owes her big break to one producer may stay beholden to him for years, recording whatever songs he picks.
The scientists turned down money from the oil company so that their findings would not look beholden to it.
Since the neighbors rebuilt her fence for free, she feels beholden to them and could hardly refuse when they asked her to mind their dog.

distractors.lemma: Turning up well past the moment it was needed.
Living without the knowledge and ideas the wider world takes for granted.
Silly with love for someone, to the point of acting like a fool.
Quick to pick fights and openly hostile toward others.
Missing something dear that has been taken away, and lost without it.

mnemonics: Beholden is an old past form of behold, which once meant to hold or keep: someone you are beholden to has a hold on you.

senses.definition: Bring a touchy or awkward subject out into the open in conversation.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To raise a hard topic out loud, such as money or a health scare.

examples.text: She waited until after dessert to broach the idea of selling the family house.
Doctors learn to broach bad news gently, starting with what the patient already knows.
Nobody on the team dared to broach the missed deadline while the boss was still fuming.
When he finally broached the idea of moving abroad, his wife admitted she had been thinking the same thing.

distractors.lemma: Fail to keep the terms you signed up to in a deal or contract.
Keep turning a worry or grievance over in one's mind, sulking.
Sear steak or chicken fast with fierce heat aimed down from above.
Act as the go-between who works out terms for a sale or a truce.
Wander through a store or a website, glancing at whatever catches the eye.

senses.definition: Tap a keg or barrel so that its beer or wine can be poured.

mnemonics: Broach comes from Old French broche, a pointed spike used to tap a barrel: broaching a touchy subject taps it open.

senses.definition: A force, belief or institution that holds firm and keeps a danger or unwanted change at bay.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Something that stands strong and keeps a threat away.

examples.text: Her sense of humor was a bulwark against the gloom of the long hospital stay.
For decades the small savings bank was the town's bulwark against the loan sharks who preyed on farmers.
The goalkeeper was a bulwark all season, stopping shot after shot as the defense in front of him fell apart.
Volunteer fire crews were the village's only bulwark against the wildfires that swept the hills each summer.

distractors.lemma: The one irritation a person grumbles about more than any other.
A town, firm or result that people watch because it tends to move first.
The patch of work or knowledge that a person treats as their own territory.
Layers of officials and forms that a request must pass through before anything happens.

senses.definition: A heaped-up earthwork that troops shelter behind when a fort is under siege.
On a ship, a solid rail rising from the deck edge, built as part of the hull.

mnemonics: Bulwark comes from Middle Dutch bolwerc, a defense made of tree trunks (bole) and work: a log wall that holds off attack.

senses.definition: Raise the standing of a person or group by adding to what they can boast of.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make people think better of someone, often after new successes.

examples.text: Winning the regional spelling bee burnished the little school's name, and more families applied the next fall.
He took the overseas posting mainly to burnish his record for a top job in Washington.
Hosting the World Cup was meant to burnish the country's standing abroad after years of bad press.
A string of glowing reviews further burnished the young chef's reputation.

distractors.lemma: Hand someone the facts or proof they have asked for.
Finish a plated dish by adding a small edible touch of color on top.
Expand fast and thrive, in numbers or in size.
Tunnel down into soil to make a hidden home or shelter.
Load someone with a heavy task, worry or duty.

senses.definition: Bring up a bright sheen on metal or a similar surface by steady rubbing.

mnemonics: Burnish comes from Old French burnir, to polish, related to brun, brown: to burnish a reputation is to rub it until it glows like polished brass.

senses.definition: Shrewd and alert to where an advantage lies, and rarely outsmarted.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Good at reading people and deals, so you usually come out ahead.

examples.text: A canny negotiator, she let the other side talk first and learned exactly how much they were willing to pay.
The canny shop owner bought winter coats in July, when suppliers were desperate to sell them cheaply.
With a few canny moves, the young senator won over both parties without giving up anything important.
Canny investors sold their shares months before the crash, while everyone else was still buying.

distractors.lemma: Weird enough to send a shiver down the spine, as if not quite natural.
Blunt about one's real views, even when keeping quiet would be easier.
Grumpy and short-tempered, often from tiredness or hunger.
Quietly mean, making little cutting remarks about others behind their backs.
Young and lacking the experience that would make one wise.

mnemonics: Canny comes from can in its old sense of know how: a canny person knows how to come out ahead.

senses.definition: Hurtle ahead in a wild, tipping run that nobody seems to be steering.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To go very fast and swing about, almost out of control.

examples.text: Caught by a gust, the empty canoe careened down the rapids and smashed against a boulder.
The skier caught an edge and careened off the trail into a stand of pines.
Kids on sleds careened past us, shrieking, as they bounced over the bumps.

distractors.lemma: Join in a rowdy drinking session that lasts well into the night.
Nitpick and grumble about trifles that no one else minds.
Herd livestock together and shut them inside a ring of fencing.
Run the food side of a party, from cooking to clearing plates.

senses.definition: Lay a ship over on a beach at low tide to work on the part normally underwater.

mnemonics: Careen comes from Latin carina, a ship's keel: sailors careened a ship by tipping it on its side, and a careening car tips and lurches the same way.

senses.definition: Give up territory or authority and let another side take it, usually under pressure.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To hand land or power over to another side, often because you must.

examples.text: Under the peace treaty, the defeated kingdom had to cede three border towns to the victors.
Spain ceded Florida to the United States in a treaty signed in 1819.
The founder refused to cede control of the family firm, even when investors demanded more seats on the board.
Neither side wanted to cede any ground on the budget, so the talks ran late into the night.

distractors.lemma: Pull a region out of the country it belongs to and set it up on its own.
Draw back slowly from the point it had reached earlier.
Take place ahead of another event, or stand before it in a line.
Become the new standard, so that an earlier law or version no longer counts.
Rise above a cap or ceiling that was set in advance.
Speak up for someone before a person who has power over them.

mnemonics: Cede comes from Latin cedere, 'to yield or go away', the root of recede and concede: to cede land is to yield it to another.

senses.definition: Collect laws, rules or customs and set them down as one orderly written system.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To write down rules or habits in an organized, official form.

examples.text: The new statute codified, in one written volume, rules that judges had applied by custom for decades.
King Hammurabi codified the laws of Babylon and had them carved into a tall stone slab.
The startup finally decided to codify its unwritten habits in a short handbook for new hires.
The guild codified its training rules in a charter so that every master taught apprentices the same way.

distractors.lemma: Shield someone from every hardship and give in to their wishes too readily.
Change some part of something while leaving the rest as it was.
Crack a cipher so that a hidden message can be read.
Let wrongdoing pass without objection, so that it seems acceptable.

mnemonics: Codify contains code: to codify a set of rules is to turn them into a written code.

senses.definition: Informed about something and taking it into account.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Knowing about something and keeping it in mind.

examples.text: Fully cognizant of the storm warnings, the captain still chose to leave port at dawn.
Doctors must be cognizant of how a patient's other medicines might react with a new prescription.
She was cognizant that every word she said to the reporter could appear in print the next day.
The bank says it is cognizant of the risks of storing customer data and has hired an outside auditor.

distractors.lemma: Built on reasons so solid that an opponent struggles to answer them.
Sprung from one shared parent word, said of terms in two related languages.
In step with a principle or aim and pulling the same way as it.
Disguised or using an assumed name to keep one's identity secret.
Warm and good-humored, so that others enjoy one's company.

mnemonics: Cognizant shares the Latin root cognoscere, 'to get to know', with recognize: when you are cognizant of a fact, you recognize it and keep it in mind.

senses.definition: A further fact or effect that comes with something else as a matter of course.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Something that is bound to happen because of something else.

examples.text: Higher rents were a predictable corollary of the city's rapid job growth.
Free speech has an awkward corollary: you must also put up with speech you dislike.
As a corollary of the merger, hundreds of overlapping office jobs were cut within a year.
Longer school days had an unplanned corollary, since after-school sports clubs lost half their members.

distractors.lemma: Confirmation of someone's account by a second, independent source.
The buying of officials' favors, so that rules bend for whoever pays.
Security pledged against a debt, which the lender keeps if the debt goes unpaid.
The pitting and crumbling of metal as rust and acid eat into it.
A notice or an edit that puts right an error that was published or handed in.

senses.definition: A minor theorem deduced straight from a larger one that has just been proved.

mnemonics: Corollary comes from Latin corollarium, a tip once handed over to buy a garland, and so a bonus: a corollary is the extra result you get for free once the main point is settled.

senses.definition: Made of flesh or other matter and so taking up space in the physical world.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Having a body made of flesh and bone, unlike a ghost or a dream.

examples.text: In the story, the ghost longs to be corporeal again so that it can hold its daughter's hand.
Medieval scholars argued over whether angels were corporeal or made of pure spirit.
After two years of video calls, meeting her online friends in corporeal form felt strange.
Unlike the ghosts in his earlier films, the villain in this one is fully corporeal and can be punched, chained and locked up.

distractors.lemma: Belonging to or connected with big business firms and those who manage them.
Carrying so much excess body fat that one looks heavy and round.
Used of the heart's arteries, as in surgery to clear a blockage in them.
Ready to sell one's office or vote to whoever offers the biggest bribe.

mnemonics: Corporeal comes from Latin corpus, 'body', as in corpse: something corporeal has a body you can touch.

senses.definition: Make something poorer in quality, worth or dignity than it was before.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To cheapen something, so it counts for less than before.

examples.text: Critics say the cooking show debases the family recipes it claims to honor, turning them into cheap stunts for the camera.
Many fans felt the legendary singer debased her talent by lending her voice to a string of cheap ads.
Some teachers worry that years of grade inflation have debased the value of an A, since nearly every student now gets one.
The once-proud brand was debased by a flood of flimsy products stamped with its logo.

distractors.lemma: Face off against a rival speaker on a set question, trying to win over the room.
Strip someone of the right to compete, practice or bid, under a formal rule.
Climb down from a boat or aircraft onto land when it arrives.
Trace why a program crashes or misbehaves and repair the code at fault.
Get a full account from someone who has just come back from an assignment.

senses.definition: Cut the value of coins by mixing cheap metal into the gold or silver.
Lead a person into immoral habits and a slow moral decline.

mnemonics: Debase pairs de-, down, with base in its old sense of low (as in base metal): to debase something is to push it down to a lower, cheaper level.

senses.definition: A state of having sunk so low morally that cruelty and vice no longer trouble one.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Deep wickedness, or behavior that is shockingly evil or immoral.

examples.text: The novel exposes the depravity of a ruler who tortures prisoners for his own amusement.
Even hardened detectives were shocked by the depravity of a con artist who robbed dying hospice patients.
Preachers of the era thundered against the city's gambling dens and brothels as proof of its depravity.
Roman historians describe the emperor's depravity in lurid detail, from poisoned rivals to murdered relatives.

distractors.lemma: Hardship caused by going without food, rest, shelter or other basic needs.
A drop in the price that a used car, a machine or a currency can fetch.
How much is at stake in a matter, and so how soberly it must be treated.
The glum, defeated mood of someone who has stopped expecting anything to go right.
Reliance on a person, drug or source of money that one cannot easily do without.

mnemonics: Depravity shares the Latin root pravus, 'crooked', with deprave: a person sunk in depravity has a crooked moral compass.

senses.definition: A mess of scattered scraps, litter and broken pieces left lying around.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Bits of rubbish and broken pieces left over after something.

examples.text: After the festival, volunteers spent two days clearing the detritus of plastic cups, flyers and broken tents from the field.
The high tide left a line of detritus along the beach: seaweed, driftwood and bottle caps.
Her desk was buried under the detritus of a long project, from empty coffee cups to crumpled drafts.
Archaeologists sift the detritus of ancient kitchens, such as fish bones and broken pots, to learn what people ate.

distractors.lemma: Damage or disadvantage suffered by a person or a cause.
A soap-like chemical added to wash water to break up grease and grime.
A threat of punishment or loss that keeps people from trying something.
A side road that drivers are sent along while the main way is shut.
A furious, drawn-out rant that tears into a person or an idea.

senses.definition: Fragments of rock, sand and silt that water, wind or ice have worn away.

mnemonics: Detritus comes from Latin deterere, 'to wear away': detritus is what is left after things are worn down, rubbed off or thrown aside.

senses.definition: Having soured on a leader, party or cause and withdrawn the loyalty one gave it before.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Fed up with a group or leader and ready to stop following them.

examples.text: Once the party's most loyal supporters, disaffected factory workers began voting for the opposition.
The rebel army recruited heavily among disaffected soldiers who had not been paid in months.
After the founder was pushed out, a group of disaffected engineers left to start a rival firm.
The poem speaks for disaffected young people who no longer trust the institutions their parents believed in.

distractors.lemma: Done for show, so that a manner or accent seems put on.
Neutral in a dispute, with no side one hopes will win.
Held back in life by poverty, poor schools or other unfair conditions.
Winning over doubters or critics with openness or humor.
Swollen or sick because germs have taken hold in a cut or in the body.

mnemonics: Disaffected is dis- ('not') plus affected in its old sense of 'fond of': disaffected people have lost their fondness for those in charge.

senses.definition: Leave someone better informed and of finer character after a lesson, talk or book.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To teach people something that also makes them better people.

examples.text: The museum hopes to edify visitors as well as entertain them, so each display explains the science behind it.
Victorian children's books were written to edify, and every story ended with a clear moral lesson.
Her grandfather's long letters were meant to edify her, full of advice on honesty and hard work.
The preacher aimed to edify his listeners, not to frighten them into obedience.

distractors.lemma: Go through a manuscript or recording, fixing errors and trimming what is not needed.
Honor a human being or an idol as divine.
Gather scattered rules or customs into one orderly written set.
Stiffen with age until nothing about it can bend any more.

mnemonics: Edify comes from Latin aedificare, 'to build', as in edifice: to edify someone is to build up their mind or character.

senses.definition: Rub out or wear away a mark or memory until it can no longer be made out.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To wipe something out, such as writing or a memory, until it is gone.

examples.text: Not even forty years could efface her memory of the night their house burned down.
The new rulers tried to efface every trace of the old regime, renaming streets and pulling down statues.
The rising tide effaced the message they had written in the sand.
Centuries of rain had slowly effaced the carvings, until the stone was smooth again.

distractors.lemma: Leave a wall, statue or page ugly by deliberately scrawling across it.
Carry through a plan so that the intended change actually takes place.
Begin a talk or piece of writing with introductory words.
Send up streams of tiny bubbles that rise and pop at the top of a liquid.
Break through the top of the water after being down below it.

senses.definition: Play down one's own part so that others get the attention.

mnemonics: Efface is e- ('out') plus face: to efface something is to wipe its face away until nothing shows.

senses.definition: Make a heartfelt, urgent plea to someone for a favor or for mercy.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To beg someone, from the heart, to do what you ask.

examples.text: The prisoner's mother entreated the governor to spare her son's life.
"Please stay a little longer," she entreated, standing in front of the door.
Villagers entreated the soldiers to leave them their last sacks of grain for the winter.
He wrote to his estranged brother, entreating him to come home before their father died.

distractors.lemma: Leave something precious, or a duty, in another person's keeping on the strength of their good faith.
Give a custom or a group in power such a firm footing that rivals cannot uproot it.
Pull back from a fight or a dangerous position.
Set up a sting that tempts an otherwise innocent person into breaking the law.

mnemonics: Entreat contains treat: picture a child at the door begging for a treat, because to entreat is to plead hard for something.

senses.definition: Take up a belief or movement as one's own and speak in its favor.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To adopt a view and publicly stand up for it.

examples.text: Early in her career she espoused free-market ideas, but she later argued for stronger regulation.
Few scientists of the time were willing to espouse Darwin's theory in public.
The band's founders espoused a do-it-yourself ethic, recording and selling every album themselves.
The senator espouses the cause of rural hospitals and has spent years pushing for more funding.

distractors.lemma: Bring a hidden wrong or secret into the open for all to see.
Spot something from far away or pick it out where it is hard to see.
Look up to a person and value them highly.
Wipe an entry off an official record as if it had never been made.
Lie down at rest, calm and still, often after effort.

senses.definition: Enter into marriage with someone.

mnemonics: Espouse shares its Latin root sponsus, 'promised in marriage', with spouse: when you espouse a cause, you take it as a partner and stand by it.

senses.definition: Remove what gives something its strength or purpose, leaving only a weak shell.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To cut out the parts that make something work, so it is left weak.

examples.text: Last-minute amendments eviscerated the privacy bill, leaving a law that protected almost nothing.
Years of budget cuts have eviscerated the city's library system, which now opens only two days a week.
Critics said the editors had eviscerated the novel by cutting the very chapters that gave it meaning.
The ruling eviscerated the old treaty, keeping its name but removing every clause that mattered.

distractors.lemma: Declare someone free of blame after a charge has been looked into.
Remove tenants from their home through a court order or the landlord's legal right.
Make an attitude or trait plain for others to see.
Wear down someone's patience until they are openly angry.
Dry up as a liquid slowly passes into the air as vapor.

senses.definition: Pull the guts out of a slaughtered animal or a body.

mnemonics: Eviscerate comes from Latin e- ('out') plus viscera, 'inner organs': to eviscerate a law or plan is to rip its guts out.

senses.definition: A close, detailed reading that explains what a written text means, most often a passage of scripture.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Working out and explaining, line by line, what a text is really saying.

examples.text: Her exegesis of a single verse from Romans ran to forty pages of footnotes and Greek grammar.
The seminary trains future pastors in exegesis, so they can explain what each passage meant to its first readers.
Legal scholars offered a line-by-line exegesis of the amendment, arguing over the meaning of every comma.
Fans of the show write endless exegesis of each episode, combing the dialogue for hidden meanings.

distractors.lemma: A mass flight from a country or region by a large share of its people.
The birth of an idea, a movement or a thing, seen as its starting point.
The opening section of a speech or essay, meant to win the audience over.
A crisis that forces drastic steps to be taken without delay.
The act of cutting a part out, often a passage from a text or a growth from the body.

mnemonics: Exegesis comes from Greek exegeisthai, to lead out or explain: an exegesis leads the meaning out of a text.

senses.definition: Unfold the reasoning behind a doctrine or view, step after step, so others can follow it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To explain an idea in great detail, often in a long talk or piece of writing.

examples.text: In a forty-page letter to his followers, the reformer expounded why the church's rules on fasting had no basis in scripture.
The tour guide expounded on the castle's drainage system for so long that half the group drifted off to the gift shop.
Each chapter of the textbook expounds one principle of physics and then works through sample problems.
Give my aunt a whiteboard and a marker, and she will expound on her plan to fix the city's bus routes for an hour.

distractors.lemma: Erase a past conviction or mark so that official files show it never happened.
Seize property by legal authority and keep it locked away for a time.
Pile a new error on top of an old one so the trouble grows.
Pour effort or funds into something until the supply runs down.
Object to a person's plan to their face and try to talk them out of it.

mnemonics: Expound comes from Latin exponere, to put out or set forth: to expound an idea is to set it out piece by piece.

senses.definition: Offering a partial excuse for a misdeed, so that it earns less blame or a lighter penalty.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Making a bad act seem less bad, because there was a fair reason behind it.

examples.text: Because of extenuating circumstances, a burst pipe that flooded his apartment, the landlord let him pay the rent a week late.
Late papers lose a grade unless there are extenuating circumstances, like a hospital stay or a death in the family.
His lawyer argued that hunger was an extenuating factor in the theft of a loaf of bread.
The panel weighed several extenuating details, including the driver's spotless record and the broken traffic light.

distractors.lemma: Thrilling in a way that lifts the spirits.
Racking the body with pain, or making a moment painfully awkward.
Not part of the thing itself, or off the point of what is being discussed.
Made up in the moment by a speaker who has not prepared.
Overpriced to an outrageous degree.

mnemonics: Extenuating comes from Latin tenuis, thin, as in tenuous: extenuating circumstances thin out the blame.

senses.definition: Work someone or something free from a trap, a tangle or an awkward situation.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To get someone or something out of a tight spot or a tangle, often with effort.

examples.text: The boy climbed halfway up the oak to extricate his kite from the branches, then had to be helped back down.
Once he had agreed to help plan his cousin's wedding, he could find no polite way to extricate himself.
The fisherman spent an hour trying to extricate his anchor from the rocks on the harbor floor.
The fox had caught its leg in a wire fence, and it took two of us to extricate it before it limped off into the woods.

distractors.lemma: Turn an accused person over to another nation that wants to try them.
Stretch a known trend out into the future or into untested cases.
Wipe out rats, insects or other pests completely, usually with poison.
Condemn someone in public with fierce, stinging criticism.
Make a bad problem, pain or conflict grow worse.

mnemonics: Extricate and intricate share Latin tricae, perplexities: you extricate yourself by working out (ex-) of a perplexing mess.

senses.definition: A sham blow or move that lures an opponent's guard to one side so the real one can land.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A fake move that fools an opponent so you can strike where they are not guarding.

examples.text: She shaped up as if to drive the ball crosscourt, and the feint froze her opponent long enough for a soft drop shot.
His knight move was a feint; while his rival rushed to guard the queen, he quietly set up checkmate on the other wing.
The sheepdog made a feint to the left, and the stray ewe bolted right, straight through the open gate.
The burglars set off a car alarm down the street as a feint, then broke into the jewelry store while the guards went to look.

distractors.lemma: A brief blackout in which a person drops to the ground.
A remarkable achievement that few people could manage.
A festive public celebration held in someone's honor.
The destiny that some say is written for each person before birth.

mnemonics: Feint comes from French feinte, a pretense, from the same root as feign: a feint is a feigned attack.

senses.definition: Leave someone stuck with a burden or product they never chose.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To push an unwanted thing onto someone, often by tricking them.

examples.text: Every year the club foisted the job of scrubbing the team bus on whoever had skipped the vote.
The software update foisted a new layout on millions of users who had liked the old one just fine.
Voters resented having a candidate foisted on them by party leaders in a back room.
The studio foisted a happy ending on the director, who had shot a much darker one.

distractors.lemma: Get a load off the ground and up high with lifting gear.
Spoil someone's scheme and keep them from getting what they wanted.
Care for a child in one's home while the child's own parents cannot.
Break a rule as if daring anyone to stop you.
Pass up a treat, right or reward one could have had.

senses.definition: Sneak a passage, clause or item into something where it does not belong.

mnemonics: Foist goes back to a Dutch word for fist: cheats at dice would hide a loaded die in the hand and foist it into play.

senses.definition: Patient self-control in holding back from anger, revenge or punishment when there is cause for it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Holding back your temper and staying kind when you have a right to be angry.

examples.text: The referee showed real forbearance, letting the furious coach shout for a full minute before sending him off.
Her years of forbearance toward his drinking ended the night he crashed her car.
The truce held only because both sides practiced forbearance when small border clashes broke out.
Only a grandmother's forbearance could survive a week of the twins' spills, tantrums and endless questions.

distractors.lemma: An uneasy hunch that trouble lies ahead.
The good sense to plan for what the future may bring.
Boldness that goes beyond what is polite or modest.
The loss of goods or land that the law takes away as punishment.
Active promotion of an aim, interest or scheme.

senses.definition: A lender's choice to hold off on collecting a debt, often by pausing payments for a set time.

mnemonics: Forbearance contains bear, as in bear with me: to show forbearance is to bear with someone instead of lashing out.

senses.definition: Heavy with trouble or risk of some kind.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Full of something bad, usually danger, trouble or worry.

examples.text: Planning a wedding that unites two feuding families is fraught with peril, as any seating chart will show.
Any plan to move the old library is fraught with legal problems, since the land was donated on strict terms.
Her first year as a manager was fraught with difficulty, from layoffs to a lawsuit.
Early heart surgery was fraught with risk, and many patients did not survive the operation.

distractors.lemma: Formed by hammering rather than by pouring into a mold.
Based on lies told to cheat others out of money or goods.
Worn thin at the edges until loose threads show.
Living cheaply and spending only on what is needed.
Weak enough to crack or snap with little force.

senses.definition: Full of nervous strain that everyone present can sense.

mnemonics: Fraught is an old cousin of freight: a ship was once fraught with cargo, and a plan can now be fraught with risk.

senses.definition: Full of rushing, chaotic activity that seems close to spinning out of control.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Wildly busy and fast, in a rushed and messy way.

examples.text: In the last ten minutes before the ferry left, the dock was frenetic, with porters sprinting and late passengers hurling bags aboard.
The toddler's birthday party grew more frenetic by the minute, until twelve sugar-fueled children were racing in circles around the couch.
Her frenetic morning routine of three alarms, two coffees and a sprint to the bus left her tired before work began.
The drummer played at a frenetic tempo, his sticks a blur as the song raced toward its end.

distractors.lemma: So devoted to a creed that no argument can reach one.
Burning with deep conviction or longing.
Concerned with how spoken words sound and how those sounds are written.
Coded in the DNA and handed on when living things reproduce.

mnemonics: Frenetic shares its Greek root, phren (mind), with frenzy: a frenetic day is one long frenzy.

senses.definition: Annoying in a way that stings one's pride or feels deeply unfair.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So annoying that it hurts your pride, often because it seems unfair.

examples.text: It was galling to watch the rival firm win the contract with an idea she had pitched a year earlier.
After decades of loyal service, the most galling part of the layoff was being walked out by a guard.
Fans found it galling that the referee who made the bad call was chosen to work the final.
It is galling to be lectured on thrift by someone who has never paid a bill.

distractors.lemma: Courtly and chivalrous in the old-fashioned way.
Glaring and flashy in color, to the point of bad taste.
So gripping that one cannot look away.
Stirring a sleepy crowd or group into a burst of effort.

mnemonics: Galling comes from gall, a sore rubbed raw by a saddle: a galling remark rubs your pride raw.

senses.definition: Gather facts or insight a little at a time from scattered or limited sources.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To piece together what you want to know from small scraps of information.

examples.text: From a few stray remarks at lunch, she gleaned that the company was about to be sold.
Historians have gleaned much of what we know about the village from old tax records and letters.
The detective gleaned a name from the torn receipt in the victim's coat pocket.
Reading the fine print, I gleaned that the free trial would renew at full price after a week.

distractors.lemma: Give back light from a polished or wet surface.
Linger over a win so as to rub it in a beaten rival's face.
Stare at someone with open anger.
Give pottery or pastry a shiny finish by brushing on a coating.
Skim over a surface in a smooth, unbroken path.

senses.definition: Pick up the leftover grain that reapers missed after a harvest.

mnemonics: Glean first meant picking up the grain left behind by reapers; now you glean facts the same way, one stray bit at a time.

senses.definition: Give a person or a work a quality that becomes part of their very nature.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To give someone a strong feeling or belief that becomes part of who they are.

examples.text: Growing up on a struggling farm imbued her with a respect for hard work that never left her.
The director imbued the old fairy tale with a dark, uneasy mood that kept audiences on edge.
Their grandfather's war stories imbued the boys with a deep sense of duty to their country.
Soft candlelight and handwritten menus imbue the little restaurant with a warm, homey feel.

distractors.lemma: Swallow drinks, usually alcoholic ones, often more than is wise.
Suggest in public that a person is lying or acting from low motives.
Shut a person away behind thick walls, as in a prison cell.
Hold up a journey, a task or a process, causing delay.
Spear a person or animal on a stake, spike or horn.

senses.definition: Soak or stain something thoroughly with a dye or liquid.

mnemonics: Imbue comes from Latin imbuere, to wet or soak: an idea that imbues you has soaked in all the way.

senses.definition: Spur someone to act by a force, inner or outer, that is hard to resist.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To drive a person to do something, often by a powerful urge.

examples.text: Grief impelled the widow to plant a garden in every empty lot on her street.
The fear of being left behind impels many investors to buy at exactly the wrong moment.
Something about the stranger's frightened face impelled the bus driver to stop and open the doors again.
A stubborn streak impelled her to finish the marathon on a sprained ankle.

distractors.lemma: Kick a member out of a club or party as punishment.
Make water bead up and roll off instead of soaking in.
Clear a worry or rumor away so it no longer hangs around.
Skewer a body on a spear or pointed post.
Put lives, plans or a good name in harm's way.

mnemonics: Impel holds the Latin pellere, to drive, also found in propel and compel: what impels you drives you on.

senses.definition: The condition of getting away with wrongdoing because no one holds the doer to account.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being free from punishment or harm after doing something wrong.

examples.text: For years the gang ran its business with impunity, because the local police were on its payroll.
Drivers speed through the school zone with impunity now that the camera has been switched off.
Because the referee never looked their way, the defenders kicked and shoved with impunity all game.
Online trolls seem to think a fake name lets them insult people with impunity.

distractors.lemma: The state of being tainted by dirt or some foreign substance.
Pushy, nagging insistence in asking for something.
Saucy, cheeky boldness in speech or manner.
Scorn or mockery aimed at religious faith.
Hot-headed rashness in rushing into things.

mnemonics: Impunity joins Latin in-, not, with poena, penalty: to act with impunity is to act with no penalty at all.

senses.definition: Fixed so firmly in place or in the mind that it never fades away.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So lasting that it cannot be cleaned away or forgotten.

examples.text: The toddler scribbled on the wall with an indelible marker, and no amount of scrubbing would lift the ink.
Poll workers dip each voter's finger in indelible ink so that nobody can vote twice.
The moon landing, seen on a neighbor's black-and-white set, stayed indelible in my grandfather's memory for sixty years.
Decades later the siege remains indelible in the town's memory, and every family still tells stories of that winter.

distractors.lemma: Not fit or safe to be eaten, because it is spoiled or poisonous.
Touching on private or awkward subjects in a crude way.
Not meeting the conditions needed to qualify or take part.
Written so messily or faintly that nobody can make out the letters.
Lacking any argument that could make it look acceptable.

mnemonics: Indelible is in- (not) plus the Latin root of delete: what is indelible cannot be deleted.

senses.definition: Too determined or brave to be defeated, tamed or worn down.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Never giving up or giving in, however hard things get.

examples.text: Even after three failed businesses and a bankruptcy, his indomitable optimism had him drafting a fourth plan within weeks.
The indomitable defenders held the fort for eleven months and refused every offer to surrender.
At ninety, my great-aunt still hikes every morning, and her indomitable spirit shames the rest of us into joining her.
Floods, fires and two hurricanes could not break the indomitable fishing town, which rebuilt each time.

distractors.lemma: So plainly true that no one could reasonably doubt it.
Certain to happen whatever anyone does to stop it.
Unfriendly to visitors, or too harsh a place to live in.
Grave enough as an offense to be tried in a criminal court.
Bossy and eager to control what other people do.

mnemonics: Indomitable comes from Latin in- (not) and domitare, to tame: an indomitable spirit is one that nobody can tame.

senses.definition: One of a kind, with a quality that no rival has managed to reproduce.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Having a style or skill that is one person's alone; others try for it and fall short.

examples.text: Many singers have covered the song, but none can match her inimitable phrasing, which fans know from the first note.
Every bistro in town has tried to copy the chef's inimitable sauce, and none of the copies taste quite right.
No other comedian has his inimitable timing: he can wait ten full seconds before a punch line, and the silence itself gets a laugh.
Forgers have tried for decades to reproduce the painter's inimitable brushwork, and experts spot the fakes at a glance.

distractors.lemma: Unfriendly, or working against someone's interests.
So vast that no boundary or end can be found to it.
Unfair, because some people get more than their share.
Able to support people or animals as a place to settle.
Short-tempered and set off by the most minor things.

mnemonics: Inimitable is in- (not) plus imitable, able to be imitated: whatever is inimitable, no one can imitate.

senses.definition: Much larger than the situation calls for or can justify.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Far too much; more than makes sense.

examples.text: He devotes an inordinate amount of time to his lawn, sometimes four hours a day trimming the edges with scissors.
The audit found the agency had paid inordinate fees to consultants, nearly triple the going rate.
Our dog has an inordinate fear of the vacuum cleaner and hides under the bed for an hour after it is switched off.
Critics said the film gave an inordinate share of its running time to car chases and almost none to the plot.

distractors.lemma: Lower in rank and taking orders from someone above.
Openly defying the orders of those in charge.
Holding equal rank or standing with another.
Not alive, and showing no signs of life.
Not made from living things or their remains.
