mnemonics: Inordinate comes from Latin in- (not) and ordinatus, set in order: an inordinate amount has gone past its proper order or limit.

senses.definition: Suggest something damaging about someone by sly hints instead of plain words.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To drop sly hints that someone is guilty of something, without saying so.

examples.text: Without ever using the word cheat, the reporter insinuated that the coach had known about the doping all along.
Are you insinuating that I took the money? If you think so, say it plainly.
Her letter insinuated, through a string of pointed questions, that the landlord had kept the deposit on purpose.
He never accused his rival outright, but in interviews he would insinuate that her degrees had been bought.

distractors.lemma: Burn something until only ashes are left.
Add a layer that keeps warmth in, keeps cold out or muffles noise.
Make someone lose their head over a person they barely know.
Stir up trouble or set a harmful action going.
Launch something new with a first official event to mark its start.

senses.definition: Work oneself gradually and slyly into a place, a group or someone's favor.

mnemonics: Insinuate comes from Latin insinuare, to wind one's way in, from sinus, a curve: an insinuation curves in sideways instead of coming straight at you.

senses.definition: Tiresomely long; seemingly without end.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Dragging on and on, long past the point of boredom.

examples.text: The delay felt interminable: we sat at the gate for nine hours while the departure time slid back again and again.
The meeting dragged through an interminable list of minor items, and half the staff dozed off before the main topic came up.
The questions from the back seat seemed interminable, since every answer led to three more.
Fans grew restless during the interminable drum solo, which went on for nearly twenty minutes.

distractors.lemma: Coming and going, on one moment and off the next.
In the middle, neither a beginner's level nor an expert's.
Able to be swapped for one another.
Not fixed, measured or settled exactly.
Lacking self-control, especially with drink or temper.

mnemonics: Interminable is in- (not) plus Latin terminare, to end, the root of terminate: an interminable speech never seems to terminate.

senses.definition: Settled for good, with no way to reverse it or call it back.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Final; once it is done or decided, there is no going back.

examples.text: Once you click Delete, the action is irrevocable, so the program asks you twice to be sure.
Selling the family farm was an irrevocable step; the developer broke ground the following week.
Under the trust's terms, the gift becomes irrevocable after thirty days, and the donor cannot ask for the money back.
Once the email reached the whole company, her criticism of the boss was irrevocable; no apology could unsend it.

distractors.lemma: Off the topic and of no bearing on the question.
Showing a playful lack of respect for serious things.
Unable to make up one's mind and act.
So good that no one can find any fault in it.
Too deeply at odds for peace or common ground to be found.

mnemonics: Irrevocable is ir- (not) plus Latin revocare, to call back, the root of revoke: an irrevocable choice cannot be called back.

senses.definition: Give up or throw out something that is now more trouble than it is worth.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To drop or throw out something you no longer want because it is holding you back.

examples.text: When costs tripled, the city jettisoned its plan for a downtown stadium and fixed the roads instead.
To win over moderate voters, the party jettisoned several of its most extreme promises.
She jettisoned half her wardrobe before the move, keeping only what fit in two suitcases.
The coach was quick to jettison a failing game plan at halftime and switch to a running attack.

distractors.lemma: Elbow one's way along, knocking into the people nearby.
Risk ruining or losing something through one's own actions.
Joke or tease instead of speaking seriously.
Mock someone loudly and rudely from a crowd.
Gush out in a thin, forceful spurt.

senses.definition: Dump cargo or fuel overboard or in flight so that a struggling vessel or plane is lighter.

mnemonics: Jettison comes from Old French getaison, a throwing, from Latin iactare, to throw: to jettison a plan is to throw it overboard.

senses.definition: Dwelling on shocking or sordid details, usually of violence or sex, in order to excite.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Shocking and full of gory or sexual details meant to grab attention.

examples.text: The tabloid ran a lurid story about the murder, lingering on every gory detail to sell more copies.
The memoir sold well, thanks largely to its lurid tales of the singer's affairs and drug binges.
The prosecutor's lurid description of the crime scene, down to the spattered walls, made two jurors look away.
Without any evidence, gossip sites spread lurid rumors about the senator's sex life.

distractors.lemma: Expressed so clearly that the meaning comes through at once.
Shaking with fury; extremely angry.
Drowsy and slow-moving, with no wish to hurry.
Heavy with sorrow in a slow, drawn-out way.
Earning a large profit for those involved.

senses.definition: Glaring or unnaturally bright in color, often with a harsh red or orange glow.

mnemonics: Lurid comes from Latin luridus, sallow or ghastly pale: a lurid story is full of ghastly details.

senses.definition: A sly, secret scheme to get one's way, often at someone else's expense.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A sneaky scheme, hatched out of sight, to get the upper hand.

examples.text: Through months of quiet machinations, the deputy turned the board against the founder and took her job.
The novel follows the machinations of a scheming duke who poisons two heirs to clear his path to the throne.
Investors knew nothing of the machinations behind the merger until leaked emails revealed secret side deals.
She saw through her cousin's machination at once: the surprise party was a trick to get her out of the house so he could search it.

distractors.lemma: The change from work done by hand to work done by machines.
The mind's ability to invent pictures, stories and ideas of its own.
The system of offices and rules by which a government or group gets work done.
A showy, exaggerated pride in being tough and manly.
The working parts inside a device, or the way they act on each other.

mnemonics: Machination comes from Latin machinari, to contrive or plot, from machina, a device, the root of machine: a machination is a device built for scheming.

senses.definition: A drained, uneasy mood with no clear cause, found in one person or across a whole community.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A dull, hard-to-explain feeling that things are not right, often shared by many people.

examples.text: A deep malaise settled over the factory town after the plant closed, and even the high school games drew thin crowds.
Economists blamed years of flat wages and rising prices for the national malaise.
By February she felt a creeping malaise, sleeping late and losing interest in the hobbies she usually loved.
The new manager hoped a fresh project would lift the office out of its malaise after a year of low morale and missed deadlines.

distractors.lemma: Spite that makes someone set out to cause harm.
A wild tangle of bodies pushing, grabbing and swinging.
Harm a patient or client suffers because a professional did the job badly.
A laughable verbal blunder: saying one word while meaning its sound-alike.
A failure in a device or system that makes it act up or quit.

senses.definition: Feeling slightly off and run-down in body without any named illness.

mnemonics: Malaise is French, from mal, bad, and aise, ease: it is literally a bad ease, a feeling that things are not right.

senses.definition: Breaking the law or betraying the public's trust while carrying out an official role.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Wrongdoing by a person in power who uses the job to cheat or break the law.

examples.text: The mayor was removed for malfeasance after investigators found he had steered city contracts to his brother-in-law's firm.
Shareholders sued the board, accusing the directors of malfeasance for hiding losses from the auditors.
The sheriff's malfeasance came to light when deputies testified that he had sold seized cars for cash.
Voters were tired of malfeasance at city hall, from padded expense accounts to bribes for building permits.

distractors.lemma: The degree to which a plan can actually be carried out.
Deep-seated spite that makes a person hope others come to grief.
A formal curse pronounced against an enemy.
Clumsiness in handling objects, tasks or other people.

mnemonics: Malfeasance comes from Old French mal, badly, and faisance, doing, from faire, to do: it is literally bad doing by someone trusted to do right.

senses.definition: Deal out punishment, justice or harsh treatment to someone as their due.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To hand out punishment or justice to someone.

examples.text: The judge meted out the harshest sentence the law allowed: twenty years without parole.
Parents should mete out discipline calmly, not in the heat of anger.
The rebels meted out rough justice to anyone suspected of helping the army.
Referees who mete out yellow cards too freely can ruin the flow of a match.

distractors.lemma: Stick one's nose into matters that are someone else's to settle.
Blend two styles or groups until the seams between them disappear.
Carry offers back and forth between opponents until they strike a deal.
Loop and double back on the way somewhere, never keeping to the direct line.

mnemonics: Mete comes from Old English metan, to measure: to mete out punishment is to measure out what each person is owed.

senses.definition: Toughness of spirit that lets a person hold firm and press on through danger or hardship.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The courage and grit to keep trying when things get hard.

examples.text: Facing a hostile crowd on her own, the young lawyer showed her mettle by refusing to drop the case.
Losing his job and his home in the same year tested his mettle, yet he kept pushing and rebuilt both.
Trailing by twenty points at halftime, the team proved its mettle with a fearless second-half comeback.
Nobody doubted the new nurse's mettle after she stayed calm through a night of back-to-back emergencies.

distractors.lemma: A habit of checking and rechecking each detail until the work is flawless.
A gloomy cast of mind that lingers for months and shades how a person sees the world.
A nosy streak that keeps a person poking into business that belongs to others.
A relaxed, easygoing warmth of temper that often comes with age.

mnemonics: Mettle began as another spelling of metal, so a person of mettle is made of tough stuff, like good steel.

senses.definition: The mix of people, ideas and customs that make up the world a person moves in.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The world of people, places and habits that surrounds someone.

examples.text: As a teenager she worked in her uncle's jazz club, a milieu of late nights, borrowed horns and musicians swapping stories.
Coming from a working-class milieu, he was startled by how casually the other law students talked about ski trips and summer homes.
Raised in a milieu of army bases and frequent moves, he learned early how to make friends within a single week.
Founders tend to thrive in a milieu where failure is treated as a lesson rather than a disgrace.

distractors.lemma: A low, foggy discontent, in a person or a whole society, that has no single source.
The bearing and facial expression by which a person comes across to others.
A disorderly brawl or crush where a crowd shoves and grapples at close quarters.
A turning point that marks how far a person or a project has come.

mnemonics: Milieu is French: mi, middle, plus lieu, place. Your milieu is the place you stand in the middle of.

senses.definition: A villain or lawbreaker, whether a petty vandal or a hardened criminal.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Someone up to no good, from small mischief to serious crime.

examples.text: Police are still looking for the miscreants who spray-painted insults across the new library wall.
A pair of miscreants slashed the tires of every car in the lot and fled before dawn.
The teacher seated the class miscreant at the front, where he could no longer flick paper at anyone.
Online, a single miscreant can flood a forum with abuse and drive away dozens of regular users.

distractors.lemma: A person whose religious life centers on direct, wordless experience of the divine.
A person with a sour, low opinion of humankind who avoids company where possible.
A person who never blends in, the odd one out at school, at work or at home.
A believer posted to a far-off land to spread the faith and win converts.
A person who scorns women and treats them with open hostility.

mnemonics: Miscreant comes from Old French mescreant, unbelieving: mes-, wrongly, and creant, believing. A heretic slowly became any villain.

senses.definition: A name or label that gives a wrong idea of the thing it is attached to.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A name that suggests the wrong thing about what something is.

examples.text: Calling the koala a bear is a misnomer, since it is actually a marsupial.
The so-called shortcut through the hills was a misnomer: it added forty minutes to the drive.
The name peanut is a misnomer, because the plant is a legume and not a true nut.
Since the express train stopped at every station, commuters joked that its name was a misnomer.

distractors.lemma: A nagging doubt that a decision already made may prove unwise.
A slip or small accident, the kind that spoils a day but is soon forgotten.
A lesser crime, the sort that is settled in a local court and rarely leads to prison.
A union, often a marriage, that pairs two people with little in common or of unequal rank.
A typing or printing error that leaves a wrong letter or word on the page.

mnemonics: Misnomer joins mis-, wrongly, with Old French nomer, to name: a misnomer names a thing wrongly.

senses.definition: The unwritten rules of conduct and moral standards that a group expects its members to follow.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: What a group sees as proper and decent behavior, even if no law says so.

examples.text: The film mocks the mores of 1950s suburbia, where every lawn was trimmed and every family secret hidden.
Workplace mores have shifted, and jeans that once raised eyebrows at the office now go unnoticed.
Anthropologists spend years learning a community's mores before they can tell a polite gesture from an insult.
Her memoir shows how the sexual mores of the 1960s changed faster than her parents could accept.

distractors.lemma: The fighting spirit of a team or army, which rises with success and sinks with hardship.
A situation so snarled with trouble that every step out of it takes great effort.
A halt called on some activity until a set date or a decision.
Human beings' shared fate of dying, which sets them apart from the immortal gods of myth.

mnemonics: Say mores as MOR-ayz. It is the Latin plural of mos, custom, the root of moral: a group's mores are its moral customs.

senses.definition: Close to death, or so far into decline that an end seems near.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Dying, or fading so badly that it will soon be gone.

examples.text: By the 1980s the town's steel mills were moribund, and most had closed within a decade.
The hospice nurse sat with the moribund patient through the night, holding her hand until the end.
A new owner tried to revive the moribund newspaper, but subscriptions kept falling until it shut.
Typewriter repair is a moribund trade, with only a handful of shops left in the whole country.

distractors.lemma: Unhealthily drawn to grisly or gloomy subjects and inclined to dwell on them.
Witty in a cutting way that stings the people it is aimed at.
Filled with shame after being embarrassed in front of others.
Glum and withdrawn, with a sour gloom that keeps others at a distance.
Quick to judge others by strict ideas of right and wrong.

senses.definition: Stuck and lifeless, showing no growth, energy or new ideas.

mnemonics: Moribund comes from Latin mori, to die, the same root as mortal: something moribund is on its way to dying.

senses.definition: Fixed on the short term or a narrow view, with little thought for what comes later.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Thinking only about what is close at hand and ignoring what comes later.

examples.text: Cutting the research budget to boost one quarter's profit was a myopic move that cost the company its lead.
Voters punished the council for its myopic plan to sell off the town's parkland for quick cash.
It is myopic to judge a new teacher on her first week instead of her whole first year.
Critics called the energy policy myopic, saying it eased this winter's shortage while ignoring the next decade.

distractors.lemma: Present in such great numbers that counting them is hopeless.
Tied to whatever story is making headlines in the news this week.
Generous with gifts of time and money to causes that serve the public.
Convinced that people are mostly selfish and better kept at arm's length.
So small that its size is measured in millionths of a meter.

senses.definition: Unable to make out distant things clearly, though near objects look sharp.

mnemonics: Myopic comes from Greek myein, to shut, and ops, eye: a myopic planner squints at what is near and misses what lies ahead.

senses.definition: The view that nothing has real worth or purpose, so moral rules and beliefs have no true basis.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The idea that nothing truly matters and no belief or rule is worth holding.

examples.text: After the war, a mood of nihilism spread among young writers who no longer trusted any cause or creed.
The villain's nihilism is chilling: he burns the city not for money but because he thinks nothing matters.
Her professor argued that Nietzsche did not preach nihilism but warned about the emptiness it would bring.
Years of broken promises left him sunk in nihilism, sure that voting, saving and planning were all pointless.

distractors.lemma: A craving for admiration joined to a puffed-up sense of one's own importance.
A political stance that puts native-born residents ahead of immigrants and distrusts newcomers.
An approach in fiction and painting that records ordinary life in faithful detail, flaws included.
A creed that rallies people around flag and homeland, often while pressing for self-rule.

senses.definition: A radical movement of young Russians in the 1860s that scorned church, state and family authority alike.

mnemonics: Nihilism comes from Latin nihil, nothing, the root of annihilate: to a nihilist, nothing has any real value.

senses.definition: Coming at a subject sideways, through suggestion, so that the point is never stated outright.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Hinting at something instead of saying it plainly.

examples.text: Rather than criticize her boss openly, she made an oblique remark about people who never read their email.
The letter's oblique mention of recent changes was the only hint that the factory would soon close.
Asked whether he would run again, the senator gave an oblique answer about serving wherever he was needed.
The poem treats grief in an oblique way, never naming the lost child but describing her empty swing.

distractors.lemma: Blind to one's surroundings, with attention fixed somewhere else.
Gone out of use or date, its job now done by a later invention.
Compulsory, so that one must do it whether one wants to or not.
Fawning over people in power and agreeing with whatever they say.
Grating and offensive in manner, so that people dread being near.

senses.definition: Sloping at an angle, so that it is neither level, upright nor at a right angle to a given line.

mnemonics: Oblique comes from Latin obliquus, slanting: an oblique remark comes at its point on a slant instead of head-on.

senses.definition: A duty that falls to one particular party, especially the task of proving a disputed claim.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The job of doing or proving something, which rests on one person or side.

examples.text: When the dishwasher broke, the onus fell on the kids to wash every plate by hand.
Since you made the claim, the onus is on you to show us the evidence.
The new law shifts the onus onto employers to show that their hiring was fair.
With the manager away, the onus of keeping the project on schedule fell to the youngest member of the team.

distractors.lemma: A solemn pledge spoken aloud, often with one hand raised, before taking office or giving evidence.
The general scorn that clings to someone whose conduct has disgraced them.
A grueling, frightening experience that a person comes out of shaken.
A furious assault, or a pile of demands or blows that keeps coming without a break.
Something seen or heard that people read as a hint of luck or trouble ahead.

mnemonics: Onus is Latin for a load, and it is the root of onerous: the onus is the burden someone has to carry.

senses.definition: Put forward for others to see and accept, whether or not it is what lies underneath.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Claimed out loud or shown on the surface, but perhaps only a cover story.

examples.text: The ostensible purpose of the new fee was to fund road repairs, yet the potholes were still there a year later.
Her ostensible errand was returning a borrowed book, yet she stayed for hours asking about the job opening.
Though the group's ostensible aim is protecting wildlife, most of its money goes to lobbying for developers.
The singer was the ostensible leader of the band, but the drummer made every real decision.

distractors.lemma: Showy and flashy, designed to catch the eye and make others envious.
Big in size, range or amount, taking in a great many parts or places.
Sound enough to hold up when someone challenges it.
Level-headed and practical, making choices that good sense would support.
Unwilling to budge from a stance no matter how good the case against it.

mnemonics: Ostensible comes from Latin ostendere, to show: the ostensible reason is the one put on show, not always the true one.

senses.definition: Flamboyant self-assurance and style in the way a person acts or performs.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Doing things with confident, eye-catching style.

examples.text: The chef plated each dish with such panache that diners took photos before taking a bite.
He wore a purple suit and a feathered hat to the gala, and carried it off with real panache.
The pianist dashed off the fiendish final passage with panache, grinning at the audience as she played.
The winger scored with panache, flicking the ball over the keeper with the outside of his boot.

distractors.lemma: A single cure claimed to fix all ills or problems at once.
A fondness or taste for something that a person keeps returning to.
A soft sheen or colored film that builds up on bronze, wood or leather with age.
A piece of art or writing that borrows and blends the manner of earlier works.
A wide sweep of scenery seen from one high spot.

senses.definition: A plume of feathers worn on top of a helmet or hat.

mnemonics: Panache first meant the plume of feathers on a knight's helmet; to do something with panache is to ride in with your plume held high.

senses.definition: The particular words and turns of phrase that a group, trade or field habitually uses.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The special words and ways of talking that a certain group of people uses.

examples.text: In sailing parlance, the left side of a boat is called port and the right side starboard.
The word selfie moved from internet slang into common parlance within a few short years.
To a stock trader a bear is not an animal; in market parlance it is someone who expects prices to fall.
The new manager's memos were full of corporate parlance such as synergy and circle back, which baffled her staff.

distractors.lemma: A talk between opposing sides to settle terms, often held during a war.
A sitting room in a house, once kept for receiving visitors.
The national body of elected members who debate and vote on new laws.
A short invented story whose events carry a moral lesson.
A sickly, washed-out look in the skin of a person's face.

mnemonics: Parlance comes from French parler, to speak: your parlance is the way your group speaks.

senses.definition: Taking an interest only in local affairs and the concerns of one's own community, while ignoring the larger picture.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Caring only about your own small area or group and not about the rest of the world.

examples.text: Living abroad for a year cured him of the parochial belief that his hometown did everything best.
The paper's coverage was so parochial that a war overseas got less space than a bake sale on Main Street.
Voters wanted a leader with a national vision, not a parochial politician who fought only for her own district's roads.
Critics called the council parochial for arguing about one street's parking fees while the whole region's water supply ran dry.

distractors.lemma: Built from claims that seem to clash with each other yet may both be true.
Added to a sentence as a side remark and set apart by brackets or commas.
Drawing food from another creature by clinging to it or dwelling in its body.
Relating to the countryside and the quiet life of farmers and shepherds.
Gripped by an unfounded fear that others are scheming to harm you.

senses.definition: Run by or tied to the church of a local district.

mnemonics: Parochial shares its Latin root, parochia, with parish: a parochial view stops at the edge of your own parish.

senses.definition: Of a size, quantity or power far beyond the normal, enough to inspire wonder.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So huge or impressive that people are amazed by it.

examples.text: She had a prodigious memory and could recite whole chapters after reading them only once.
The young pitcher's prodigious arm sent fastballs across the plate at over a hundred miles an hour.
Building the cathedral took a prodigious amount of stone, labor and money over two centuries.
Even by the standards of competitive eating, his appetite was prodigious: forty hot dogs in ten minutes.

distractors.lemma: Careless with money, spending it fast and without thought for tomorrow.
Held in high regard because of a long record of success.
Reaching a grown-up level of skill or behavior while still a young child.
Pointing to a good outcome, and so well suited for starting something.
Spreading harm gradually and out of sight until it is hard to undo.

mnemonics: Prodigious is related to prodigy, a person with amazing gifts: both come from Latin prodigium, a marvel or omen.

senses.definition: Hold out or put forward something for another person to take or turn down.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To hold out your hand, a gift or an idea for someone to take.

examples.text: He stood and proffered his hand, but she walked past without shaking it.
The waiter proffered a tray of champagne glasses to each guest who came through the door.
Several experts proffered explanations for the crash, though none could be proven.
When her rival finally proffered an apology, she accepted it with a stiff nod.

distractors.lemma: Declare in public that you hold a belief or skill, whether or not you really do.
Like one choice better than the others available.
Insult or misuse something that people hold sacred.
Grow successful and well off over time.
Supply the force that sends something moving forward.

mnemonics: Proffer is pro-, forward, plus offer: when you proffer something, you put an offer forward.

senses.definition: Actively seek converts to one's own religion, or press any belief on others with the same zeal.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To keep pushing other people to join your religion or agree with your beliefs.

examples.text: The missionaries went door to door to proselytize, handing out pamphlets and inviting families to Sunday services.
Ever since he went vegan, he proselytizes at every dinner, lecturing his friends about the evils of meat.
The street preacher tried to proselytize anyone who paused, promising salvation if they would only join his church.
Company rules forbid managers to proselytize at work, so talk of faith is kept out of staff meetings.

distractors.lemma: Take a person accused of breaking the law to trial and argue for a conviction.
Lie flat on the ground, face down, to show worship or total surrender.
Declare something forbidden by an official ruling.
Foretell what will happen, claiming the knowledge comes from God.
Multiply quickly and spread in large numbers.

mnemonics: Proselytize comes from proselyte, Greek for one who has come over: a person who proselytizes wants you to come over to their side.

senses.definition: The source of something: the place, maker or setting it first arose from.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Where a thing started out, or who first made it.

examples.text: Before buying the painting, the museum hired experts to trace its provenance back to the artist's studio.
Botanists used the seeds' DNA to pin down their provenance: a single valley high in the Andes.
Shoppers increasingly want to know the provenance of their coffee, down to the farm where the beans were grown.
Linguists have traced the provenance of the word ketchup to a fish sauce from southern China.

distractors.lemma: Good fortune that believers credit to God's watchful hand.
A major region of a country that runs some of its own affairs.
A catch tacked onto a deal or promise, naming what must hold for it to stand.
What a doctor expects will happen to a patient over the coming weeks or years.
A brief, familiar saying that sums up a piece of everyday wisdom.

senses.definition: The paper trail showing each hand a valuable object has passed through since it was made.

mnemonics: Provenance comes from French provenir, to come from: an object's provenance tells you where it came from.

senses.definition: The field of questions or tasks that an official, office or court has the power to decide.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The set of things someone is in charge of or allowed to deal with.

examples.text: Zoning disputes fall outside the school board's purview, since only the city council has the power to change land rules.
The new law widened the agency's purview, giving its inspectors power to audit online banks as well as traditional ones.
The clerk said refunds were not within her purview and pointed me to a supervisor who could approve them.
Questions about the drug's price lie beyond the safety panel's purview, because the panel was set up only to rule on side effects.

distractors.lemma: The business of keeping a household, army or ship stocked with food and goods.
A slow, close read of a document that takes in every line.
A hunt for someone on the run, kept up until they are caught or get away.
The aim behind an action, or the use a thing was designed to serve.
A stretch of misery that must be sat through before any relief arrives.

senses.definition: The extent of what a person can see or understand.

mnemonics: Purview comes from Anglo-French purveu, provided, a word that opened old laws. It also ends in view: matters within your purview are in view of your authority.

senses.definition: A predicament so tangled that each effort to get free only sinks one deeper.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A messy problem you get stuck in, which only gets worse the longer it lasts.

examples.text: What began as a quick border operation became a military quagmire, with troops unable to win or withdraw for a decade.
Each new lawsuit sank the company deeper into a legal quagmire, with no way out that did not cost millions.
The renovation became a financial quagmire, as every wall they opened revealed another costly problem.
Lawmakers set out to simplify the tax code but got stuck in a quagmire of competing interests and loopholes.

distractors.lemma: A falling-out between friends, relatives or neighbors that turns loud and bitter.
A waiting period in isolation that travelers or animals must serve before mixing freely.
A calm spell during which something normally active lies still for a time.
The event that finally silences something for good, including a person's death.

senses.definition: Ground so soft and waterlogged that it sinks under a person's weight.

mnemonics: Quagmire joins quag, an old word for a bog, with mire, deep mud: step into a quagmire and you sink.

senses.definition: The mending of a rift between former rivals, especially states, so that they can cooperate again.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: When two sides that were enemies or rivals start to get along again.

examples.text: After decades of hostility, the two countries' rapprochement began with a quiet exchange of ambassadors.
The brothers' rapprochement came at their father's funeral, where they shook hands for the first time in years.
Nixon's 1972 visit to Beijing marked a rapprochement between the United States and China after years without diplomatic ties.
Hopes for a rapprochement between the union and management faded when talks collapsed for the third time.

distractors.lemma: A rebuke delivered more in sorrow than in anger.
A creeping advance past a boundary into space that is not yours.
An act of revenge carried out against an enemy who caused harm.
A last-minute halt to a sentence, sparing someone from the penalty for now.
A rough working figure, good enough for planning though off by a little.

mnemonics: Rapprochement comes from French rapprocher, to bring back together, built on approcher, to approach: old rivals approach each other again.

senses.definition: The repeated lawbreaking of an offender who has already been convicted, whether on probation, on parole or after release.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: When people already caught and punished for crimes go on to commit more.

examples.text: Prisons that offer job training report lower recidivism, since fewer of their inmates are rearrested after release.
Within three years of release, nearly half the inmates were back behind bars, a recidivism rate that alarmed officials.
The judge hoped drug treatment would break the young man's cycle of recidivism, which had already brought him back to court four times.
Backers of the reading program in juvenile jails point to its effect on recidivism: few of its graduates ever return.

distractors.lemma: The practice of reworking accepted accounts of history or doctrine.
A period in which a country's economic activity shrinks and jobs are lost.
The give-and-take between people or nations who repay each other's favors in kind.
An ingrained habit of digging in one's heels whenever someone in charge gives an order.
The belief that no moral rule holds everywhere, since each society sets its own.

mnemonics: Recidivism comes from Latin recidivus, falling back: recidivism is falling back into crime.

senses.definition: An accusation made in return against someone who has blamed you, often as part of a bitter exchange.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Blame thrown back at someone who has blamed you first.

examples.text: After the team lost the final, the locker room filled with recriminations as players blamed each other for the missed tackles.
At the reunion, old classmates fell into recriminations about who had leaked the exam answers twenty years earlier.
Rather than waste time on recrimination over the failed launch, the manager asked what they could fix by Monday.
When the bridge collapsed, the builders and the city traded recriminations, each insisting the other had cut corners.

distractors.lemma: The denial of fair chances in jobs, housing or law on grounds of race, faith or sex.
Play, sport or hobbies taken up for pleasure in time off from work.
The rest and healing time a body needs to bounce back after sickness or surgery.
A public taking back of something one said or believed earlier.
The money a person is paid for doing a job, including wages and benefits.

mnemonics: Recrimination joins re-, back, with Latin criminari, to accuse: you throw the charge back at your accuser.

senses.definition: Compensation or other action that makes up for an injustice a person has suffered.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Making up for harm done to someone, by fixing it or paying them back.

examples.text: The workers sued the company, seeking redress for the wages it had illegally withheld.
Customers who were overcharged can apply for redress through the state's consumer protection office.
Decades later, the government offered formal redress to families forced from their land: an apology and cash payments.
When the airline lost her luggage, the only redress it offered was a voucher worth a fraction of her loss.

distractors.lemma: Needless doubling of words or parts that serve the same purpose.
A reshuffling of who holds wealth, land or goods, often by government policy.
A short break from work, school or a court session.
The hiding of sensitive passages in a record so readers see only what is safe to share.
A slipping back to a cruder stage that had been left behind.

mnemonics: Redress is re- plus dress in its old sense of set straight: redress sets a wrong straight again.

senses.definition: The group following and attending to some important person.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The helpers, guards and staff who go everywhere with a famous or powerful person.

examples.text: The queen arrived at the cathedral with a retinue of guards, ladies-in-waiting and secretaries trailing behind her.
The pop star's retinue of stylists, bodyguards and publicists took up an entire floor of the hotel.
The visiting chess champion traveled with a retinue of coaches, a chef, a doctor and two bodyguards.
The sultan walked through the market while his retinue of servants and courtiers held a parasol over his head and cleared a path.

distractors.lemma: The total money brought in by a company or a state over a period.
A meeting again of people who once spent much time together, often marked by a party.
Whatever clings to a dish, pipe or surface after the main contents have gone.
A stage entertainment with no single story, built from one quick act after another.
The few survivors still holding together after most of a group has been lost.

mnemonics: Retinue comes from Old French retenue, a body of people kept on, from retenir, to retain: a great person retains a retinue to travel at their side.

senses.definition: A reply that turns a remark or criticism back on the speaker, delivered without delay and with wit.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A clever line shot straight back at someone who has just taken a dig at you.

examples.text: When a heckler shouted that she was boring, the comedian's riposte got a bigger laugh than any joke in her set.
Asked whether he was too old to run again, the senator fired back a quick riposte about his rival's own birthday.
Her riposte to the critic who called her novel slight was a single line: so was his review.
He thought of the perfect riposte to his boss's jab only hours later, standing in the shower.

distractors.lemma: A warm, easy understanding between people who get along well.
A correction in which a speaker or paper withdraws an earlier claim and owns the error.
A final afterthought jotted beneath a letter's signature.
A courteous ask, spoken or written, for a favor or a service.
A brief let-up that gives someone a chance to breathe during a hard time.

senses.definition: In fencing, the attack a fencer makes in return as soon as the other's blade has been knocked aside.

mnemonics: Riposte comes from Italian risposta, an answer, a cousin of respond: a riposte is a reply that strikes back fast.

senses.definition: A rupture in a once-united body of people, after which its parts treat each other as rivals.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A split that turns one group into rival sides that no longer agree.

examples.text: The vote on the merger caused a schism in the union, and a third of the members left to form their own.
What began as a quarrel over the club's rules grew into a schism, with each faction electing its own president.
Historians trace the party's collapse to the schism between its free-trade and protectionist wings.
The founders' bitter schism over the company's direction divided the staff into two loyal camps.

distractors.lemma: A muscle cramp or twitch that strikes all at once and cannot be stopped at will.
Reasoning that hides a flaw under polished words, offered to win a point rather than find the truth.
A slip in grammar or usage, or a lapse in polite behavior.
The stance of someone who questions what others readily believe.

senses.definition: The breaking away of a church or part of one, so that two bodies now each claim to be the true church.

mnemonics: Schism comes from Greek schisma, a split or cut: a schism cuts one group into two.

senses.definition: A thin, surface version of something that passes at a glance but would not hold up to a close look.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Just enough of something to look real on the surface, even if there is little behind it.

examples.text: After weeks of chaos, the new manager restored some semblance of order to the warehouse.
The trial had only a semblance of fairness, since the verdict had been decided before it began.
She forced a smile and kept up a semblance of calm until the last guest had gone home.
Months after the fire, the family had rebuilt a semblance of their old routine, though nothing felt quite the same.

distractors.lemma: A ceremony, a day or a keepsake set aside so that the dead are honored and not forgotten.
A company of players or singers who rehearse and appear together.
A formal gathering of members, students or lawmakers called to meet in one hall.
The capacity of a living being to feel pain, pleasure and other sensations.
An old flag code, read by sailors and soldiers, in which each arm angle stands for a letter.

mnemonics: Semblance comes from Old French sembler, to seem, the root of resemble: a semblance only seems to be the thing itself.

senses.definition: A cluster of incidents of one kind, packed close together in time.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A run of the same sort of event, each one close on the heels of the last.

examples.text: After a spate of bike thefts outside the station, the city put in locked racks and a camera.
The airline faced a spate of lawsuits after three of its flights were canceled in a single week.
After a spate of injuries to key players, the coach had to start two rookies in the final.
The new law followed a spate of crashes, five in one month, all involving drivers who were texting.

distractors.lemma: A petty row between people close to each other, often over chores or plans.
The lineup of candidates a party puts forward together for one vote.
A glib stream of talk recited from memory to draw in a crowd or a buyer.
A spending binge on treats one would normally go without.

senses.definition: A river running high and fast after a storm or a quick thaw.

mnemonics: Spate first meant a river in sudden flood, so a spate of events is a flood of them arriving all at once.

senses.definition: Grimy, shabby and decaying, with the look of a place nobody can afford to keep up.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So filthy and broken-down that no one should have to live there.

examples.text: Twelve workers were crammed into one squalid room with no running water and rats in the walls.
Reporters who visited the camp described squalid tents surrounded by open sewage.
The landlord rented out squalid basement rooms where sewage seeped under the doors and the windows were nailed shut.
Inspectors shut the kitchen down after finding squalid conditions, with mold on the walls and food rotting on the counters.

distractors.lemma: Quick to turn pale and queasy at anything gory or disgusting.
Prone to gusts that blow up out of nowhere and pass quickly, often with rain.
Unexcitable and plodding, with a face that rarely gives away a feeling.
Having a washed-out, colorless face from sickness or staying indoors.
Short and stocky, thicker through the middle than its height suggests.

senses.definition: Shameful and cheap in conduct, with nothing decent about the motives.

mnemonics: Squalid comes from Latin squalere, to be caked with dirt, which also gives squalor, the state of a squalid home.

senses.definition: Unshaken in loyalty, the kind of supporter a cause can count on year after year.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Loyal and reliable, someone you can count on to stick with you.

examples.text: A stalwart member of the choir, he has not missed a Thursday rehearsal in twenty-two years.
Even when the team lost twenty games in a row, its stalwart fans filled the stands each Sunday.
The senator thanked her stalwart door-knockers, who had walked the district in rain and snow through three elections.
He remained a stalwart ally of the union long after his colleagues had abandoned it.

distractors.lemma: Shrill and jarring, whether in the sound of a voice or in the force of a protest.
Wooden in speech or writing, as if every phrase had been rehearsed.
Sly and hushed in movement, so as to slip by unnoticed.
Stuck in sensible old habits and wary of anything daring or fun.
Lofty and solemn in bearing, suited to a palace or a coronation.

senses.definition: Big-boned and brawny in build.

mnemonics: Stalwart comes from Old English stael, place, and weorth, worth: a stalwart friend is worth their place at your side.

senses.definition: Force apart things or people that were joined, so that they cannot easily come back together.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To split up what was together, so badly that it may never be whole again.

examples.text: A single bolt of lightning sundered the ancient oak, leaving one half standing and the other on the ground.
A bitter fight over their father's will sundered the brothers, who did not speak for twenty years.
The civil war sundered families, sending cousins to fight on opposite sides.
Nothing, she promised, would ever sunder the bond between the two sisters.

distractors.lemma: Stroll along at an easy, lazy pace with no need to hurry.
Throw away wealth or a rare opening through careless, wasteful use.
Smear a rival out loud with lies meant to turn others against them.
Lay down arms and yield to the side one was fighting.
Send a command that brings a person before a judge, a ruler or a meeting.

mnemonics: Sunder comes from Old English sundrian, built on sundor, apart, which also gives asunder: to sunder something is to tear it asunder.

senses.definition: Replace a person or thing and leave the earlier one cast aside or forgotten.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To replace something, so the one before falls out of use or loses its power.

examples.text: Streaming services have largely supplanted the video rental stores that once filled every mall.
The young general plotted for years to supplant the king and seize the throne himself.
Within a decade, solar power had supplanted coal so completely that the region's last coal plant shut down.
She feared that the charming new hire meant to supplant her as head of the department.

distractors.lemma: Add an extra amount to fill out what is already there.
Beg a god or a powerful person for help, in a meek and pleading way.
Fit a device or graft of tissue into a patient's body by surgery.
Move a rooted seedling or shrub from one bed or pot into another.
Crush a protest or uprising with police or troops.

mnemonics: Supplant comes from Latin supplantare, to trip up, built on planta, the sole: you trip a rival and step into their place.

senses.definition: Dangle something a person craves where they can see it but never have it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To tease someone with something they long for but cannot quite get.

examples.text: The hungry dog sat beside the table, tantalized by a steak it was not allowed to touch.
For years the old treasure map tantalized explorers, who could never find the island it showed.
Glimpses of the sea between the buildings tantalized us all afternoon, but we never found a path down to the beach.
The one surviving page of the lost manuscript has tantalized scholars for a century, since the rest has never been found.

distractors.lemma: Rub someone the wrong way until they turn hostile.
Give a frightened animal a shot that leaves it limp and drowsy.
Daydream about wishes coming true, in scenes that exist only in the mind.
Wind strands of rope, wire or hair around each other into a knotted clump.

mnemonics: Tantalize comes from Tantalus, a king in Greek myth made to stand in water under fruit trees: the water sank and the fruit rose whenever he tried to drink or eat.

senses.definition: Serving as a figurehead whose title brings honor but no command.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Called the leader, but only for show, without any power to act.

examples.text: The king is only the titular head of state; parliament and the prime minister run the country.
Every child in the club got a titular job, such as Keeper of Snacks, that came with no actual duties.
As titular chair of the board, the founder attended dinners and cut ribbons but had no vote.
The retired coach was named titular captain for the final game, so he tossed the coin while the real captain called the plays.

distractors.lemma: Acting as a patron spirit or protector that keeps watch over a home or town.
Of a scale or force so vast that it dwarfs everything around it.
Spicy enough to give a little thrill of shock or desire.
Hesitant and fearful, shrinking back from anything bold.

senses.definition: Being the figure that a story, song or show is named after.

mnemonics: Titular comes from Latin titulus, a title or label: a titular leader has the title and little else.

senses.definition: Grinding toil or hardship that wears a person down over time.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Very hard work or a painful struggle that goes on for a long time.

examples.text: Her memoir describes the travails of raising three children alone while working two jobs.
After months of travail on the farm, the drought wiped out the harvest anyway.
The book traces the travails of a small family bakery trying to survive a decade of rising rents.
Few tourists who climb the cathedral steps think about the travail of the masons who carved every stone by hand.

distractors.lemma: Making trips away from home, often to distant lands.
A crude imitation so poor that it insults the real thing.
Odd scraps of fact that are fun to know but of little use.
An outburst of furious scolding that goes on and on.
A thorough scholarly study that sets out one subject in depth.

senses.definition: The pain and effort of giving birth.

mnemonics: Travel began as the same word as travail: long journeys were once such hard, painful work that one word covered both.

senses.definition: Hands-on teaching in which a more skilled person directs and corrects a learner's work.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being trained by someone who shows you how and checks your work.

examples.text: Under the tutelage of a retired concert pianist, the shy teenager learned to play Chopin with real confidence.
She spent three years in the kitchen under the chef's tutelage before opening a restaurant of her own.
The young lawyer flourished under the tutelage of a senior partner who read and marked up every brief she wrote.
Without his grandfather's patient tutelage, he would never have learned to repair old clocks.

distractors.lemma: A noisy uproar in which a crowd falls into confusion.
Wicked, shameful conduct that breaks basic moral standards.
The work of plowing and turning soil so that crops can be grown in it.
The knack of sensing an answer before one can say how one reached it.
Money and favor from a rich sponsor that keep an artist or a cause afloat.

senses.definition: The protective care of a guardian who is responsible for someone.

mnemonics: Tutelage shares a Latin root with tutor, tueri (to watch over): under someone's tutelage, a tutor watches over your learning.

senses.definition: Beyond any realistic challenge from rivals trying to overtake it or critics hunting for a flaw.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Too strong or too well proven for anyone to attack or beat.

examples.text: With a twenty-point lead and three games left, the team's place at the top of the league looked unassailable.
The prosecutor's case seemed unassailable, since the DNA evidence, the video and two witnesses all pointed to the same man.
Her reputation for honesty was so unassailable that even her rivals trusted her figures.
Critics spent years hunting for a flaw in the proof, but it remained unassailable.

distractors.lemma: Producing no useful result despite all the effort put in.
Modest in manner and content to stay out of the spotlight.
Odd and mysterious, leaving everyone at a loss to say what caused it.
Bold and unembarrassed, making no effort to hide what one thinks or does.

senses.definition: Too well defended to be attacked or captured by force.

mnemonics: Unassailable is un- plus assail, to attack: an unassailable lead or argument is one that no attack can break.

senses.definition: Unfair, cruel or excessive to a shocking degree, beyond any decent excuse.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: So wrong or unfair that it is shocking and cannot be defended.

examples.text: Charging a stranded family five hundred dollars for a two-mile tow is unconscionable.
The judge threw out the contract, ruling that its hidden penalty clause was unconscionable.
Patients waited an unconscionable eight hours in the emergency room before a doctor saw them.
It is unconscionable that the company kept selling the heater after learning it could catch fire.

distractors.lemma: Out cold and unresponsive, with the senses temporarily shut down.
Offered in full, with no terms or requirements attached.
Breaking from custom, with methods or habits that few others follow.
Overcome by a grief that resists every attempt at comfort.

senses.definition: Lacking any inner sense of right and wrong.

mnemonics: Unconscionable comes from conscience: an unconscionable act is one that no conscience could allow.

senses.definition: Utter and total, with no saving feature to lessen it; said mostly of bad things.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Complete and total, with nothing good to make it any better.

examples.text: The class trip was an unmitigated disaster: the bus broke down, it rained all day, and the museum turned out to be closed.
The report called the scheme unmitigated nonsense, without a single claim that held up under scrutiny.
The refugees endured weeks of unmitigated hardship, with no shelter, no medicine and no break in the cold.
To the critics, the remake was an unmitigated failure, with nothing in it worth saving, not even the music.

distractors.lemma: Direct and firsthand, passing through no agent or channel on the way.
Lacking the drive or interest to work hard at anything.
Plainly identifiable, since nothing else looks or sounds quite the same.
Heedless of something that one ought to be paying attention to.
Not stirred to any feeling by what one sees or hears.

mnemonics: Unmitigated is un- plus mitigate, to ease or soften: an unmitigated disaster has nothing that makes it easier to bear.

senses.definition: Wrong for the occasion, in a way that offends the manners people expect there.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Not proper or fitting for the place or the moment.

examples.text: Laughing loudly on his phone during the funeral struck the mourners as unseemly.
The two candidates got into an unseemly shouting match on live television, trading insults about each other's families.
Some board members thought it unseemly for the charity's director to accept a luxury car from a donor.
There was an unseemly rush for the buffet before the host had even finished her toast.

distractors.lemma: Inclined to avoid parties and conversation, keeping to oneself.
Out of line with the weather normally expected in that month or season.
Overlooked by the public even though one's contribution was real and important.
Looking toward something without taking any of it in.
Green and untested, having had little time to learn a trade or role.

mnemonics: Unseemly is un- plus seemly, a formal word for fitting or proper: unseemly conduct does not suit the occasion.

senses.definition: Taking part in something without knowing its true nature or purpose.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Not knowing what is really going on, even though you are part of it.

examples.text: The smugglers hid the drugs in a tourist's suitcase, turning her into an unwitting courier.
Thousands of shoppers were unwitting test cases: the app quietly showed them different prices and never said so.
The con artist made his elderly neighbor an unwitting accomplice, having her cash checks she believed were refunds.
By forwarding the fake email to his whole team, he became the unwitting source of the virus.

distractors.lemma: Holding back from an action because one would rather not do it.
Bulky and awkward, so that it is a struggle to carry or manage.
Different from what someone normally does or shows; unaccustomed.
Shabby enough to bring shame on the person who did it.
Quick to turn a clever phrase that leaves listeners amused.

senses.definition: Done by accident instead of on purpose.

mnemonics: Unwitting keeps wit in its old sense of knowing: an unwitting helper does not know what he is helping with.

senses.definition: What a situation finally amounts to once all the twists and arguments are over.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: What happens in the end because of everything that came before.

examples.text: The two sides argued for hours, and the upshot was that the meeting would be held again next week.
Sales fell for three straight years; the upshot was that the store closed in March.
The upshot of all the testing was simple: the bridge needed new cables before it could reopen.
We talked it over with the landlord, and the upshot is that we can stay until June.

distractors.lemma: Great disorder caused when a society or a life is abruptly overturned.
A sharp climb in the amount or intensity of something after a calmer spell.
The regular repairs and bills that come with owning a house, car or other property.
An outbreak of armed or mass resistance to a government or occupying army.
A person's speed at grasping what is meant or explained.

mnemonics: Upshot first meant the final shot of an archery match; now it means how anything finally turns out.

senses.definition: Install oneself in a post or power with no lawful claim, displacing the person entitled to it.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To push out a rightful leader and take their power for yourself.

examples.text: The general used the army to usurp the presidency while the elected leader was abroad.
In the play, Macbeth murders the king in order to usurp the Scottish throne.
Local councils complained that the new state agency had usurped powers the law gave to them.
The prince's uncle usurped the crown and sent the rightful heir into exile.

distractors.lemma: Beat a rival or top one's own earlier best.
Get the better of a problem or hurdle that stands in the way.
Walk with visitors and show them into a room or to their seats.
Interfere with a meeting, service or routine so badly that it stalls.
Treat a hunch as likely on the strength of a few hints.

senses.definition: Push aside and take over the role or place of something else.

mnemonics: Usurp comes from Latin usurpare, to seize for one's own use: a usurper takes a power and uses it as if it were theirs.

senses.definition: Having its surface broken up by marks of a second or third color.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Having blotches or stripes in more than one color.

examples.text: The variegated leaves of the ivy are splashed with cream and pale yellow along their edges.
The cat's variegated coat mixed patches of black, orange and white, so no two photos of her looked alike.
Polished slabs of the marble showed variegated bands of gray, rose and white.
She knitted the scarf from variegated yarn that shifts from blue to green to purple along its length.

distractors.lemma: Bulging and twisting under the skin, said of enlarged leg veins.
Given a protective, see-through coat that leaves a surface shiny.
Lush with new growth, so that fields or hills look green.
Of a hot, orange-tinged red shade.

senses.definition: Full of variety; diverse in makeup or character.

mnemonics: Variegated comes from Latin varius, meaning varied or spotted: a variegated leaf shows varied colors.

senses.definition: Brag about something, crediting it with more glory than it has.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To show off about something and make it sound better than it is.

examples.text: The company vaunted its new phone as the fastest ever made, but reviewers found it slower than last year's model.
He liked to vaunt his connections at every dinner party, dropping the names of senators and film stars whenever there was a pause.
The mayor vaunted the new stadium as a boost for the city, though it has stood empty most of the year.
Instead of vaunting her prize, she quietly put the medal in a drawer and told no one.

distractors.lemma: Jeer at someone with cruel remarks meant to provoke them.
Shake someone's confidence so that a task seems too hard to attempt.
Stay with someone as a painful memory they cannot shake off.
Put one's own name behind someone's good character or a story's truth.

mnemonics: Vaunt goes back to Latin vanus, empty, the source of vain: to vaunt is to boast in a vain, empty way.

senses.definition: Felt in the gut as an instant, instinctive reaction that comes before any reasoning.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Felt strongly in your gut, as a reaction that comes before thinking.

examples.text: Many viewers had a visceral reaction to the footage of the crash, turning away before they could think about it.
Her dislike of the man was visceral; she could not explain it, but her stomach tightened whenever he entered the room.
The drummer's playing had a visceral pull: the crowd was swaying and stamping before anyone had even caught the tune.
For the veterans, the sound of fireworks brought a visceral fear that no argument could calm.

distractors.lemma: Taken in secondhand, as if another person's thrill or pain were one's own.
Having a heavy, syrupy consistency that resists pouring.
Concerned with sight and the images the eye takes in.
Savage and spiteful in nature, and set on causing others harm.
Ahead of its time in imagination, foreseeing changes others cannot yet see.

senses.definition: Relating to the soft organs inside the chest and belly.

mnemonics: Visceral comes from viscera, the body's internal organs: a visceral reaction is one you feel in your gut.

senses.definition: Sharpen or awaken a desire, especially an appetite or a person's curiosity.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make you hungrier for food, news or fun than you were before.

examples.text: The smell of garlic drifting from the kitchen whetted our appetites long before dinner was served.
The trailer reveals just enough of the plot to whet viewers' curiosity without spoiling the ending.
A summer job at the museum whetted her interest in ancient history, and she changed her major that fall.
The free first chapter is meant to whet readers' appetite for the rest of the book.

distractors.lemma: Splash or sprinkle water on something so it is no longer dry.
Win a small favor from someone by being sweet to them on purpose.
Cut a list, a debt or a staff down a little at a time.
Bring a litter of pups or cubs into the world.
Struggle for breath, with a rattle or whistle in the chest on every intake.

senses.definition: Draw a knife or scythe across a stone until it cuts cleanly again.

mnemonics: Whet is the old word for sharpening a blade on a whetstone: when something whets your appetite, it sharpens your hunger.

senses.definition: Pry something from another's grip, whether a thing in their hands or their control of a place or group.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To fight someone for something they are holding onto and come away with it.

examples.text: After a long tug-of-war, the toddler finally wrested the toy truck from his older sister's hands.
Rebel forces fought for months to wrest control of the port from the government.
After a long proxy battle, the investors wrested the company from its founder.
She wrested the steering wheel away from her drunk friend and pulled the car onto the shoulder.

distractors.lemma: Pause from activity and relax until one feels refreshed.
Inflict heavy damage or punishment on people or places.
Encircle or cover something with a ring of flowers, leaves or curling smoke.
Leave a ship, car or plan in ruins by crashing or spoiling it.

senses.definition: Get something, such as an answer or a living, out of a difficult source through great effort.

mnemonics: Wrest is related to wrestle: to wrest something away is to twist and pull it free, as a wrestler would.
